entries.name: about-story
entries.title: About story
entries.description: The story of a company in long form: a large statement, two columns of text beside a tall picture, and a strip of the facts that anchor it.

components.name: AboutStory
components.summary: The story of a company in long form, for an about page that should sound like people wrote it: a large statement sentence, a two-column body of story paragraphs beside a tall picture with its caption, and under it a strip of the facts that anchor it in tabular numbers. Paragraphs keep a comfortable measure, and on a phone the picture follows the first paragraph instead of leading; on a tablet it keeps a width of 28rem instead of filling the column. On wide, tall screens the picture stays in view while a long story scrolls past it; set `--sticky-top` (for example `className="[--sticky-top:4rem]"`) to the height of your sticky header.

props.name: eyebrow
props.doc: A small line above the statement: "Our story".

props.name: statement
props.doc: The opening sentence, set large. One idea, a sentence or two.

props.name: statementAs
props.doc: The statement's element: "h2" (the default) inside a page, "h1" when this opens the page.

props.name: paragraphs
props.doc: The story in paragraphs, three reads best. On a phone the picture follows the first one.

props.name: image
props.doc: A tall picture with its caption. Drawn at 4 to 5.

props.name: facts
props.doc: The facts that anchor it: founded, team, places, customers. Three to five read best.

props.name: signature
props.doc: Who is telling the story.

props.name: action
props.doc: A link on to the next page: "Meet the team".

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the action link. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: renderImage
props.doc: Draws the picture: plug in next/image or any optimiser. Defaults to a plain .

entries.docs: Three paragraphs read best, and on a phone the picture follows the first one. Draw the picture at 4 to 5. Pass renderImage to plug in next/image.

entries.name: accessibility-statement
entries.title: Accessibility statement
entries.description: The accessibility statement a site must publish: conformance in the heading, known gaps with workarounds and dates, how you tested and who to tell.

components.name: AccessibilityStatement
components.summary: The accessibility statement a site is expected to publish, kept honest by a date. A panel opens the page with the verdict written into its heading ("This website partially conforms with WCAG 2.2 level AA"), so the status never depends on a badge or a colour, then the standard, the level, the day it was assessed and how. Under it come what works, the known limitations with a workaround and a planned fix date each, the technologies relied on, how to report a problem and who to turn to when the answer is not enough. It follows the structure of the European model statement.

props.name: subject
props.doc: What the statement covers, as the start of the heading: "This website" or "northwind.example".

props.name: standard
props.doc: The standard assessed against: "WCAG 2.2".

props.name: level
props.doc: The level aimed for: "AA".

props.name: status
props.doc: Where the site stands. It is written out in the heading.

props.name: assessed
props.doc: When it was assessed. A statement without a date cannot be trusted.

props.name: method
props.doc: How it was tested: "Self-assessment with automated checks and manual tests with NVDA and VoiceOver".

props.name: works
props.doc: What works, one statement each.

props.name: limitations
props.doc: What does not, with a workaround and a date. Pass an empty list to say there are none.

props.name: technologies
props.doc: The technologies the site relies on: "HTML", "WAI-ARIA", "CSS", "JavaScript".

props.name: contact
props.doc: How to report a problem.

props.name: enforcement
props.doc: Who to turn to when your answer is not enough.

props.name: title
props.doc: The page's own heading: "Accessibility statement".

props.name: description
props.doc: A line under the title.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the title. The status heading and the section headings sit one level below it, or take this level when there is no title.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the headings and terms, for a site that is not in English.

entries.docs: status is written into the heading as words (fully conforms, partially conforms, does not conform), so it never relies on a badge or a colour. Pass assessed with a dateTime so the date is a time element, and keep it honest: test again after every redesign and update the date. limitations={[]} states that there are none, and leaving it out drops the section. fixBy takes a string or the dated object. Pass labels to translate the headings and the heading sentence.

entries.name: allergen-matrix
entries.title: Allergen matrix
entries.description: Every dish against the fourteen EU allergens in a sticky-header table, with chips that hide dishes containing what you cannot eat.

components.name: AllergenMatrix
components.summary: Every dish against the fourteen allergens, as the real table food businesses in the EU have to publish. Dishes are the row headings, grouped by course; allergens are the columns. A cell says Contains or May contain in words for assistive technology and draws a solid disc or a ring for everyone else, so the two never depend on colour. A row of toggle chips lets a reader pick what they cannot eat and hides every dish that contains it (and, unless they switch that off, every dish that may), announcing how many are left. The first column and the header row stay in place while the table scrolls inside its own region, so a phone keeps the dish name and the allergen in view, and a soft shade along the right and bottom edge shows while there is more behind it. Column heads use short names; the full name is the accessible one. Set `--matrix-max-height` on the component (it is 40rem by default, a…

props.name: dishes
props.doc: The dishes, in the order you want them. They are grouped by course.

props.name: allergens
props.doc: The columns. The fourteen EU allergens by default (EU_ALLERGENS, from the item's allergens file).

props.name: value
props.doc: The ids of the allergens the reader cannot eat, for a controlled matrix.

props.name: defaultValue
props.doc: The same, to start from when the matrix keeps its own state.

props.name: onValueChange
props.doc: Called with the ids of the picked allergens each time a chip is toggled or the chips are cleared.

props.name: defaultHideMayContain
props.doc: Whether a dish that only may contain a picked allergen is hidden too. On by default: when in doubt, leave it out. The reader can switch it off.

props.name: legend
props.doc: Extra words about the marks: what May contain means in your kitchen. Shown under the table.

props.name: updated
props.doc: When the table was last checked against the recipes, as an ISO date: "2026-10-12".

props.name: note
props.doc: A note the reader must not miss: tell your server about an allergy, the kitchen handles every allergen. Set in a panel under the table.

props.name: title
props.doc: The matrix's own heading, when the page has no other: "Allergens".

props.name: description
props.doc: One or two sentences under the title.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the title.

props.name: caption
props.doc: The table's name: the caption screen readers announce on arrival and the name of the scrolling region.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for numbers and the date.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: Time zone for an updated date that carries a time; a date without one is never shifted.

entries.name: article-footnotes
entries.title: Article footnotes
entries.description: Footnote references and a notes list with working back links, so a long article can cite sources without breaking the flow.

components.name: Footnotes
components.summary: Holds the notes of one article so every FootnoteRef knows its number and every FootnoteList knows its notes. Wrap the article in it; it renders no element of its own. Numbers follow the order of the list, and the anchors are built from each note's id, so deep links survive an edit.

props.name: notes
props.doc: The notes in the order they are numbered. A reference takes its number from its place in this list, not from where it sits in the text.

props.name: idPrefix
props.doc: Start of every anchor on the page: "fn" gives #fn-<id> for a note and #fnref-<id> for the spot in the text. Change it when two articles share a page.

props.name: children
props.doc: The article: the text with its references, and wherever the list belongs.

components.name: FootnoteRef
components.summary: A superscript number in the text that links to its note. It is a small pill with a larger touch target than it looks, it keeps its place when you come back from the note, and following it moves focus to the note as well as the page, so a keyboard or screen reader user lands where the eye does.

props.name: note
props.doc: The id of the note this points to.

props.name: mention
props.doc: Which mention of the note this is, when the text refers to it more than once. 1 by default.

props.name: label
props.doc: Start of the link's accessible name; the number follows it: "Footnote 3".

components.name: FootnoteList
components.summary: The notes of an article as an ordered list with the source of each claim: the text in the muted colour at a readable size (never below 14px), the source on its own line in the foreground colour with the day it was read, and a back link that returns to the exact spot in the text. Every note has a stable anchor, so a reader can link to one, and the note that a link or a reference points at is highlighted and takes focus. For essays, reports and explainers that need to show their work.

props.name: notes
props.doc: The notes, when the list is not inside <Footnotes>. Inside it, leave this out: the references and the list must share one list to agree on the numbers.

props.name: title
props.doc: The heading above the list. "Notes" by default.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the heading: 2 by default.

props.name: backLabel
props.doc: Start of each back link's accessible name; the number follows it: "Back to reference 3".

props.name: idPrefix
props.doc: Start of every anchor, when the list is not inside <Footnotes>.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for the day a source was read.

entries.docs: Wrap the article in Footnotes with a list of notes, each with a stable id, its content and optionally a source (label, href and the day you read it). Put FootnoteRef note="id" in the text where a claim needs one and FootnoteList wherever the notes belong, usually at the end. A reference takes its number from the place of its note in the list, so numbers follow the list while the anchors (#fn-id for a note, #fnref-id for the spot in the text) keep working when notes are added or moved. Following a reference puts focus on the note, which is also highlighted when a link targets it; the back link returns focus to the exact sentence. A note that is cited twice sets mentions to 2, and the second FootnoteRef passes mention=2. Notes use the muted colour at 14px or larger, with the source line in the foreground colour. Pass labels, title and backLabel to translate the fixed words, and locale for…

entries.title: Article layout
entries.description: A reading layout with header, byline and cover that styles the plain prose elements you pass in.

components.name: ArticleLayout

props.name: author

props.name: date
props.doc: Formatted for the reader, plus the ISO value for the time element.

props.name: cover

props.name: children

entries.name: article-series-outline
entries.title: Series outline
entries.description: Where you are in a multi-part series: every part in order, with Read, You are here and Soon told in words, as a card or a strip.

components.name: ArticleSeriesOutline
components.summary: Where you are in a multi-part series: every part in order, each with its number, title and reading time, and a word for where it stands: Read, You are here, or Soon with the date it is due. Status is always spelled out, so it never depends on colour or on an icon. Parts that are not out yet are plain text rather than dead links, and the part you are reading carries aria-current. A card suits an article's sidebar or the end of the piece beside the pager; the strip runs across the top of the body and shows the whole series at a glance. Both follow the width of their own column, not the screen. The outline is a navigation landmark named after the series; when a page carries two of them, give each its own `aria-label` so they can be told apart.

props.name: series
props.doc: The series itself: its name, and a link to its landing page when it has one.

props.name: parts
props.doc: Every part, in order. A part is its position in this list.

props.name: current
props.doc: The number of the part this page is, counting from 1. Leave it out on the series' own page, where nothing is current.

props.name: layout
props.doc: A card for a sidebar or the end of an article, or a compact strip across the top of the body.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the series name: 3 by default, for a sidebar under an h2.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the series and part links. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for the dates and the numbers.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: Time zone for a release date that carries a time; a date without one is never shifted.

entries.docs: Pass the series (a title and an optional href) and the parts in order. current is the number of the page you are on, counted from 1; leave it out on the series' own page. A part before it is Read, the current one is You are here and carries aria-current, and a part after it is plain text marked Soon, with its releaseDate when it has one, unless it has an href: then it is a published part and links. Set state on a part to override that, for a site that knows what each reader has read. layout is card (a sidebar, or the end of an article beside the pager) or strip (across the top of the body); both follow the width of their own column. Upcoming parts are never dead links. The outline is a navigation landmark named after the series; give two outlines on one page their own aria-label. Pass linkAs={Link} to route the links and labels to translate the words.

entries.name: blog-index-sidebar
entries.title: Blog index with sidebar
entries.description: A blog front page in two columns: your post list beside a sticky sidebar of search, topics with counts, popular posts and a slot for a sign-up.

components.name: BlogIndexSidebar
components.summary: A blog front page in two columns: your post list on the left, and on the right a sidebar that sticks below the header on wide screens and drops under the posts on a phone. The sidebar holds four optional widgets, each its own labelled region so screen reader users can jump between them: search first (a plain GET form, or your own handler that also hears the field being cleared), topics with post counts and the current one marked, a numbered list of popular posts, and a slot for a newsletter. It sticks below the header; one taller than the window pins by its bottom edge instead, so the last widget stays in view while the page scrolls. Set `--sticky-top` (for example `className="[--sticky-top:4rem]"`) to the height of your sticky header.

props.name: children
props.doc: The main column: a PostFeed, a BlogList or your own list.

props.name: searchAction
props.doc: Where the search form sends its GET request, with the field as `q` (see `searchName`). The search widget shows when this or `onSearch` is given.

props.name: searchName
props.doc: The field's name in the query string.

props.name: onSearch
props.doc: Handle the search yourself instead of navigating. Receives the trimmed query on submit, and an empty string when the field is cleared (the clear button, Escape or deleting the text), so a filtered list can return to everything. Works inside a Client Component.

props.name: searchLabel
props.doc: The search form's accessible name, which also labels the field.

props.name: searchPlaceholder
props.doc: The field's placeholder.

props.name: topics
props.doc: Topics as links with their post counts.

props.name: topicsTitle
props.doc: The heading of the topic list.

props.name: currentTopic
props.doc: The `slug` of the topic being shown; its row is marked with aria-current.

props.name: popular
props.doc: Posts to point at, as a numbered list.

props.name: popularTitle
props.doc: The heading of the popular list.

props.name: aside
props.doc: A slot at the end of the sidebar: a newsletter sign-up, an about card.

props.name: asideLabel
props.doc: Gives the aside slot a landmark name, so it joins the other regions.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the widget headings: 2 (the default) under a page title, 3 under a section heading.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the topic and popular-post links. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: sidebarLabel
props.doc: The sidebar's landmark name.

props.name: countLabel
props.doc: Read after each topic's count: "12 posts".

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for the post counts.

entries.docs: Pass a PostFeed, a BlogList or your own list as children. Give searchAction for a plain GET form, or onSearch inside a Client Component; it also gets an empty string when the field is cleared, so reset your list there. The sidebar sticks under your header, and one taller than the window pins by its bottom edge so the last widget stays in view. Set --sticky-top to your header's height, for example className="[--sticky-top:4rem]".

entries.name: class-timetable
entries.title: Class timetable
entries.description: A weekly timetable for a gym, school or studio: the week at a glance on wide screens, a day at a time on a phone, with spots left and full classes in words.

components.name: ClassTimetable
components.summary: A weekly timetable for a gym, school or studio. When it is wide enough (64rem, about 9rem a day) it is the week at a glance: one column per day, Monday first, with the classes as cards in time order, each with its time, name, trainer and level and a note on the places left. Narrower, and on a phone, it is one day at a time under day tabs, opening on today. A class with no places left is not hidden: it stays in the list, flagged "Full" in words and with a dashed edge, and offers the waitlist when you give a link. Every day is a list rather than a table, so it reads in order on every screen, and today is marked with a word, never only a tint.

props.name: days
props.doc: The days of the week, Monday first. Seven read best; the week view takes any number up to seven.

props.name: today
props.doc: The id of today's day. It opens first on a phone and is marked in words in both views. Leave it out for no marker: the page then renders the same everywhere.

props.name: legend
props.doc: A line under the timetable: how often the places are updated, how to cancel.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the day headings: 3 by default.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the class and waitlist links. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for the times. en-US writes "6:30 PM", en-GB and most others "18:30".

entries.usage:
import { ClassTimetable } from "@rhs-ui/marketing/class-timetable"; export default function Demo(): React.JSX.Element { return (

A studio week on Tuesday: today is marked, three classes are full and two of them offer a waitlist

Five days, no day marked, times on the 24-hour clock (en-GB)
entries.docs: Pass days with Monday first, each with its classes (start and end on the 24-hour clock; 9:30 and 09:30 both work, and the classes are listed by the clock). The week is a grid once the timetable itself is 64rem wide, about 9rem a day; narrower, and in a narrow column on a wide screen, day tabs open on today. today is the id of the current day: work it out for your visitor's time zone, or leave it out and nothing is marked. spots: 0 flags a class as Full in words and with a dashed edge, and waitlistHref adds the waitlist link only then, named after its class for screen readers (labels.waitlistFor words that). locale decides how times are written: en-US 6:30 PM, en-GB 18:30. A range that does not fit its card wraps after the dash. legend is a line under the timetable. Pass linkAs={Link} to route the class links.

entries.name: code-of-conduct
entries.title: Code of conduct
entries.description: A community code of conduct people will read: the promise, expected and unacceptable behaviour in pairs, how to report, and what happens next.

components.name: CodeOfConduct
components.summary: A code of conduct people will actually read: a short promise, then what is expected and what is not accepted side by side, each behaviour with a one-line example, how to report with the contact, the response time and the confidentiality promise, and a ladder of consequences as an ordered list. The two lists use words and icons together, never colour alone, and the reporting contact is the first link after the promise, so it is easy to find on a bad day. Every section and every behaviour has an anchor, so a moderator can link to a clause. The layout follows the width of its column, not the screen, so the contact never breaks across lines in a narrow column. For open-source projects, communities, events and clubs.

props.doc: The page's own heading, when the page has no other: "Code of conduct".

props.name: promise

props.name: unacceptable

props.name: consequences
props.doc: The ladder of consequences, mildest first.

props.name: scope

props.name: updated

props.name: labels

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for the date.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: Time zone for an updated date that carries a time; a date without one is never shifted.

entries.docs: Give each behaviour a title and a one-line example. report.contact is the first link after the promise, so it is easy to find in a bad moment: an https link opens in a new tab and shows an arrow, a mailto or tel link stays plain. Every section and every behaviour has an anchor (#conduct-reporting); set idPrefix when a page holds two codes. scope says where the code applies, and labels translates the headings. The layout follows the width of its column, not the screen: the two lists sit side by side from 672px and the three reporting facts from 896px, so the contact never breaks across lines.

entries.name: directions-by-mode
entries.title: Getting here
entries.description: How to arrive by train, bus, car, bike and on foot, with routes that start at the station, a facts line for each and a step-free access panel.

components.name: DirectionsByMode

entries.name: docs-page-layout
entries.title: Docs page layout
entries.description: A three-column documentation page: your sidebar, the article with breadcrumbs and meta, and an on-this-page rail that tracks your place.

components.name: DocsPageLayout

entries.name: document-library
entries.title: Document library
entries.description: Downloadable documents grouped by category: format, size, pages, language and date on every row, real download links and optional search.

components.name: DocumentLibrary
components.summary: A page of downloads for sites that live on their PDFs: investor relations, municipalities, schools, associations. Documents are grouped by category, and each row says what it is before it asks for a click: a tile with the file type, the title, a line about it, and the size, page count, language and date. Each Download is a real link with the download attribute, and its accessible name carries the title, the type and the size ("Download Annual report 2025, PDF, 2 MB"), so a list of twelve of them is not twelve identical words. An optional search narrows the list as you type and announces how many documents are left. Rows stack on a phone with the button across the full width. The links are plain anchors on purpose: a download is not a route.

entries.docs: Every Download is a plain anchor with the download attribute, and its name reads Download, then the title, the type and the size. Pass filename when the saved name should differ from the file on the server. searchable adds a field that filters by title, description, type and language and announces how many documents are left. Dates follow locale, and a date without a time is never shifted. Downloads are not routes, so there is no linkAs. The block is a client component because of the search: use it from a Server Component with plain data. labels are plain strings too, with {query}, {shown}, {total} and {noun} as placeholders, so they can cross from a Server Component.

entries.name: faq-sidebar-categories

Each question is a heading with a permalink button that updates the hash and confirms in words, and the ids are stable, so links from support replies keep working and the targeted answer is highlighted on arrival. The current category follows the scroll and carries aria-current; below lg the list becomes a scrolling row under the title. Unlike FaqTabs, every answer stays in the DOM, which is what search engines and support teams link to. Set `--sticky-top` (for example `className="[--sticky-top:4rem]"`) to the height of your sticky header.

entries.name: founder-letter

components.name: FounderLetter

An optional postscript is a paragraph of its own and is never hidden behind a click. There is nothing decorative and no handwriting font, because the words are what earn the trust. For about pages, launch announcements, price-change explanations and apologies, where a company has something to say and a person to say it.

props.name: date
props.doc: The day the letter is dated. Shown with the place, above everything else.

props.name: title

props.name: salutation

props.name: children

props.name: signoff
props.doc: The words before the signature: "Thank you for staying with us,".

props.name: signer
props.doc: Who signs, with a role and a small portrait.

props.name: postscript

props.name: labels

entries.docs: Pass the date (a label and an ISO dateTime), the place, a salutation and the paragraphs as children: plain p, ul, ol, blockquote, strong and a elements are styled, so Markdown output works as it is. signoff is the line before the signature and signer is a name, a role and a portrait URL; initials stand in until the portrait loads or when it fails. postscript is inline content that gets a paragraph of its own and is never collapsed; links and strong in it are styled like the body. title adds a subject line (an h2 unless you set headingLevel). The column is 38rem wide at a generous line height, and nothing about it is decorative. Pass labels to change the words that open the postscript.

entries.name: help-article-list
entries.title: Help article list
entries.description: A help centre collection: its title and article count, then articles grouped by section with a one-line summary each.

components.name: HelpArticleList
components.summary: A help centre collection: its title, how many articles it holds and when it last changed, then the articles grouped by section, each a whole row with a title, a one-line summary and a chevron that moves on hover. With more than three sections a jump row of anchors appears above the list. Rows carry no dates on purpose, because help is judged on being right today, and each is at least 56px tall so it is easy to hit with a thumb. The aside at the end is yours: tell people how to reach a person. It sits beside its heading once its column is 768px wide, whatever the screen, and your own content can use container variants such as `@3xl:` for the same reason.

props.name: count

props.name: sections

With more than three sections a jump row of anchors appears; give two lists on one page their own idPrefix. contact is your own node for the Can't find it? aside, so say how to reach a person there. Rows carry no dates on purpose. Pass labels to translate the counts and the date, and linkAs={Link} for your router. The aside sits beside its heading once its column is 768px wide, whatever the screen, and your contact node can use container variants such as @3xl: for the same reason.

components.name: HowToGuide

A closing block says what the reader now has and links to the next guide. The steps are an ordered list with anchors, so a reader can link straight to step 4 (#step-4). For help articles, setup guides and repair manuals; unlike ProcessSection it is meant for pages that run long.

props.name: labels

entries.name: incident-postmortem
entries.title: Incident postmortem
entries.description: A blameless post-incident report: severity in words, impact in tabular figures, a UTC timeline, the root cause in plain words and actions with owners.

components.name: IncidentPostmortem
components.summary: A post-incident report that a customer can read in order: what happened in one box (severity in words, when it started and ended in UTC, how long it lasted, what was affected), then the summary, the impact as tabular figures, a timestamped timeline, the root cause in plain words, what went well and what did not, and the actions with an owner, a date and a status in words. Blameless by design: owners are teams unless you pass a name. Every section has an anchor and a link beside its heading, so a customer can be sent straight to the timeline, and a contents list that follows the reader sits beside the page on a wide screen and as a row of links above it on a phone. All times are written in one zone, UTC unless you say otherwise.

props.name: incident
props.doc: The incident itself: its title, severity, when it started and ended, what it affected and a summary.

props.name: impact
props.doc: The numbers: customers affected, requests failed.

props.name: timeline
props.doc: What happened and when, in any order. It is sorted by time.

props.name: rootCause
props.doc: Why it happened, in plain words.

props.name: lessons
props.doc: What worked and what did not. Leave it out to skip the section.

props.name: actions
props.doc: What will change, with an owner and a date. Blameless by design: owners are teams unless you pass names. Leave it out to skip the section.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the ticket links. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the title: 1 by default, because this is the page. Sections go one level below it.

props.name: idPrefix
props.doc: Put this in front of every anchor when a page holds more than one postmortem: "inc-2417" gives #inc-2417-timeline.

props.name: note
props.doc: The note at the end. A sentence on how the review was written by default; pass null to leave it out.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for dates and numbers.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone every time is shown in. UTC by default, so a customer in another zone reads the same clock as your team.

entries.docs: Pass the incident (id, title, severity as critical, major or minor with an optional code such as SEV 2, start and end as ISO times, what was affected, and a summary that can be several paragraphs), the impact (figures with a label, a number or text, and a note, plus a body), the timeline (events with a time, text and an optional milestone word such as Detected, Mitigated or Resolved), the rootCause (a one-sentence summary, an explanation and contributing factors), the lessons (wentWell and wentPoorly) and the actions (title, owner, due date and status as done, in-progress or planned, with an optional ticket and link). Blameless by design: owners are teams, and a person is shown only when you pass person. Every section has an anchor and a link beside its heading, so #timeline sends a customer straight to the timeline; idPrefix keeps the anchors apart when a page holds more than one repor…

Dates are calendar days, so a range crossing the new year or a time zone never shifts one. The layout follows the width of its column, not the screen, so it holds in a prose column as well as across a page. For schools, clubs, studios and offices that publish the year in advance.

entries.docs: Dates are calendar days, sorted by their first day; a range is written once with both ends in time elements. Pass today as an ISO date for stable rendering, otherwise the current day in timeZone is used. groupBy is month, term (each date names its term) or none, and calendar is a slot for an Add to calendar link on each row. A day-first locale such as en-GB writes 24 Dec, a month-first one Dec 24. labels translates the markers. The layout follows the width of its column, not the screen: dates, labels and types sit in three columns from 672px, the month or term moves beside its rows from 896px, and below that each date stacks.

That is the difference from Callout, which is not a landmark. Pass labels to translate the reading time, the audience words and the jump label.

entries.name: leadership-bios

entries.name: open-source-credits

components.name: OpenSourceCredits
components.summary: The libraries your product ships, with their version and licence, as the attribution page that MIT, Apache, BSD and other licences ask for. Packages are grouped by licence family with a count for each, and sorted by name within a licence. A licence's name opens its full text in a dialog, so the requirement is met without leaving the page, and a button copies that one text for a notice file; a browser that will not copy gets the text selected instead. A dual licence such as "MIT OR Apache-2.0" opens either text. The search field narrows the list by package name and says how many are left. Package names link to their repositories and are read out as opening a new tab. Licence texts are yours to supply, because the one that applies carries each project's own copyright line.

entries.name: pay-bands-table
entries.title: Pay bands table
entries.description: Published salary bands by role family and level, with a zone switch, a bar for each range and a plain note on how pay is set.

components.name: PayBandsTable
components.summary: Published pay, as the table it is: role families as row groups, levels as rows, and for each the annual minimum and maximum in tabular numbers, with a bar that draws the band on one shared scale so overlaps between levels can be seen. A zone switch changes the figures without leaving the table and says where the zone applies. Under it sit the rest of the package (bonus, equity, review cycle) and a plain paragraph on how the bands are set. Built for pay transparency: the range sits next to every role. On a phone each bar moves under its level so the table fits; a table that is still too wide (long names, big figures) scrolls sideways inside its own container, with the level column held in place.

props.name: families
props.doc: The role families, each with its levels. Every level carries a band per zone.

props.name: zones
props.doc: The pay zones. Two or three work best; with one the switch is left out.

props.name: currency
props.doc: The ISO 4217 code the bands are in: "EUR".

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for the amounts and the date.

props.name: notes
props.doc: Short facts about the rest of the package: the bonus, the equity, how often pay is reviewed.

props.name: methodology
props.doc: A plain paragraph on how the bands are set.

props.name: updated
props.doc: When the bands last changed, as an ISO date: "2026-10-01".

props.name: zone
props.doc: The chosen zone, when you control it.

props.name: defaultZone
props.doc: The zone chosen first. The first zone by default.

props.name: onZoneChange
props.doc: Called when the reader picks another zone.

props.name: title
props.doc: The page's own heading, when the page has no other: "Pay bands".

props.name: description
props.doc: One or two sentences under the title.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the title. The methodology heading sits one level below it, or takes this level when there is no title.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the headings and terms, for a site that is not in English.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: Time zone for an updated date that carries a time; a date without one is never shifted.

entries.docs: bands are keyed by zone id; a level without a band in the chosen zone says so in words. The bars share one scale across every zone, so they move when the zone changes, and the two ends of the scale are written in the Range heading. Pass zone and onZoneChange to control the switch, or defaultZone to start on another zone; with a single zone the switch is left out. Amounts are written from currency and locale without decimals. List the levels from the first rung up. On a phone each bar sits under its level so the table fits; one that is still too wide scrolls inside its own container with the level column held in place. notes takes the facts about the rest of the package (bonus, equity, review cycle) and methodology a plain paragraph on how bands are set.

entries.name: portfolio-grid
entries.title: Portfolio grid
entries.description: Selected work for a studio or a freelancer: filter chips by discipline, a grid of covers with title, client and year, and wide projects across two columns.

components.name: PortfolioGrid
components.summary: Selected work for a studio or a freelancer: filter chips by discipline, a grid of covers with title, client and year, and wide projects across two columns. Every card is one link; the filter is a group of toggle buttons with the count announced.

entries.name: post-feed
entries.title: Post feed
entries.description: Posts as a reading feed: author, date and read time, then title, standfirst and topic chips, with a square thumbnail on the right.

components.name: PostFeed
components.summary: Posts as a reading feed, the way a publication streams them: who wrote it, when and how long it takes, then the title, a two-line standfirst, topic chips and a square thumbnail on the right (under the byline on a phone). Where BlogList is date-led and text only, this one is author-led with pictures, and a row without a picture keeps the same measure. The title link is stretched over the row, so the whole post is one target while its accessible name stays the title; its focus ring reaches 12px past the row on each side, so do not clip the feed with overflow-hidden. Rules, not cards, separate the rows; a `loadMore` slot closes the list.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of every post title: 2 (the default) under a page title, 3 under a section heading.

props.name: loadMore

props.name: empty
props.doc: Shown in place of the list when there are no posts, for example a no-results message.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the title and topic links. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: renderImage
props.doc: Draws a thumbnail: plug in next/image or any optimiser. Defaults to a plain .

props.name: label
props.doc: The list's accessible name.

entries.docs: Dates arrive formatted, with the ISO value in dateTime. Rows without an image keep the same measure. Pass a LoadMore, a pager or a link as loadMore, and renderImage to plug in next/image.

entries.name: press-release-list
entries.title: Press release list
entries.description: Your own announcements by year: headline, date and optional PDF per row, with the company boilerplate and the media contact in sticky cards beside them.

components.name: PressReleaseList
components.summary: Your own announcements, set out the way journalists use them. Releases are grouped by year, newest first, each row a dated headline that goes to the release page with its tag, and a PDF link that says the file type and the size. Beside the list on wide screens, two cards stay in view while the list scrolls, as long as the screen is tall enough to show them whole: the company boilerplate with a copy button that confirms in words, and the media contact with the email, the phone and how fast they answer. Where PressQuotes shows what others said about you, this is what you said. Below 1024px the cards follow the list.

props.name: releases
props.doc: Your announcements, in any order. They are grouped by the year of `dateTime`, newest first.

props.name: title
props.doc: The page's own heading, when the page has no other: "Press releases".

props.name: description
props.doc: One or two sentences under the title.

props.name: boilerplateTitle
props.doc: The boilerplate card's heading.

props.name: contactTitle

props.name: labels

props.doc: Locale for numbers and for dates that you did not write out yourself.

entries.docs: Pass releases with an ISO dateTime: the year groups and the order (newest first) come from it, and a dateTime with a time is filed under the year it falls in timeZone, the same day the row shows. date is the short form shown in the row; leave it out and dateTime is written with locale. A release without pdfHref has no download link, and the PDF link is named by what it fetches: Download, the headline, PDF and the size. The boilerplate and contact cards are optional and sit beside the list from 1024px, held in view below --sticky-top (6rem by default; set it to the height of your sticky header) on screens at least 46rem tall, so a short laptop screen never cuts them off; without them the list takes the full width. Only the copy button is a client component, so the block works in a Server Component. Pass labels to translate the fixed words and linkAs={Link} to route the release links.

The rights row takes its columns from how many rights there are and from the width of its column, so no row ends on a tile of its own.

entries.name: recipe-layout
entries.title: Recipe layout
entries.description: A recipe page that cooks well: times and servings up front, ingredients that rescale, large-numeral steps with timers and a nutrition panel.

components.name: RecipeLayout
components.summary: A recipe page that cooks well: the times and the servings up front, the ingredients beside the method on a wide screen (they stay in view while the steps scroll past) and one after the other on a phone. A servings stepper rescales every quantity, written the way a cook writes it (1½ tbsp, 750 g, 1.2 kg) and announces the new count. Steps are an ordered list with large numerals; a step may have a picture and a timer that counts down in place, and where the browser can do it a switch keeps the screen on. The Recipe data for search engines is made from the very same props, so the page and its markup cannot disagree.

props.name: title
props.doc: The recipe's name: "Slow-roasted tomato spaghetti".

props.name: intro

entries.docs: Pass title, intro, times (prep, cook and total in minutes; the total is worked out when left out), servings (the number the quantities are written for), ingredients (quantity, unit, name, note, with unitPlural and plural for words that change, and group for a heading such as For the sauce), steps (text, an optional image and an optional timer in minutes), nutrition per serving, tips and onServingsChange. The stepper rescales every quantity the way a cook writes it: halves, thirds and quarters as fractions (1½ tbsp), grams and millilitres to the nearest 5 once they are big and as kilograms and litres past a thousand, 3 tsp as 1 tbsp, and a line without a quantity never scales. Set whole on an ingredient such as eggs to keep it a whole number. The new count is announced, and an amount that changes lights up for a moment. entries.name: roadmap-columns
entries.title: Roadmap columns

components.name: RoadmapColumns
components.summary: A public roadmap in horizons, not dates: Now, Next and Later (and, if you like, Shipped) as columns of cards, each with a title, one line on why it matters, an area tag and a status in words. A horizon is a promise you can keep, where a date is one you cannot, and a "Plans change" footnote is built in for that reason. A card with a link is one stretched link and the rest stay plain, so nothing is clickable that goes nowhere. Columns are labelled lists with their counts in the heading; on a phone they stack, each under its own heading, and from 768px they sit side by side as lanes.

props.name: title
props.doc: A heading for the roadmap: "What we are building".

props.name: description
props.doc: One or two sentences under the title.

props.name: columns
props.doc: The columns, left to right. Three or four read best; five or more wrap.

props.name: shippedHref
props.doc: Where the full record of shipped work lives, usually the changelog. Shows as a link under the board.

props.name: note
props.doc: The footnote. It defaults to a plain "Plans change" line; pass null to leave it out.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the title. Column headings sit one level below it, or take this level when there is no title.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the card links. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.docs: Pass three or four columns. A column with the id now, next, later or shipped also gets that phase's mark in its heading; any other id can pass phase. A card with an href is one stretched link and a card without one stays plain. Write statuses in words (In progress, Designing, Exploring) and keep dates out: that is the point. Each column is a labelled list with its count in the heading, and the cards of every lane start on one line from 768px. shippedHref adds a link to your changelog under the board, and note replaces the built-in Plans change footnote (pass null to leave it out). Pass linkAs={Link} to route the card links.

entries.name: search-results-list
entries.title: Search results list
entries.description: The body of a site search page: result count, type filters with counts as links, results with path and marked snippet, and pagination.

components.name: SearchResultsList

It keeps no state, so every filter and every page has a URL and the page works as plain HTML; the snippet is highlighted by splitting the text on the query, never by injecting HTML. With nothing found it hands over to EmptySearch. The count sits in a polite live region, so a client-side update is announced once. On a phone the pager shrinks to Previous, "Page 2 of 12" and Next, so it never wraps however many pages there are.

entries.name: sitemap-page

It gives people a second way to find a page, which WCAG asks for, and works as an index for anyone lost on a large site.

props.name: sections

props.name: label

entries.title: Support and SLA table

entries.name: topic-hub
entries.title: Topic hub header
entries.description: The top of a topic page: description, a fact strip, a numbered Start here reading path and related topics as chips.

components.name: TopicHub
components.summary: The top of a topic page: the topic's name, what it covers and a few facts on the left, and on the right a Start here panel with a numbered path through the best pieces, each with its reading time and a line about it. Under them, related topics as chips that link to their own hubs. It turns a tag archive into somewhere a new reader can begin. The path is an ordered list, so the sequence is announced, and each row is one stretched link rather than a title and a "read more". Unlike SubpageHeader it has a point of view about where to start.

props.name: eyebrow

props.name: description

props.name: facts

props.name: startHere

props.name: related

entries.name: troubleshooting-guide
entries.title: Troubleshooting guide
entries.description: Problems listed by what the user sees, each opening to the likely cause and numbered fix steps with code or a screenshot, grouped by area.

components.name: TroubleshootingGuide
components.summary: Problems listed by what the user sees, in the order people actually debug: the symptom in their words, the likely cause, then numbered fix steps with optional code to copy or a screenshot, and a Still stuck? line that links to support with the symptom pre-filled. Problems are grouped by area (Sign-in, Billing, Sync), open in an accordion one at a time, and have stable ids, so support can link straight to one: a link that targets a problem opens it on arrival, and opening one writes its id to the address bar for copying. It differs from an FAQ by that fixed order of symptom, cause and fix. Areas are h2 and problems h3, so the guide sits directly under your page's h1.

props.name: areas
props.doc: Problems grouped by area, in the order they should be read.

props.name: supportHref
props.doc: Your support page. Each "Still stuck?" link adds the symptom to its query string, so the form arrives pre-filled.

props.name: symptomParam
props.doc: The query parameter that carries the symptom.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.doc: The id of a problem that starts open, for a deep link you resolve on the server. A link that targets a problem opens it either way.

props.name: syncHash
props.doc: Write the open problem's id to the address bar, so support can copy the URL of what they see. On by default.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the support links. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: renderImage
props.doc: Draws a screenshot: plug in next/image or any optimiser. Defaults to a plain .

props.name: labels
props.doc: Replaces any of the fixed words, for another language.

The Still stuck? link adds the symptom to supportHref as ?symptom=. Areas are h2 and problems h3, so place it under your page h1.

entries.title: Values rows

components.name: ValuesRows

The pairs are what separate real values from posters, so the component asks for them instead of accepting a bare list. Each column has its own icon and its own words, so neither depends on colour. Rows stack on a phone with the name first. Three to six values work best.

props.name: eyebrow
props.doc: A small line above the title: "How we work".

props.name: title
props.doc: The section's title: "Four things we hold ourselves to".

props.name: description
props.doc: One or two sentences under the title.

props.name: values
props.doc: The values, in the order they appear. Three to six work best: more than that is a list nobody remembers.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the title: 2 by default. The value names sit one level below it.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the row links. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: labels

entries.docs: Pass an eyebrow, a title and three to six values. Each value needs a name, a one-sentence meaning, and one behaviour for does and one for doesNot, each checkable in a day at work; the component asks for the pair so a bare list is not possible. A value with an href gets a link under its pair, set with labels.more and routed with linkAs. Rows are an ordered list with an index, and stack on a phone with the name first. The two columns carry their own icon and words, so neither relies on colour. headingLevel is the section title's level; the value names sit one below it.

entries.name: version-support-table
entries.title: Version support table
entries.description: Which versions you still support: release date, end of active support, end of life and a status in words, with the next change flagged.

components.name: VersionSupportTable
components.summary: Which versions of a runtime, SDK or API you still support, and until when: one row per version with its release date, the end of active support, the end of security fixes and a status in words. A date that has passed says Ended, and the one date that will change a status next is flagged where it sits, so a reader sees at once what is about to stop. Every status is a word and every date sits in a time element; nothing depends on colour. Dates are written year first by default, which aligns in a column and cannot be misread as day or month. Below 768px each row becomes a card that keeps every label. Pass a fixed `today` and the table renders the same on every machine, which is what a test wants.

props.name: versions
props.doc: One row per version, in the order you want them. Newest first is the usual order.

props.name: today
props.doc: Today as an ISO date. It decides which dates are marked Ended and which date is next. Pass a fixed one for stable rendering; without it the current day in `timeZone` is used.

props.name: caption
props.doc: The table's name, shown above it and read out by screen readers: "Supported versions of the Halcyon SDK".

props.name: note
props.doc: A short note under the table: what active support and security fixes mean, and how long you support a version.

props.name: dateFormat
props.doc: How a date is written. `iso` (the default) writes 2026-10-31, which sorts, aligns and means the same in every locale; `medium` writes it the way `locale` does.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of each version's heading in the stacked layout on a phone: 3 by default.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the release-notes links. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the headings, the statuses and the markers, for a site that is not in English.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for `medium` dates.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: Only decides which day "today" is when you do not pass one. The dates themselves are calendar days and are never shifted.

entries.docs: Pass versions with a name, an ISO released date, activeUntil and securityUntil, and optionally a status (current, supported, security-only or end-of-life) and a notesHref. Without a status it is worked out from the dates; Current is always your call. A date that has passed says Ended, and the one date across the table that will change a status next is flagged where it sits, so colour is never the only signal. Dates are written year first by default (dateFormat iso) and sit in time elements; dateFormat medium writes them with locale. Pass a fixed today for stable rendering and tests; without it the current day in timeZone is used. Below 768px each version becomes a card that keeps every label. note sits under the table for what active support and security fixes mean. Pass linkAs={Link} to route the release-notes links.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: Time zone for a date that carries a time; a date without one is never shifted.

components.name: CallUsSection

entries.description: The next intake of a course or programme: start date, length, price, seats left and an enrol button, with the application deadline.

components.name: CohortSignup
components.summary: The next intake of a course, bootcamp, workshop or accelerator, as a card that answers the questions before they are asked: when it starts, how long it runs, when the live sessions are and how many seats are left, with a meter, the application deadline as a time element, the price as the biggest number and one button. Every date is written in the time zone you pass, and the deadline names it. When the seats run out the card says Full in words, the button becomes Join the waiting list and the meter stays full. Once the deadline has passed on the reader's clock (or on the moment you pass as now) the button closes; the server never claims that, so a page built ahead of time cannot go stale. On a wide section the facts sit beside the enrolment panel; on a narrow one they stack. The only client JavaScript is that clock; a function passed to it must come from a client component.

entries.description: Ask for a postcode and answer yes, not yet or check the address, with a notify-me field for the places you do not serve.

components.name: CoverageCheck
components.summary: "Do you reach me?" answered in one step: a field for a postcode or an address and one button, and then the answer in place of the form, one of three. Covered says what it means (delivery days, an install date) with facts as label and value; not yet offers an email field to be told when you arrive; unknown asks the visitor to check the address. Every answer has a heading and its own icon, so none leans on colour. The answer is a status message that takes focus, so a screen reader reads it, and Check another address brings focus back to the field with the old text selected. The text is checked against a pattern you can change before anything is sent. For delivery areas, fibre or service coverage, local installers and franchises.

components.name: CreditPacks

Each pack shows its credits as the biggest thing on the card, then the price, the price of one credit and the saving against the smallest pack. The saving and the best value badge are worked out from the packs you pass, never typed in, so they cannot drift when a price changes. The packs are a radio group (arrow keys move, one tab stop) with a button under it that hands the chosen pack to onSelect, and the rule buyers ask about first, such as credits never expiring, sits beside that button. Under 672px every pack is a compact row with the price on the right; from there the packs become cards that share their rows, so the credits, prices and savings line up from one card to the next.

entries.name: email-course-signup
entries.title: Email course signup
entries.description: A five-day email course: the lesson outline day by day beside a signup field, so the promise is concrete before the email is given.

components.name: EmailCourseSignup

entries.name: join-count-cta

components.name: JoinCountCta
components.summary: A closing ask anchored by a big number: how many people already did it. A short lead-in, the count set very large with what it counts, a stack of faces, one sentence on what they get, the button and a small note. The count is formatted for the locale and, when the band scrolls into view from below, rises once to its value; where it is already on screen when the page loads, or the reader prefers less motion, it simply stands there. The faces are decoration and hidden from assistive technology, and the heading carries the whole figure as text, so the number is the same for everyone. Use a count you can verify, and pass asOf so the figure is dated underneath it.

entries.docs: Pass count, unit, action and, for the full effect, avatars, description, note and asOf. The heading carries the whole figure as text (Join 48,213 teams) in the locale's number format, so the count is the same for everyone and for search. The number is set very large, with a size that follows the width of the band. When the band scrolls into view from below, the number rises once to its value; where it is already on screen when the page loads, or the reader prefers reduced motion, it stands still, so the figure is never wrong and nothing flashes. The faces are decoration and hidden from assistive technology; a face without a picture shows initials. Use only a count you can verify, and pass asOf (an ISO day or a date) so the figure is dated underneath it, written for locale in a time element. labels translates the dating line; lead is the word before the number.

entries.name: limited-offer-panel

components.name: LimitedOfferPanel

The count is yours and the state follows it: while places are left the button takes the buyer in, and when claimed reaches the total the meter reads All claimed and the panel closes: the price is struck and marked as no longer available, and the button turns into the waiting list, so the panel can never sell what is gone. An optional end date is written in a time element in an explicit time zone; once it has passed the panel closes the same way. For lifetime deals, early-bird pricing, pre-orders and crowdfunding with finite stock.

props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.name: paywall-gate
entries.title: Paywall gate
entries.description: The subscribe-to-keep-reading moment: a fade over the last lines of an article, the offer, the price and a sign-in link for members.

components.name: PaywallGate
components.summary: The subscribe-to-keep-reading moment, placed under the visible paragraphs of an article. The last lines fade into the page with a mask (a functional fade that hides where the preview ends, not decoration) and a card rises over the fade with the offer: a headline, three benefits, the price with its period, the primary button and a sign-in link for members. The fade carries no information: the teaser is ordinary text a screen reader reads in full, and the card has a heading of its own. For publishers and membership sites that meter their content. Mark the article up for search engines too, or the wall can read as cloaking: describe it with JSON-LD that sets isAccessibleForFree to false and a hasPart whose cssSelector matches the gated part of the page (pass a className such as paywall to this block), and send crawlers the same teaser readers see. It needs no client JavaScript.

It is the honest version of urgency: a real code, a real date and the small print. No timer runs in the page. Once the end has passed the band says This offer has ended and the code is no longer in the page. entries.name: rate-card
entries.title: Rate card
entries.description: Metered pricing as a plain table: each resource with what is included free, then the price per unit, so developers can estimate without a calculator.

components.name: RateCard
components.summary: Metered pricing as a plain table, for products billed by usage. Each resource is a row with what is included free in a billing period, then the price per unit and a note, grouped by product under their own headers, so a developer can read off what a month will cost without a calculator. Prices are tabular figures and units are spelled out ("per 1,000 requests"). The caption says how the product is billed and the day the prices were checked, and both are required: a rate card that does not say how old it is goes stale without anyone noticing. You pass the numbers, so the card never drifts from them. It is a reference, not an estimator. On a phone each row becomes a stacked block that keeps its labels, so there is no sideways scrolling; the table keeps its roles in both layouts, so a screen reader still meets a table.

components.name: RsvpForm
components.summary: The reply to an invitation, for weddings, parties, open days and company events: the event, its day, its place and the day the hosts need an answer by, then the form. The reader gives a name, chooses yes or no on two large cards and, when the answer is yes, says how many guests they bring (a number with a limit) and ticks any dietary needs. Choosing no takes the guest and dietary questions away, so nobody answers what does not apply. A message to the hosts is optional. Mistakes are said in words beside their field once the reader has been there or tried to send, and the first one takes focus. The confirmation repeats the answer in words, lists what was noted, offers Add to calendar to people who are coming, and has a Change my answer that reopens the form with everything as it was.

entries.name: savings-receipt
entries.title: Savings receipt
entries.description: What you would pay for the tools this replaces, added up like a receipt against your single price and the saving it makes.

components.name: SavingsReceipt
components.summary: What you would pay for the tools this replaces, added up like a receipt against your single price. A real table: a row per replaced tool with a dotted leader to its price in tabular figures and a total row with the sum struck through; then your own price in large type and one computed line, such as You save $1,584 a year (52 percent). The arithmetic is done from the numbers you pass, in whole cents, so it cannot disagree with the rows; the percent is rounded down, so the claim is never larger than the sum; and when your price is not lower, the receipt says there is no saving instead of claiming one. The date the prices were checked is required, because price comparisons age fast, and it is printed under the button next to a line on how the comparison was made.

props.doc: How the comparison was made, in a sentence: "List prices of each tool's cheapest plan for ten people."

props.doc: The language the prices and the date are written in. "en-US" by default.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone a full date and time is read in. A plain ISO day is read as that calendar day. "UTC" by default.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the heading: 2 by default.

props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.name: sticky-cta-bar
entries.title: Sticky CTA bar
entries.description: A bar fixed to the bottom that appears once the hero has scrolled away, with the product, a price or promise and one action; it can be dismissed.

components.name: StickyCtaBar
components.summary: A bar at the bottom of the screen that makes one ask once the reader has seen enough of the page: the hero has scrolled away, and the product, an offer and a single action stay in reach. It watches with IntersectionObserver rather than scroll handlers, slides in with a short transform that becomes a fade when the reader prefers less motion, hides itself while the footer or a form is on screen, and adds room at the bottom of the page while it shows, so it never covers the last lines or a focused field. It respects the safe area of a phone, can be dismissed for the session (from the keyboard, focus goes back to where it came from), and is out of the tab order and the accessibility tree whenever it is hidden. A sticky ask lifts mobile conversion without a popup.

props.name: label
props.doc: The ask in a few words: the product and the offer, "Halcyon Pro, free for 14 days". It also names the bar. On a phone it may take up to three lines beside the button, so keep the button's text short too.

props.name: description
props.doc: One short line of support under the label: a price, a promise. Hidden on a phone, where the label and the button are enough.

props.doc: The one action: a Button, or a link styled as one. Give it size="sm".

props.name: showAfter
props.doc: When the bar appears. A number is a distance in pixels from the top; a string is the id of an element, usually the hero, and the bar appears once that element has scrolled out of view above the screen. 480 by default.

props.name: hideWhen
props.doc: The id of an element, a sign-up form or the footer, that hides the bar for as long as any part of it is on screen: the bar never covers the thing it points at.

props.name: dismissible
props.doc: Shows a close button. Without it the bar stays for as long as its conditions hold.

props.name: onDismiss
props.doc: Called when the reader closes the bar.

props.name: storageKey
props.doc: Remembers a dismissal for the rest of the browser session under this key, so a closed bar stays closed on the next page.

props.name: dismissLabel
props.doc: The accessible name of the close button.

props.name: scrollRoot
props.doc: The element that scrolls, when it is not the window: a preview frame, a dialog, an app pane. The bar is then positioned inside the nearest positioned ancestor instead of fixed to the screen, and the room it needs at the end of the page is added to this element. Leave it out for a page that scrolls normally.

entries.description: A closing ask led by real people: faces, names and roles, a first-person heading, two actions and a status dot with words for how fast they reply.

components.name: TalkToUsCta
components.summary: A closing ask led by real people, for the moment when a person converts better than a form: one to three faces, their names and roles, a heading in the first person, two actions, and a line that says whether they are there and how fast they answer. Place it after a FAQ, beside pricing, or above the footer, to catch the visitor who has a question rather than an objection. Availability is a dot and words together, never colour alone, and it is a polite status region that stays quiet until it changes.

props.name: people
props.doc: One to three people who will answer. More than three are not shown.

props.doc: The ask, in the first person if you can: "Not sure which plan fits? Talk to Maya."

props.doc: When and how fast they answer, in words: "Online now, replies in about 10 minutes". Say the state in the text too; the dot beside it repeats it and is hidden from assistive technology. It is a polite status region, so a change is announced once and nothing is read when the page loads.

props.name: status
props.doc: Whether they are there right now. The dot is solid when online, a ring when away and a thin ring when offline. Online by default.

props.name: actions

The faces overlap on a ring in the card colour and are hidden from assistive technology because the names are written below them; three names share one row in three equal columns, so none is left alone on a second line. Status is a dot and words together: the dot is solid when online, a ring when away and a thin ring when offline, and the availability text must say the state too, for example Online now, replies in about 10 minutes. The line is a polite status region, so a change is announced once and nothing is read on load. The actions stack on a phone and sit side by side when there is room. Place it after a FAQ, beside pricing or above the footer.

components.name: TicketTiers

A tier that is sold out, ended or not on sale yet keeps its place with a disabled button and a clear label, so the reader sees the whole range and what they missed. Until the clock is known a tier with a sale window shows as checking (no badge, a muted price, a disabled button that says so), so the server never renders a tier open that the browser would close; pass `now` from the server and nothing is ever checking. components.name: TrialTimeline
components.summary: A free trial told as it will happen: what you get today, when you are reminded and what happens when the trial ends. Most trial drop-off comes from one fear, "will I be charged?", and a row of ticks only asserts the answer; a short timeline shows it. The moments are an ordered list laid out in a row when the section has the room and in a column when it does not, so it holds on a phone and in a sidebar. The connecting line is decoration. The last moment is emphasised by weight, a filled marker and a heavier title, never by colour, because it is the one that answers the fear.

The connecting line is decoration and hidden from assistive technology. The last moment is the answer to what happens at the end, so it is emphasised by weight, a filled marker and a heavier title, never by colour. Without an icon a moment shows its step number. entries.name: welcome-offer-signup

components.name: WelcomeOfferSignup
components.summary: Trade an email for a first-order discount, and show the code right there. A split section: the offer on one side, and on the other one email field and a button with the consent line beside it. On submit the form gives way to the code in a copy field that says Copied in words, the conditions as a short list and a Start shopping button. The code is never in the page before the address is sent: it arrives with the response, so a crawler or a view source gets nothing. When the response says the address signed up before, the same path reads Welcome back and hands the code over again. The result takes focus so a screen reader reads it. For shops and direct-to-consumer brands.

The code is not in the page until that response arrives, so view source and crawlers get nothing; defaultResult is the one way to start on a code, for a visitor who is meant to have it. The consent line is required and sits beside the button, and the terms show under the form as one line and next to the code as a list. The base URL sits over the list in a copy field. Chips filter by method, show how many endpoints each holds, and say politely how many are on screen. Rows sit under group headings such as Climate, People and Supply chain, and a tally says how many are in each state. The progress is a real progressbar named after its commitment, with the same figures as its value text ("62% of 100%"), so a screen reader hears what the bar shows. The age is judged when the section renders, so a page that is generated once needs revalidating, or a `now` that is kept fresh. Weight, icons and words tell the statuses apart, never colour alone, and a missed goal is listed with…

entries.description: How far you can bend the product, from no-code to code: custom fields, rules, webhooks, plugins and the API, each with its level, examples and a guide.

components.name: ExtensionPoints
components.summary: How far you can bend the product, from no-code to code: a ladder of four or five mechanisms (custom fields, automation rules, webhooks, plugins, the API), least technical first. Each row has the mechanism's name, its level written out, a sentence on what it lets you change, example chips ("Add a field", "Send to Slack") and a link to its guide. A step marker on the left grows by one bar on every row, so the list reads as a climb; it is decoration, because the level is a word and the list is an ordered list. The levels you pass set the order, so a ladder can never be shown upside down, and a key above it says what each level takes when you describe them. It answers "can it do what we need" for buyers who fear being locked in. No state, no script: it renders on the server. The link moves under the chips on a narrow block.

A step marker on the left grows by one bar on every row; it is decoration and hidden from assistive technology, because the list is an ordered list. When any level has a description a key above the ladder says what each level takes; the levels sit in equal columns by their number, or stack, and never as two and one. A chip is only offered when at least one feature belongs to it, and each shows how many features it holds. components.summary: Each feature paired with the result a named customer measured. A ruled list: the feature's name as a link, one line on what it does, and on the right a large figure with what was measured and who measured it. It is proof per feature, where a stats band elsewhere on the page proves nothing in particular. Honest by construction: the customer is always named and the note under the list says how and over what period it was measured. Figures use tabular numbers and never wrap; a signed figure is spelled out as up or down for a screen reader. Under 672px of width each row stacks as feature, description, figure.

entries.name: feature-with-quote
entries.title: Feature with quote
entries.description: One feature explained on one side and the customer who proves it on the other: description, points and a quote card with the result.

components.name: FeatureWithQuote
components.summary: One feature explained on one side and the customer who proves it on the other. On the left an eyebrow, the title, a paragraph, three points and a link; on the right a card with the customer's words set large, their picture, name, job and company, and underneath the result they got as one bold line. Evidence beside the claim it supports persuades more than a wall of testimonials further down the page. The words are a blockquote with the person in its caption, and the result sits outside the quote on a band of its own, so it reads as a fact the customer measured and not as something they said. Under 768px of width the two stack, feature first; `reverse` swaps the sides above that. The card sizes its type and padding from its own width, so it holds in a narrow column too.

props.name: quote
props.doc: The customer on the other side, with the result they got.

props.doc: Puts the quote on the left and the feature on the right from 768px. On a phone the feature always comes first.

entries.docs: Pass feature (an eyebrow, a title, a description, three points, an href and the link's text) and quote (the words, the name, the role, the company, the address of a picture and the result). The words are a blockquote with the person in its caption: their picture (their initials until it loads, or when there is none), name, job and company. The result is one bold line on a band under the quote, outside it, so it reads as a fact the customer measured and not as something they said; leave it out for a quote without a number. On a phone the feature comes first; reverse swaps the sides from 768px of width. The card sets its padding and type from its own width, so it holds in a narrow column. headingLevel sets the level of the title, and labels translates the word over the result and the button's default text.

components.name: GoodFitSection
components.summary: Who it suits and who it does not: two honest columns on one bordered surface, "A good fit if" with checks and "Probably not if" with dashes. It saves the wrong customers a trial and reassures the right ones, because a visitor who sees their own situation named as not a fit believes the other column. A line under the second list points to what to use instead, and the action sits under the first. Both are real lists under real headings, and the check and the dash repeat what the headings already say, so they are decoration. The good-fit column comes first on a phone, where the two stack.

props.name: notFit

entries.docs: Pass title, fit and notFit (four to six short lines each), alternative (the line and its href) and cta (a label and an href). Two columns sit on one bordered surface under "A good fit if" with checks and "Probably not if" with dashes; the second is tinted so it reads as the quieter one. The action sits under the first list and, under the second, a line points to what to use instead; the whole line is the link when you give an href. Both lists are real lists under real headings, and the check and dash icons repeat what the headings already say, so they are hidden from assistive technology. Under 768px of width the columns stack with the good fit first. align centres the heading; labels translates the two column heads.

components.name: ImportSources
components.summary: The reader's switching worry, answered with specifics: a grid of the tools you can import from, each tile with its name (and a mark if you have one), what comes across as short chips, how long it takes in plain words and a link to its guide. The whole tile is the link, named by the tool and "import guide", so a list of eight does not read as eight identical words. The chips and the estimate claim nothing beyond what you pass in. The grid ends in a dashed tile for a CSV upload, which every tool can feed, and an optional help line for the reader whose tool is not on the list. It needs no script and no state, so it renders on the server. For migration pages and the footer of a comparison, where the question is never whether but how painful.
