entries.docs: Pass sources (an id, the tool's name, an optional mark, what comes across as short names, a time estimate in plain words and the link to its import guide), plus csv for a closing dashed tile and help for the line under the grid. Each tile is one link: the name is a link stretched over the tile, named by the tool and import guide. The chips and the estimate say only what you pass in. A tool without a mark shows its first letter. The block has no state and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels.

entries.name: industry-index
entries.title: Industry index

components.name: IndustryIndex
components.summary: Where the use cases grid gives a few audiences a card each, this carries the long tail: twelve to thirty industries as a quiet index, grouped by sector, each a link with how many customers you have there. Sector headings sit over lists that flow into columns by the width of the block, and no industry is split across two of them. A featured industry leads its sector and is marked in words. With `filterable` a search field narrows the index as you type, says how many are left, and when nothing matches it says so and offers your contact link, because a missing industry is a lead and not a dead end. The numbers are tabular and quiet, and a screen reader hears them as customers.

props.name: title

props.name: description

props.name: sectors

entries.docs: Pass sectors (a label and its industries, each with a name, an href, optionally a customer count and a featured flag). A featured industry leads its sector and is marked Popular in words; counts are tabular, quiet and read out as customers. Lists flow into one, two or three columns by the width of the block, and no industry is split across two. Set filterable to add a search field that narrows the index as you type and says how many are left; when nothing matches it says so and offers the contact link. entries.name: keyboard-features
entries.title: Keyboard features
entries.description: A keyboard-first product's shortcuts as cards: the keys, what they do, and a card that lights up when you press them.

components.name: KeyboardFeatures
components.summary: The shortcuts of a keyboard-first product as a grid of cards: the keys drawn as keycaps, a title that starts with a verb and a line of detail. It is playful and it is also the index of what the keyboard can do. Press a real shortcut while no field has focus and its card lights up for a second, its keys turn solid, and its title is announced politely to a screen reader; a sequence such as G then P lights its first key and waits a moment for the second. Under reduced motion nothing fades, lifts or flips: the card gets a bold outline instead. Mod is Cmd on a Mac and Ctrl elsewhere, chosen after hydration, so the server HTML says Cmd/Ctrl and no reader is shown a key they do not have. Every key is text, with a spoken name where it is a symbol, so the cards read as a plain list of shortcuts without scripting. Nothing is taken from the browser unless you ask for it.

props.name: title
props.doc: The heading: "Everything is a keystroke away".

props.name: description
props.doc: One or two sentences under the heading.

props.name: shortcuts
props.doc: Six to nine shortcuts, the ones people learn first at the top. They are also the index of what the keyboard can do, so every key is written out as text.

props.name: platform
props.doc: Which keyboard to write the keys for. "auto" reads it after the page has loaded, and until then Mod says Cmd/Ctrl, so the server never shows a Mac key to a Windows reader. "mac" and "other" fix it, for a page that knows.

props.name: cta
props.doc: The action under the cards: a Button or a link styled as one, such as "See every shortcut".

props.name: preventDefault
props.doc: Stops the browser from doing its own thing with a shortcut that matches a card: no quick find on "/", no address bar on Ctrl+K. Off by default, because a marketing page should not take keys from its visitor.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the heading: 2 by default. Each card's title sits one level below it.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.docs: Pass title, description, shortcuts (six to nine, each with an id, keys, a verb-first title and a line of detail) and optionally cta, platform and preventDefault. Keys are written as text: Mod+K is a chord (Mod is Cmd on a Mac and Ctrl elsewhere), G then P is a sequence, and ? or Esc are single keys; the modifiers are Mod, Ctrl, Alt, Shift and Meta. Press a real shortcut while no field has focus and its card lights for a second, its keys turn solid and its title is announced politely; in a sequence the first key lights and the second has a moment to follow. Under reduced motion the card gets a bold outline instead and nothing lifts, fades or flips. platform is auto by default, which reads the keyboard after hydration, so until then Mod is written Cmd/Ctrl and no reader is shown a key they do not have; mac and other fix it. Mac symbols come with their spoken names, so every key is also te…

entries.name: materials-section
entries.title: Materials section
entries.description: What it is made of and where it comes from: materials with share, origin and certification beside a short story, for products that must prove it.

components.name: MaterialsSection
components.summary: What it is made of and where it comes from, for products that have to prove it: fashion, food, furniture and cosmetics, where the label is part of the pitch. On the left a short story and a care list; on the right a ruled list of materials, each with a swatch in the material's own tone, its name, its share, the place it comes from and what certifies it. The share is written as text first and the thin bar under it is decoration, hidden from assistive technology; origins are plain places and a certification is a word, not a seal. The shares should add up to 100, and while you develop the block warns you in the console when they do not. No state, no script: it renders on the server. The two halves sit side by side by the width of the block, not of the screen.

props.name: materials

props.name: care

entries.docs: Pass a title, a story and materials (a name, a share in percent, an origin, an optional certification and a swatch, a CSS colour for the material's own tone), plus care, a short list for washing or maintenance. The share is written as text first and the thin bar under it is decoration, hidden from assistive technology. The shares should add up to 100: while you develop, the block warns in the console when they do not. Origins are plain places and a certification is a word in a badge. The halves sit side by side by the width of the block. The block has no state and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels, and the shares follow locale.

entries.name: membership-tiers
entries.title: Membership tiers
entries.description: A loyalty or membership ladder: tiers earned by spend or time, with thresholds, perks and a marker for where the member stands.

components.name: MembershipTiers
components.summary: A loyalty or membership ladder: tiers that are earned, not bought, with what each takes and what each gives. The tiers are an ordered list joined by a rail, as columns on a wide section and one under the other on a phone. Give it the member's tier and how far they are towards the next, and their own tier is marked in words (Your tier, with aria-current), the tiers below it say Reached, the rail is filled up to where the member stands with a marker between the two tiers, and a progress bar says it in numbers and words: "€180 to go until Gold". Without a member it is the ladder a visitor sees, and nothing is marked. Different from a pricing table, where each column is a purchase: here the thresholds are the point. For shops, clubs, airlines, hotels and anyone who rewards people for staying.

props.name: title
props.doc: The heading: "Earn your way up".

props.name: description
props.doc: One or two sentences under the heading: what counts towards a tier and when it is reviewed.

props.name: tiers
props.doc: Three or four tiers, lowest first. They are earned in order, so the order is the ladder.

props.name: current
props.doc: The `id` of the member's own tier. Leave it out for a visitor who is not a member: no tier is marked.

props.name: progress
props.doc: How far the member is towards the next tier. It needs `current`; the marker sits between the two tiers, and the words say how far is left.

props.name: cta
props.doc: The action under the ladder: a Button or a link styled as one, such as "Join the club".

props.name: note
props.doc: Fine print under the action: "Tiers are reviewed every January, on the last twelve months."

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: The level of the heading: 2 by default. Each tier's name sits one level below it.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.description: Up and running in three commands: numbered steps, each with a copyable command and what you should see, and a package manager switch.

components.name: QuickstartSteps
components.summary: The first five minutes, made checkable: three or four numbered steps, each with the command in a copy field and, under it, what the terminal should print, so a developer can tell at every step whether it worked before they commit to the product. An optional switch swaps all commands to the reader's package manager (pnpm, npm, yarn, bun, or any list of your own) and says so politely. The expected output is plain, selectable text, never an image, and every copy button carries its step number in its name, so a screen reader does not hear three identical "Copy" buttons. Nothing is tracked or stored: the choice lives in the block until the page is left, and `onManagerChange` hands it to you if you want it kept. A last node links on to what comes next.

A map would look nicer and tell a buyer less about data residency than one row does. Chips filter by tag, show how many regions each holds and say, politely, how many are on screen; the tag you filter by is marked in every row it appears in. A planned region has no latency and says so instead of showing a dash. On a wide block the list is a real table with headers and a caption; on a narrow one each region is a card under its continent, with the latency written out as a sentence ("about 12 ms from Amsterdam"). A region can link to wherever choosing it goes. Words are translated through labels.

Time is the axis, so a buyer of a bigger product sees when it pays back and what is asked of their team. The first milestone is marked Start and the last Outcome (or the one you flag), in words under the time label, and the outcome gets a filled marker and a heavier title. The time labels and the owners are text, never colour or an image, and the spine is drawn with a border. It is an ordered list. On a wide section the heading sits beside the plan and each row has the time label, the spine and the milestone in three columns; on a phone the time label stacks above the title. Give a feature a marker and its number is drawn on the screenshot where the feature lives, so the eye can go from the column to the place and back. The alt text describes the screen in a sentence; the marks and the dots are decoration, and the marks are sized from the picture, so on a phone they shrink with it instead of covering what they point at. components.name: SdkGrid
components.summary: The first question a developer asks of a product with an API: is there a library for my stack? One card per language or framework, each with the name, the current version, who stands behind it as a written word (Stable, Beta or Community, each with its own shape so colour is never the only cue), the install command in a copy field, and links to the docs and the source. The command is real text you can select, and a copy button announces itself by language, so a page of eight does not give a screen reader eight identical buttons. A last, dashed card sends the reader to a list of community libraries and says in words that those are not official, instead of padding the grid with logos it does not stand behind. It needs no state of its own, so it renders on the server; the copy buttons are the only client parts.

The install command is real text in a copy field, and each copy button is named after its language, so a page of eight does not give a screen reader eight identical buttons. A command that does not fit beside its button wraps, with the button under it, instead of hiding behind a scrollbar. Give an sdk a mark (a logo or glyph at 22px) or let the card show the first letters of its name. The block has no state of its own and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels.

entries.description: Commitments in numbers: response times by priority, each defined in a sentence, and uptime targets with the downtime they allow and the credit owed.

components.name: ServiceLevels
components.summary: What a buyer can hold you to, in two compact tables: how fast people answer at each priority, and how much downtime a month the uptime target allows and what you owe if it is missed. It replaces "24/7 support" with numbers. Every priority is defined in a sentence exact enough to argue about, the percentage is translated into minutes, and every figure is tabular. Side by side on a wide block, stacked on a narrower one; on a phone both tables become lists of cards with the very same labels under the same titles, so nothing hides in a horizontal scroll. Both are real tables with captions, and a line under them says when support applies. No state and no script: it renders on the server.

Add hours for the line under the tables that says when support applies, and slaHref for a link to the full agreement. The two tables sit side by side from 76rem, the inside of an 80rem page container, and stack on anything narrower so neither column is cramped; both switch together between real tables and lists of cards with the same labels, so on a phone nothing hides in a horizontal scroll. Figures are tabular, and both tables have captions. Words are translated through labels.

entries.name: spend-breakdown
entries.title: Spend breakdown
entries.description: Where every 100 goes: a ten-by-ten unit chart in tones and patterns, beside a legend that says what each share pays for.

components.name: SpendBreakdown
components.summary: Where the money goes, as one hundred squares: each square is one per cent, filled in proportion to the parts, so "82 of every 100" is something you can count rather than a slice to estimate. Beside the squares a legend table says, for every part, its percentage (and its amount when you give the total), its name and a sentence on what it pays for. The squares are decoration and hidden from assistive technology; the table is the content. The squares are allotted by the largest remainder method, so the grid is always exactly full even when the shares are 33.4, 33.3 and 33.3, and each part has a tone and a pattern of its own, so the chart still reads in greyscale and in print. Hovering a row of the legend lights its squares. For charities, marketplaces, payment providers and public bodies that owe their audience a plain answer to "where does it go?".

The shares are read as percentages of a hundred, and if they do not add up to 100 they are scaled, so the grid is always full. entries.name: stack-layers
entries.title: Stack layers
entries.description: Your architecture as horizontal layers, edge to storage: each with its technologies, a one-line promise and a metric, along a rail that marks a request's path.

components.name: StackLayers
components.summary: Your architecture as horizontal layers, top to bottom in the order a request meets them: edge, API, compute and storage. Each band has the layer's name, the technologies that do the work as chips, a one-line promise and a small metric at the right, with hairlines between the bands and a thin rail down the left that marks the path a request takes. For infrastructure and security-minded buyers who want to see the engine: the point is the layers, not a movement through them, so nothing animates. It is an ordered list read from top to bottom, and the metric is plain text. On a narrow block each band becomes a card, and a short line between the cards keeps the path. No state, no script: it renders on the server.

The block is an ordered list read from top to bottom; the metric is plain text, and the rail on the left is decoration that marks the path of a request. On a wide block the layers are bands separated by hairlines; on a narrow one each becomes a card, joined to the next by a short line. A layer without a metric simply has none. Add a footnote for where the figures come from. Nothing animates, the block has no state and it renders on the server.

entries.name: sync-mapping
entries.title: Sync mapping
entries.description: What syncs between two tools: object pairs, direction, how often and what stays manual, in a clear table with the limits listed underneath.

components.name: SyncMapping
components.summary: What syncs between two tools, in the table people actually look for: one row per pair of objects, your object on the left and the other tool's on the right, the direction between them (an arrow and the words One way or Two way), how often it runs and what stays manual. Direction is announced in full, "Contacts to Customers, two way", and never left to an arrow. Under the table is a plain list of what does not sync, because that is the honest detail integration pages usually leave out. On a narrow block the table scrolls sideways inside its own region, which can be reached and scrolled with the keyboard, and says so underneath; the first column, your object, stays in view while it scrolls, so a row never loses its name. No state, no script: it renders on the server.

The direction is drawn as an arrow and written out, and a screen reader hears it in full ("Contacts to Customers, two way"). The table scrolls sideways in a region of its own on a narrow block, which can be focused and scrolled with the keyboard, and says so underneath. The first column, your object, stays pinned while it scrolls, so a row never loses its name. The region is a tab stop at every width, also where the table fits: a scroller that cannot be reached by keyboard is worse, and knowing that it overflows takes a script. The block has no state and renders on the server. Words are translated through labels.

components.name: ThemePreview

Give it your own markup as children, and your own palettes as themes, to show a design system, a white-label product or a dashboard that takes dark mode seriously. entries.description: A platform explained to both sides: what buyers get and what sellers get, mirrored around a centre line, each side with benefits and an action of its own.

components.name: TwoSidedFeatures
components.summary: A platform explained to both of the people it serves: what buyers get and what sellers get, mirrored around a centre rule. Each side has an audience tag, a heading, a ruled list of benefits with a small icon and its own action, and the benefits sit on the same rows across the rule, so each pair reads straight across whatever the length of the words. Both sides carry the same structure, size and button, so neither reads as an afterthought. It is made for marketplaces, booking platforms, hiring sites and any other two-sided network. On a narrow block the sides stack with a labelled divider ("and") between them. The block has no state of its own and renders on the server; the sides come in two columns by the width of the block, not of the screen.

entries.description: If you are this, pick that: scenario rows that point each kind of buyer to the right plan, model or product.

components.name: WhichOneGuide
components.summary: "If you are this, pick that": a ruled list of situations in the reader's own voice, each pointing at the option that fits, so a visitor finds themselves in one sentence instead of comparing a feature table. A row reads scenario first, then an arrow, then the recommended option as a chip with a line on why and a link; on a medium block (a tablet) the row is two columns, the scenario beside the answer, with the arrow leading into the chip; on a narrow block the arrow turns downward and the answer sits under the scenario. It is a plain list: no quiz, no state, nothing that needs JavaScript, so it renders on the server and works with scripts off. The chip names the option in words and the row says "Recommended" to screen readers, so the arrow is only decoration. A fallback row catches the reader nobody wrote a sentence for.

entries.docs: Pass rows (a scenario in the reader's own voice and the recommendation: a name, a one-line reason and a link) and, optionally, a fallback for the reader nobody wrote a sentence for. A row reads scenario, arrow, then the option as a chip with its reason; on a medium block it is two columns, the scenario beside the answer, with the arrow leading into the chip; on a narrow block the arrow turns downward and the answer sits under the scenario. The chip names the option in words and screen readers hear Recommended before it. It is a static decision aid with no quiz and no state, so it renders on the server and works with JavaScript off. Words are translated through labels.

A pill over the portrait can say whether the adviser is taking clients. Nothing else competes with the person: no carousel, no second button.

entries.name: big-number-hero
entries.title: Big number hero
entries.description: One figure as the picture: a huge number at the largest size its container allows, what it measures, a dated source and the action that follows.

components.name: BigNumberHero
components.summary: One figure as the picture: a huge number, what it measures, and the action that follows from it. The value is set at the largest size its container allows, from a phone to a wide page, so a long figure shrinks to fit and a short one fills the width, with its unit beside it. Under the figure go a sentence of context, a source line with the day the figure was true as a time element, and the actions. With `animate` the figure counts up from zero the first time it is on screen, in tabular figures inside a box as wide as the final value, so nothing shifts while it runs. The page holds the final value from the first render, for screen readers, search engines and print: what counts is a copy for the eye, hidden from assistive technology, and under reduced motion there is no count at all. For nonprofits, public bodies and data products whose strongest statement is a number.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The heading's element: "h2" inside a page that has its own h1 (the default), "h1" when the hero opens the page.

props.name: value
props.doc: The figure. It is the heading, together with its label, and its final value is in the page from the first render.

props.name: unit
props.doc: What it is a count of, set smaller beside the figure: "million litres", "years", "%". A short one stays beside it everywhere; a longer one drops under it on a narrow screen.

props.name: label
props.doc: What the figure measures, in a line over it: "Drinking water saved since 2019".

props.name: description
props.doc: A sentence of context under the figure.

props.name: source
props.doc: Where the figure comes from, as words or as words with a link.

props.name: asOf
props.doc: The day the figure was true: an ISO day ("2025-12-31"), a timestamp or a Date. It is printed after the source, in a time element, so the figure is dated.

props.name: actions
props.doc: The actions that follow from it. The first is the solid button and the rest are outlined; two read best.

props.name: format
props.doc: How the figure is written, as options for Intl.NumberFormat: `{ maximumFractionDigits: 1 }`, `{ style: "percent" }`.

props.name: animate
props.doc: Count up from zero, once, the first time the figure is on screen. The page always holds the final value, and a reader who asked for less motion gets it at once. Default false.

props.name: duration
props.doc: Seconds the count takes. Default 1.6.

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the figure and the date. Default "en-US".

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone a full timestamp is read in. A plain ISO day is that calendar day everywhere. Default "UTC".

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.docs: value is the figure, unit what it counts ("million litres", "years", "%"), label what it measures, and format takes options for Intl.NumberFormat, such as { maximumFractionDigits: 1 } or { style: "percent" }. The figure is set at the largest size its container allows, from a phone to a wide page: a short unit stays beside it, a longer one drops under it on a narrow screen. The heading holds the label and the final value as text from the first render. animate counts up from zero once, the first time the figure is on screen, using AnimatedNumber; duration is in seconds; under reduced motion, or without IntersectionObserver, the final value is simply there. source is words or { label, href }, asOf the day the figure was true (shown in a time element) and actions the buttons, the first of them solid. Pass locale and timeZone, and labels to translate the fixed words.

entries.name: book-hero

components.name: BookHero

The object is drawn with CSS transforms alone, no 3D library, and lies flat under reduced motion. Two or three lines of praise can be stepped through with Previous and Next, and nothing ever advances them by itself; the room for the longest is reserved, so the page never jumps. The buy button is a menu of shops named in text, or a plain link when there is one. For novels, non-fiction, cookbooks and self-publishers.

components.name: BreathingHero
components.summary: A wellness opening where the demo is the pitch: a ring that breathes. It grows while you breathe in, rests, and shrinks while you breathe out on a 4, 4 and 6 second rhythm (or yours), the phase is written in the ring and announced politely each time it changes, and under it come the title, a line and the button that starts a session. The ring is driven by CSS animations that take their length from the pattern, so there is no script per frame; the one timer only wakes at each change of phase to update the words. A Pause and Resume button is always there, as WCAG asks of anything that moves by itself. Under reduced motion the ring stays still, and the words and a thin progress line in three named parts, one per phase ("In 4s", "Hold 4s", "Out 6s"), carry the timing instead. Other props, an id for a nav anchor, aria or data attributes and a ref, go to the section.

entries.description: A community opening built from its members: a mosaic of faces, the member count, the channels busy right now and one join button.

components.name: CommunityHero
components.summary: A community opening built from its members. The promise and one join button stand in the middle of a staggered mosaic of faces, pictures or initials on a calm grid; under the button come the total ("12,480 members") and the channels that are busy now with how many people are in each. The mosaic is decoration and gets one sentence for screen readers instead of eighteen faces; its pictures load lazily, so a phone, which shows eight, never fetches the rest. Where the container is wide the faces flank the text, and where it is narrow they become a row above and a row below it. For clubs, chat communities, alumni networks and open-source groups, where the people are the product.

The mosaic is decoration: a screen reader gets one sentence naming the first few members, and the labels prop translates it with the other fixed words. Pass the page's own content as children and the card stays beside it while it scrolls. Prices use tabular figures. Payment lives elsewhere: the button hands your app the click, or links to your checkout.

props.name: locale

entries.name: creator-hero
entries.title: Creator hero
entries.description: A link-in-bio opening for a creator: avatar, handle, a line of bio, three audience numbers and a column of link buttons, designed at 320px.

components.name: CreatorHero
components.summary: A link-in-bio opening for a creator, designed at 320px and left that way: one narrow column with a large avatar, the name and handle, a line of bio, three audience numbers in compact notation (48.2K, and the full figure for screen readers) and a stack of full-width link buttons, each with an icon, a label and an optional New tag, then profiles named in text. The stack is a real list, the first link can be set in solid colour as the one to press, and a link that leaves the page opens in a new tab with a rel and says so. For creators, speakers, musicians and small brands.

props.name: nameAs
props.doc: The name's element: "h2" inside a page that has its own h1 (the default), "h1" when the hero opens the page.

props.name: name
props.doc: Your name.

props.name: handle
props.doc: "@marlowe.makes"

props.name: bio
props.doc: One line about you.

props.name: avatar
props.doc: A square picture, as a URL or a data URI. Leave it out and your initials are drawn.

props.name: stats
props.doc: Three fit best: the numbers that make a stranger stay.

props.name: links
props.doc: The stack of buttons: what you want people to do next, in order.

props.name: socials
props.doc: A row of profiles under the stack, named in text.

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the numbers. Default "en-US".

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.docs: Give name, handle, bio and an optional square avatar (without one the initials are drawn). stats are numbers, not strings: 48200 is shown as 48.2K in the locale you pass and read in full to a screen reader. links is the stack of buttons: a label, an href, an icon from @rhs-ui/icons, an optional badge ("new", "beta" or "soon") and featured for the one link to set in solid colour. A link to an absolute http(s) address opens in a new tab with rel="noopener noreferrer" and says so to screen readers; pass external to override. socials are profiles named in text, not logos. Use nameAs="h1" when the hero opens the page, and labels to translate the fixed words.

entries.name: dashboard-hero
entries.title: Dashboard hero
entries.description: A SaaS opening with the product drawn in HTML: the pitch on the left, a cropped dashboard with KPIs and a table on the right.

components.name: DashboardHero
components.summary: A SaaS opening with the product drawn in HTML: the pitch and two actions on the left and, on the right, a window with a hairline border, three quiet dots and a title, holding a dashboard made from your data: a slim sidebar, a row of figures with how they moved, and a table whose every row ends in a status word. The window runs off the right and bottom edges of its stage, so it reads as a product bigger than the picture, and because it is real markup it follows light and dark and never needs a screenshot. To a screen reader the drawing is one sentence, made from its own figures; it is hidden and inert, so nothing in it takes focus. Under 768px it sits below the copy, still cropped. Depth comes from the hairline and one soft shadow, never from a gradient or a glow.

props.name: titleAs

props.name: secondary

props.name: window

entries.name: desktop-download-hero
entries.title: Desktop download hero
entries.description: The opening of a desktop app: one primary download button for the visitor's system, the other platforms a click away.

components.name: DesktopDownloadHero
components.summary: The opening of a desktop app: one large download button for the visitor's system, the other platforms and architectures in a menu beside it, the version, size and date under it, and the app in a window on the right. The system is read from the browser only after hydration, so the server HTML lists every platform as an equal button and never shows the wrong one; if detection fails, that list simply stays. With a single build there is no menu, and without a window the copy takes the whole width. Every platform is a real download link, and the system requirements fold into a details element.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The title's element: "h2" inside a page that has its own h1 (the default), "h1" when the hero opens the page.

props.name: title
props.doc: The headline beside the download button.

props.name: description
props.doc: The support line under the headline.

props.name: platforms

props.name: version

props.name: releasedAt

props.name: requirements

props.name: detect
props.doc: "auto" reads the browser after hydration, so the server HTML shows every platform as an equal button and nothing flashes. A platform id fixes the choice. An id that matches nothing, such as "none", keeps the equal list.

props.name: window
props.doc: The app, drawn in a window frame beside the copy. Leave it out and the copy takes the whole width. It is a picture next to the copy: give a screenshot alt text, and hide a drawing made of markup with aria-hidden.

props.name: windowTitle
props.doc: The title in the window's bar.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for the date.

props.name: timeZone

entries.name: donation-hero
entries.title: Donation hero
entries.description: A nonprofit opening with the gift on the first screen: one-off or monthly, four amounts, your own, a campaign meter and what each gift pays for.

components.name: DonationHero
components.summary: A nonprofit's opening with the gift on the first screen: a short centred headline over one wide card. The left half is a picture of the cause with the amount and what it pays for written over it, changing as the visitor chooses. The right half is the form: a campaign meter whose figures are in words as well as a bar, a one-off or monthly choice, four amounts in a toggle group, a field for any other amount, a live summary ("You give $25 every month") and a Give button that always says the amount and how often. An own amount under the minimum is explained in words and cannot be given. Payment is not in here: the hero hands your app the choice.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The title's element: "h2" inside a page that has its own h1 (the default), "h1" when the hero opens the page.

props.name: eyebrow
props.doc: A small line over the title: the campaign or the season.

props.name: title
props.doc: The ask, in a line: "Warm meals for every winter night".

props.name: description
props.doc: One or two sentences under the title on who is helped and how.

props.name: amounts
props.doc: The suggested amounts, in minor units, in the order they are shown. Four is the design.

props.name: defaultAmount
props.doc: The amount chosen at the start, in minor units. One that is not among `amounts` opens in the own-amount field; null starts with nothing chosen. Default: the second of `amounts`.

props.name: defaultFrequency
props.doc: Default "one-off".

props.name: minimum
props.doc: The lowest amount allowed in the own-amount field, in minor units. Anything lower is explained in words and cannot be given. Without it only amounts above zero are allowed.

props.name: currency
props.doc: The ISO 4217 code of the currency. Default "EUR".

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the amounts and the decimal sign. Default "en-US".

props.name: impactFor
props.type: (amount: number, frequency: DonationFrequency) => string | null | undefined
props.doc: What a gift pays for, as the end of a sentence: "pays for a week of meals". It is written over the picture under the amount and changes with every choice; return null for an amount you have nothing to say about. The frequency is passed too, so a monthly gift can say "every month". It must be a pure function of its arguments. Leave it out for a picture with no sentence. A function cannot be passed from a Server Component: use the hero inside a Client Component.

props.name: campaign
props.doc: The campaign meter: a bar and its numbers in words. Leave it out when there is no goal to show.

props.name: image
props.doc: The picture of the cause, on the left of the card.

props.name: note
props.doc: A line under the button: how the money is handled, whether it is tax-deductible.

props.name: onDonate
props.doc: Called when the visitor presses Give with a valid amount. Payment is yours: this only hands you the choice. If it returns a promise, the button shows it is busy until the promise settles; handle errors inside it.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.docs: All money is in minor units, hundredths of the currency's unit, like CurrencyInput and most payment APIs: pass 2500 for 25.00. impactFor(amount, frequency) returns the end of a sentence ("pays for a week of meals") that is written over the picture and changes with every choice. onDonate({ amount, frequency, currency }) is where your checkout starts; return a promise and the button shows it is busy until it settles. impactFor and onDonate are functions, so use the hero inside a Client Component.

entries.name: gallery-hero
entries.title: Gallery hero
entries.description: A full-bleed photograph opening a series: the picture, caption and credit, a counter with Previous and Next, and thumbnails that switch it.

components.name: GalleryHero
components.summary: A full-bleed photograph as the opening of a series. One picture fills the frame, the series title stays small in one corner and a link sits in the other, and a quiet caption bar underneath gives the title and place on the left, the year and credit on the right, and a "03 / 08" counter with Previous and Next. A strip of thumbnails switches the picture, and so do the arrow keys, Home and End while focus is inside the gallery, and a swipe on a touch screen. Changing the picture fades the new one in over the old and fetches the pictures either side of it; the caption is announced through a polite live region; and no timer ever advances it. For photographers, architects and studios whose work is a picture.

entries.name: inline-image-hero
entries.title: Inline image hero
entries.description: An agency statement set at display size with small rounded pictures between the words, so the sentence and the work read together.

components.name: InlineImageHero
components.summary: An agency's statement set at display size with small rounded pictures sitting between the words, so the sentence and the work read together: the pattern of studio sites, built so it cannot break the heading. The sentence is data, words and pictures in order, and is one heading; the pictures are pills that are part of the line, wrap with it and are as high as the line itself, the most a line can hold without being pushed apart. They are sized in em, so they shrink with the type on a phone and the rhythm of the line holds. A picture is decorative unless you give it an alt, and the heading reads to a screen reader as the plain sentence. A kicker sits over it, and under it a rule with a few small facts and the one action.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The heading's element: "h2" inside a page that has its own h1 (the default), "h1" when the hero opens the page.

props.name: parts
props.doc: The sentence as data: words and pictures in the order they are read, `["We design", { image }, "brands for", { image }, "people who care"]`. Words are joined with a space; a picture is set between them as a pill.

props.name: kicker
props.doc: A small line above the sentence: what the studio is and where.

props.name: cta
props.doc: The one action, as a button under the sentence.

props.name: meta
props.doc: Small facts along the foot of the hero: services, a city, when there is room for a new project.

entries.docs: parts is the sentence as data: strings and { image, alt?, ratio? } in the order they are read. Words are joined with a space and each picture is set as a pill between them, as high as the line itself and sized in em, so it wraps with the line and shrinks with the type on a phone. The heading reads as one plain sentence: a picture is hidden from assistive technology unless you pass an alt, which is then read at its place in the sentence. kicker sits above the sentence; meta is a list of small facts and cta the one button, both along a rule under it. titleAs makes the heading an h1 when the hero opens the page.

components.name: IntegrationHero

The two tiles are one image to a screen reader ("Acme and Northwind") and nothing is drawn with the partner's brand beyond the mark you pass, so one template can give every integration its own landing page without copied badges.

entries.name: lineup-hero
entries.title: Lineup hero
entries.description: A festival or conference poster set in type: the dates and the city as display type, and the names sized by billing, wrapping like a poster.

components.name: LineupHero
components.summary: A festival or conference poster set in type. The dates and the city are display type across the top, the festival's own name sits small above them like the mark on a poster, and the names run underneath in three sizes by billing: headliners large, the middle tier at half that, the rest small and quiet. Names are separated by thin slashes and wrap like a poster; a name with an address is a link, a role is set small after the name, and every tier is a heading for assistive technology. The sizes follow the width of the names' own column, so the poster reflows in a narrow column as well as a wide page and a long name wraps instead of overflowing. There are no portraits to load, which is the point: for festivals, conferences and symposia.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The title's element: "h2" inside a page that has its own h1 (the default), "h1" when the hero opens the page. The tiers' headings sit one level below it.

props.name: title
props.doc: The name of the festival or the conference. It is the heading, set small like the mark on a poster.

props.name: dates
props.doc: The dates as they should be set: "12–14 June 2027".

props.name: venue
props.doc: Where it is: a city, or a city with the place.

props.name: tiers
props.doc: The billing, largest first. The first tier is set largest, the second in the middle and every other tier small, so three read best.

props.name: ticketsHref
props.doc: Where to buy tickets. Leave it out for no button.

props.name: programmeHref
props.doc: Where to read the programme. Leave it out for no button.

props.name: showTierLabels
props.doc: Write the tier labels on the page, in a column beside the names, instead of leaving them to assistive technology.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.docs: Pass the festival's title, the dates as you want them set ("12–14 June 2027"), the venue (a city, or { city, name } to set the place small under it) and tiers: an array of { label, names } with the largest billing first, where each name is { name, role?, href? }. The first tier is set largest, the second at half that and every later tier small and quiet. The sizes follow the width of the names' own column, so the poster reflows inside a narrow container as well as on a wide page, and a long name wraps instead of overflowing. Each tier is a heading for screen readers; showTierLabels also writes it on the page, in a column beside the names. A name with an href is a link, and a role is set small after it. ticketsHref and programmeHref add the two buttons. Pass labels to translate the fixed words.

entries.name: local-business-hero
entries.title: Local business hero
entries.description: The front of a local business: name, open or closed now in its own time zone, a call button, directions and a card with the week's hours.

components.name: LocalBusinessHero
components.summary: The front of a local business: its name, whether it is open right now, and a call button, all on the first screen. Beside them a card with a photo, the address in an address element, today's hours and the full week folded into a details element. The status ("Open now, closes 18:00", "Closed now, opens tomorrow 13:00") is worked out in the business's time zone in the browser while the server renders only the hours, so there is never a wrong "Open" flash; the pill holds its place and fades in. Phone and email are real tel: and mailto: links. For shops, garages, salons and practices, where the first question is whether you are open and where you are.

props.doc: The business's name.

props.name: tagline
props.doc: One line on what it does.

props.name: phone

props.name: email
props.doc: An email address. It becomes a mailto: link in the card.

props.name: address
props.doc: The address, as lines ("Kerkstraat 14", "6511 AB Nijmegen") or as one string.

props.doc: The week as seven days in the shape of OpeningHours: a name and the hours, null for a closed day. The status is worked out from the hours text, written as 24-hour times: "09:00 to 18:00", or "09:00 to 12:30, 13:30 to 18:00" with a break. Hours it cannot read (12-hour times, fewer than seven days) show the card and the week as written, and no status.

props.name: directionsHref
props.doc: Where the directions link leads: a map link for the address.

props.name: image
props.doc: The photo at the top of the card. Leave it out for a card without one.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The business's own time zone as an IANA name: "Europe/Amsterdam". Required, because "open now" is a statement about the clock where the business is, not where the visitor is.

props.name: weekStartsOn
props.doc: Which day `hours` starts on: 1 for Monday (the default), 0 for Sunday.

props.name: now

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text and the status sentences, for a site that is not in English. `{time}`, `{day}` and `{phone}` are filled in.

entries.name: marketplace-hero

components.name: MarketplaceHero

entries.name: podcast-hero
entries.title: Podcast hero
entries.description: A podcast's opening: cover art, the latest episode with a Play button that hands off to your player, and where to listen as plain text links.

components.name: PodcastHero
components.summary: The opening for a podcast: a square cover on the left, and on the right the show name, who hosts it, one sentence of pitch, the latest episode as a card and the places to listen. The card holds the number, the title, the length and the day, and a Play button that calls `onPlay`; the player itself is yours and lives elsewhere, which keeps the hero a hero. Hand `playing` back and the button says Pause and the card says Now playing. The length is written "48 min" and spoken "48 minutes", both are time elements, and the listen links are services named in text rather than logos. A show with no cover art gets one set in type from its name, black on white or the reverse.

Hand its state back with playing and the button says Pause and the card says Now playing; onPause is called then, or onPlay again if you leave it out, so one handler can toggle. listenLinks are services named in text, such as Apple Podcasts, Spotify and RSS, instead of logos, in a list named after the show so two shows on a page are told apart. entries.name: promo-slider-hero
entries.title: Promo slider hero
entries.description: A hero that carries several campaigns: slides with their own copy and image, manual controls and a polite counter, never moving by itself.

components.name: PromoSliderHero
components.summary: A hero that carries several campaigns at once: each slide is a full panel with its own eyebrow, headline, line, button and picture, laid on native scroll snapping, so a swipe or a trackpad works with no script. Previous and Next buttons, numbered dots and a "2 of 4" counter announced politely move the visitor around; the arrow keys, Home and End work anywhere in the region. Nothing ever advances on a timer, slides that are off screen are inert so Tab never lands on a button nobody can see, and the first slide's picture loads with priority. The dots and the counter follow the track as it moves, but the announcement and `onSlideChange` wait until it has come to rest, so a jump from the first slide to the fourth is read out once, for the slide it lands on. The calm answer to the auto-rotating banner: a retailer gets several promotions into one hero and the visitor stays in control.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The slide headlines' element: "h2" inside a page that has its own h1 (the default), "h1" when the hero opens the page. Only the current slide is exposed to assistive technology, so a page never has more than one.

props.name: slides
props.doc: The campaigns, in the order you want them seen. Two to six read best.

props.name: label
props.doc: The region's accessible name: "Current promotions".

props.name: initial
props.doc: The slide to start on, counting from 0.

props.name: onSlideChange
props.doc: Called with the new slide's index once the visitor has come to rest on it, by a button, a dot, a key or a swipe. A jump across several slides reports only the one it lands on. It is optional; a Server Component cannot pass a function, so leave it out there.

props.name: labels
props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.name: prompt-hero
entries.title: Prompt hero
entries.description: An AI product opening where the first action is typing: a large prompt box with example chips that fill it.

components.name: PromptHero
components.summary: An AI product's opening where the first action is typing: a large prompt box that grows to six lines, a submit button with a keyboard hint, and example chips that fill the box. Enter submits and Shift+Enter adds a line; on a touch screen, which has no Shift+Enter, Enter adds the line and the button submits. An empty prompt disables the button and says why in words. There is no streaming and no model logic here: the prompt is handed to your app, typically to carry it through sign-up. The text is uncontrolled by default; pass value and onValueChange to clear it after a send or to keep a draft.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The title's element: "h2" inside a page that has its own h1 (the default), "h1" when the hero opens the page.

props.name: description

props.name: examplesLabel

props.name: errorMessage

entries.name: property-search-hero
entries.title: Property search hero
entries.description: A real-estate opening with Buy, Rent and Sold tabs over one search row: place, price range, bedrooms and popular places with counts.

components.name: PropertySearchHero

Switching tab swaps the price steps (rent per month against a purchase price), keeps a price the new list has, clears one it does not, and announces the change politely. The row is one line when there is room, two lines on a tablet and one field per line on a phone, by the width of the panel. A search with no place is allowed and the button says "Search everywhere", so it never ends in nothing. A photograph can sit behind the panel through the `background` slot.

entries.name: recipe-hero

components.name: RecipeHero
components.summary: The top of a recipe, for the visitor who wants the recipe first and the story second. The photo is on one side; beside it the title, a short description, the stars with their count, the author and the date, and the facts that decide whether to cook it tonight: prep, cook, total, servings and difficulty, each with an icon, as one region named Recipe facts. Times are time elements with ISO durations, written "25 min" and spoken "25 minutes". Diet chips follow, and three actions: Jump to recipe, an anchor that skips the story; Save, which reports pressed or not; and Print, which opens the print dialog unless you say otherwise.

entries.docs: Pass the title, a photo with its alt, a description, the author (a name, or { name, href }), publishedAt, the rating ({ value, count, href? }), the facts and the diet chips. facts are prep, cook and total in minutes (total is prep plus cook when you leave it out), servings (a number or words) and difficulty; each one you leave out is left out of the row, which is one region named Recipe facts and then the title, so two recipes on a page are told apart. Times are time elements with ISO durations, written "25 min" and spoken "25 minutes". jumpHref is the id of the recipe further down the page. Save reports aria-pressed: pass saved to control it or defaultSaved to start it saved, and onSave(saved) is where you keep it. Print opens the browser's print dialog unless you pass onPrint. Pass locale and timeZone for the numbers and the date, and labels to translate the fixed words. onSave and on…

components.name: ReservationHero
components.summary: A restaurant's opening with the table first: a tall photograph beside the name, one line and a compact form. The visitor sets the party (a stepper, one to twelve) and a day (starting on today, or the first open day), and the times for that day appear as chips in a toggle group the arrow keys move through. A time that is taken stays in the row, disabled and tagged "Full" in words. Whenever the party or the day changes the chips are asked for again, and a polite message says what is shown: "Showing 4 times for 2 guests on Friday". Until a time is chosen the button waits, and the reason is written under it. "Today" is the restaurant's own and is read from the browser's clock once the page is live, so a page built days ago never shows the day it was built: until then the date is a placeholder and the times a skeleton. There is no booking engine in here: you give it the times, and it gives y…

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The name's element: "h2" inside a page that has its own h1 (the default), "h1" when the hero opens the page.

props.name: name
props.doc: The restaurant's name. It is the heading.

props.name: description

props.doc: The photograph, tall, on the left.

props.name: slots
props.doc: The same times for every open day. Use `slotsFor` when they depend on the day or the party.

props.name: slotsFor
props.type: (date: string, party: number) => readonly ReservationSlot[] | Promise<readonly ReservationSlot[]>
props.doc: The times for a day and a party size, from your booking system: an array, or a promise of one. It is asked again whenever the party or the day changes, and an answer that arrives after they have changed again is ignored. It wins over `slots`. A function cannot be passed from a Server Component: use the hero inside a Client Component.

props.name: closedDays
props.doc: The days the restaurant is shut: weekdays (0 is Sunday, 1 is Monday) it is always shut, and dates ("2026-12-25") it is shut on. They cannot be picked, and the date starts on the first open day.

props.name: defaultParty
props.doc: How many guests to start with. Default 2.

props.name: maxParty
props.doc: The largest party the stepper allows. Default 12.

props.name: defaultDate
props.doc: The day to start on, as "2026-11-06". Default: today, or the first open day after it.

props.name: daysAhead
props.doc: How far ahead a table can be reserved, in days. Default 90.

props.doc: The restaurant's own time zone as an IANA name: "Europe/Amsterdam". "Today" is worked out there, not on the visitor's clock. Default "UTC".

props.name: today
props.doc: A fixed day to treat as today ("2026-11-06"), for server HTML, previews and tests. Leave it out and the day is read from the browser's clock once the page is live: until then the date shows its placeholder and the times a skeleton, so a page built days ago never shows the day it was built.

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the dates and times. Default "en-US".

props.name: hourCycle
props.doc: "h23" writes 18:30 whatever the locale, "h12" writes 6:30 PM. Default "h23".

props.name: weekStartsOn
props.doc: Which day the calendar's week starts on: 1 for Monday (the default), 0 for Sunday.

props.name: onReserve
props.doc: Called when the visitor presses Reserve with a time chosen. The booking is yours: this only hands you the choice. If it returns a promise, the button shows it is busy until the promise settles; handle errors inside it.

props.doc: Words for the fixed text, for a site that is not in English.

entries.docs: Pass slots (the same times every day) or slotsFor(date, party), which may return a promise. Dates are plain yyyy-mm-dd strings in the restaurant's own calendar and times are the strings you give; closedDays takes weekdays (0 is Sunday) and dates. Answers that arrive late for a party or date that has since changed are ignored. onReserve({ party, date, time }) is where your booking starts. Today is the restaurant's own day in timeZone and is read from the browser's clock once the page is live: until then the date shows its placeholder and the times a skeleton, so a page built days ago never shows the day it was built. Pass today ("2026-11-06") to pin it for server HTML, tests and previews. slotsFor and onReserve are functions, so use the hero inside a Client Component.

entries.name: service-start-hero
entries.title: Service start hero
entries.description: The start page of a service: what it is, how long it takes, what to have ready and one clear Start button, in plain text with no image.

components.name: ServiceStartHero
components.summary: The page a service starts on, with nothing else on it: what the service is, how long it takes, one large Start button, and a list of what to have ready so nobody gets halfway and has to stop. Other ways to apply are one quiet line, and the date the page was last checked sits in a time element. Everything is text and one link, set in the strongest contrast the theme has, with no image to load or wait for. For public bodies, insurers, banks and any flow people dread, where clarity beats persuasion.

props.name: title
props.doc: What the service is, in the words people use for it: "Apply for a resident parking permit".

props.name: lead
props.doc: One or two sentences: who it is for, what happens at the end and how soon.

props.name: start
props.doc: The one action. It is a link to the first step of the service, so it works without script and opens in a new tab like any link.

props.name: duration
props.doc: How long the service takes, written as a sentence: "Takes about 10 minutes". It sits beside the button and is read with it.

props.name: requirements
props.doc: What to have ready before the first step, in the order it is asked for.

props.name: alternatives
props.doc: Other ways to reach the same result, as a quiet line of links under the list.

entries.name: timetable-hero
entries.title: Timetable hero
entries.description: A studio opening with today's sessions in a row of tiles: time, class, coach and spots left, each a link to book.

components.name: TimetableHero
components.summary: Today's classes for a studio, as a row of tiles that does the arithmetic: the start in large tabular figures, the class and its coach, and the places left as a thin meter with the number beside it. A full class says "Full, join waitlist" and a class that has begun is dimmed and tagged Started, both in words, so no state is carried by tone alone. Every tile is one link. The day and the times are worked out in the studio's own time zone, so a visitor on the other side of the world sees the studio's day; when the last class of today has begun, the row shows the first class of the next day and says so. The row scrolls sideways with snap on small screens, and opens on the first class that has not begun. For gyms, yoga studios, dance schools and climbing halls.

The hero shows today's sessions in the studio's zone and, when none are left, the first one of the next day with sessions. Leave `now` out and the browser's clock is read once the page is live; pass it for server HTML, tests and previews. On a small screen the row opens on the first class that has not begun, so the next one you can book leads.

Where they still do not fit, such as on a phone, the marks scroll sideways and snap instead of wrapping into a second row, the edge with more past it fades out so it is plain that there is …

entries.docs: Pass title, actions, proofLabel ("Trusted by 4,200 teams"), logos (the Logo shape of LogoCloud: a name, a mark and an optional link) and, optionally, eyebrow, description and a rating with a score, a count and a source. The hero is at least 100svh tall with the strip pinned to its foot, so the proof is on the first screen; pass a min-h class that takes a header's height off when a bar sits above it. From 1280px the label, the six marks and the rating share one line; below that the label and the rating share a line above the marks. Where the marks still do not fit, such as on a phone, they scroll sideways and snap instead of wrapping, the edge with more past it fades out so it is plain there is more, and the strip is a stop for the keyboard only while there is something to scroll. Each mark is named for a screen reader and reaches full strength on hover and focus, and nothing animates.

entries.name: ui-snippets-hero
entries.title: UI snippets hero
entries.description: A product opening where small interface cards flank a centred headline, instead of one big screenshot underneath.

components.name: UiSnippetsHero
components.summary: A product opening where small interface cards flank a centred headline, in place of one big screenshot underneath. Each side holds two or three cards described by data (a task with its assignee and due date, a comment with a reply field, an activity toast, a status card) and drawn with the real checkbox, badge and avatar, so they look like the product. The cards float at different heights and are moved sideways by a few plain CSS translations, with one soft shadow; on wide screens they bleed a little past the content. To a screen reader they are one sentence, they are inert, and nothing in them depends on a pointer. Below 1024px they gather in a quiet stack under the actions, two columns on a tablet and, on a phone, the first two cards of each side in one column. A calm alternative to a hero image for collaboration and workflow tools: no glow, no glass and no gradient.

A card is a task (a title, an assignee, a due date, a label, done), a comment (an author, text, a time, a reply placeholder), an activity toast (a sentence and a time) or a status card (a title, a status, progress and a detail line). They are drawn with the real checkbox, badge and avatar, float at different heights with plain CSS translations and one soft shadow, and bleed a little past the content on wide screens. The cards are hidden and inert, and a screen reader hears one sentence for each (or your summary). components.name: BreadcrumbBar
components.summary: One slim row between the header and the content: where this page sits on the left, a slot for page actions on the right, and when it last changed. From md up the left side is the full ordered trail ending in the current page (aria-current), with the middle folded into a menu once it is longer than maxItems; below md it is one Back link to the parent, which is what people want on a phone. The trail has priority over everything else on the row: its crumbs never wrap, and when the row runs short only the current page gives way and ends in an ellipsis. It is deliberately smaller than SubpageHeader, for sites that need orientation without a title band. No state of its own, so it renders on the server.

entries.title: Docs header
entries.description: The top bar of a documentation site: brand, a row of section links, a search field and icon links, folding into a menu on a phone.

components.name: DocsHeader
components.summary: The top bar of a documentation site, in two rows. The first holds the mark, a search field that is really a button opening your own palette (with the right shortcut for the platform, and an icon button in its place below sm), icon links to the repository and the community, and a slot for a theme or version control. The second lists the top-level sections with the current one underlined. The sections are plain links with aria-current, not an ARIA tablist, because each one goes to another page. Under md the section row scrolls sideways with fade edges and the icon links fold into one menu. Pairs with a docs sidebar on the left and an on-this-page rail on the right. onSearchOpen is a function, so use the header from a Client Component, next to the palette it opens.

The sections are plain links, not an ARIA tablist, because each one goes to another page. onSearchOpen opens your own command palette from the field and from the shortcut (shortcutKey, Ctrl or Command and K), so use the header from a Client Component, next to the palette. links are icon links to the repository or the community: they open in a new tab and say so, and below md they fold into one menu. children is one compact control at the end of the first row, a theme toggle or a version select, and it stays on a phone. Below md each column is a button with aria-expanded and a plus or a minus, and defaultOpen lists the titles that start open. The desktop heading and the phone button are separate elements, and the links are in the page either way, closed or not. Columns animate their height and snap open under reduced motion. aside is a slot beside the brand (a newsletter, a status link), social takes icon or text profiles, and legal with legalLinks fills the bottom bar. Pass linkAs={Link} for your router's links, and navLabel and labels to translate the fixed words.

Three short groups (product, company, legal) stay together instead of floating in three sparse columns, links wrap with no fixed column count, and on a phone each label sits above its links. Pass linkAs={Link} for your router's links, and navLabel and labels to translate the fixed words. Where FooterSection spreads groups across columns and FooterMinimal gives everything one row, this suits a few short groups: product, company, legal.

components.name: FooterRegionSelector

On a phone the group becomes one button that opens a dialog with the same three fields, so the footer stays short. entries.docs: options lists the countries (leave countries out for all of them), the suggested countries that come first, the languages, each named in itself, and the currencies. Control it with region and onRegionChange, or let it keep the state with defaultRegion; either way the callback gets the full triple { country, language, currency } on every change and nothing navigates. The summary line says the choice in words, and the country names come from Intl.DisplayNames in the language of locale. Below md the group is one button, named by the summary, that opens a dialog with the same three fields. onRegionChange is a function, so use the footer from a Client Component or pass a Server Action. labels translates every visible word, the headings and the empty message of the country list included, navLabel names the footer navigation, and linkAs renders your router's Link.

entries.name: locale-suggestion-bar
entries.title: Locale suggestion bar
entries.description: A polite bar that offers the local version of the site once, with Switch and Stay actions, and leaves remembering the answer to you.

components.name: LocaleSuggestionBar
components.summary: A polite bar that offers the version of the site in the visitor's language, once: a short question in that language, a primary Switch button, a quiet Stay button and a close. It never redirects by itself and never guesses from an IP address: you decide when to show it, for instance when Accept-Language differs from the page, and you store the answer. It is a region whose lang is the suggested language, so a screen reader pronounces the question right, and the type asks for every word of the bar (the question and the names of the three buttons), so none is left in English by accident. Translations run long: when the buttons do not fit side by side, Stay drops under Switch. It slides in once, instantly under reduced motion, and any choice removes it for good. The callbacks are functions, so use the bar from a Client Component, or pass Server Actions.

props.name: current
props.doc: The version the visitor is on now. It is handed back to onStay so you can store it.

props.name: suggested
props.doc: The version you offer, and the question and button words in its own language.

props.name: onSwitch
props.doc: Called when the visitor takes the offer, as the link is followed. Store the choice here.

props.name: onStay
props.doc: Called when the visitor keeps the version they are on. Store the choice here, and do not show the bar again.

props.name: onDismiss
props.doc: Called when the visitor closes the bar without choosing.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the Switch link. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

entries.docs: Decide when to show it, for instance when Accept-Language names a language you have a version in and the page is another, and store the answer yourself: the bar never redirects, never guesses from an IP address and removes itself on any choice, so render it only if you have not asked before. suggested carries the question and the words of the buttons in the suggested language (switchLabel, stayLabel and closeLabel are all required, so nothing on the bar is left in English by accident), and its code becomes the lang of the region, so every word on the bar is pronounced right. When the buttons do not fit side by side on a narrow screen, Stay drops under Switch instead of being cut off. Switch is a link to suggested.href, so linkAs can be your router's Link; onSwitch, onStay (which gets current) and onDismiss are where you store the choice. The bar slides in once, and instantly under reduc…

components.name: MobileNavDrilldown
components.summary: The phone menu that navigates the way a native app does. A menu button opens a sheet from the left that holds a stack of panels: the root lists your groups, and a group with links slides them in as a panel of its own, with a Back row that names where it returns to. Focus moves to the first row of a panel that opens and back to the group's row when you return, Escape goes up a level and only then closes the sheet, and the panels you cannot see are inert, so their links are never tabbable. Reduced motion swaps the slide for an instant change. Better than folding groups open in place once a group holds more than six links. The sheet starts over at the root each time it opens, and every link closes it. onOpenChange is a function, so use the menu from a Client Component if you control it.

props.name: className

entries.docs: Pass brand, the groups and, if you like, actions (sign in, start free) and current, the href of the page you are on. A group with links opens as a panel of its own; a group without links is a plain link, and one with links and an href offers an All row first that leads to the group's own page. Every link closes the sheet. Escape goes up a level before it closes the sheet, Up, Down, Home and End move between the rows, and the panels you cannot see are inert, so their links are never tabbable. DrilldownMenu is the same menu without the sheet, for a container of your own, and defaultGroup opens one panel first. The menu button is shown at every width: pass className="md:hidden" to hide it from md up, or trigger to use a button of your own. open, defaultOpen and onOpenChange control the sheet, labels translates the fixed words, and linkAs renders your router's Link. onOpenChange is a functi…

components.name: NavbarCenteredLogo
components.summary: A navbar with the mark in the middle: links on the left, actions on the right and the brand on the true centre of the bar, because the three zones are one grid and a long list of links never pushes it off. Props match Navbar, so one can replace the other, and groups open as panels in the shared navigation menu. The current page is marked with aria-current and a thin underline that grows from the centre on hover and focus. The links only sit beside the mark where they fit: below md for up to three links, below lg for four and below xl for more (foldBelow sets it), they move into a sheet opened from a menu button on the left, so they do not run over the mark. The brand stays centred, and below md the actions fold into one icon button on the right. For fashion, hospitality and editorial brands, where the mark is the loudest thing on the bar. No state of its own, so it renders on the server.

entries.name: navbar-onepage
entries.title: One-page navbar
entries.description: A navbar for single-page sites: section links that scroll to their section, the current one marked, and one call to action.

components.name: NavbarOnepage
components.summary: The navbar for a site that lives on one page: the mark on the left (it scrolls to the top), a link to each section in the middle, with the one in view marked as you scroll, and a call to action on the right. Links are real fragment links, so they work before any script loads; give each section a scroll-margin as tall as the bar (scroll-mt-20 for the default offset) so they also clear it when a visitor arrives with the hash in the address. On a phone the links move into a sheet that closes itself when one is chosen and then moves focus to that section's heading. Scrolling is smooth, and instant under reduced motion. For tradespeople, studios and event pages.

props.name: brand
props.doc: Your mark. It is wrapped in a link that takes the reader back to the top.

props.name: brandHref
props.doc: Where the mark links. "#top" scrolls to the top of the page, with or without an element of that id. Pass "/" with your router's Link to leave the page.

props.name: brandLabel
props.doc: The accessible name of the mark's link, when the mark is only a picture.

props.name: sections
props.doc: The sections of the page, in order: each link scrolls to the element with that id.

props.name: action
props.doc: The call to action: on the right, and at the foot of the phone menu. A link to a section (href="#contact") scrolls like the rest.

props.name: offset
props.doc: The pixels the bar covers. A section counts as current once its top passes this line, and a link scrolls it to rest just below. Match it to the scroll-margin of your sections.

props.name: currentId
props.doc: The section to mark as current. Leave it out and the bar follows the scroll.

props.name: onNavigate
props.doc: Called with the id of the section a link took the reader to.

props.name: linkAs
props.doc: Renders the mark's link. Defaults to "a"; pass your router's Link.

props.name: sticky
props.doc: Keep the bar at the top of the window as the page scrolls. On by default.

props.name: menuLabel
props.doc: The name of the menu button, and the title of the sheet it opens on a phone.

props.name: navLabel
props.doc: The name of the navigation landmark, for a site that is not in English or a page with two bars.

entries.docs: Give sections as an id and a label each, in the order they appear; every link is a real fragment link, so it works before script loads. Give each section scroll-mt-20 (as tall as offset, 80px by default) so a visitor who arrives with the hash in the address also clears the bar. The section in view is marked with aria-current="location" as you scroll; pass currentId to mark one yourself. A click scrolls smoothly (instantly under reduced motion), moves focus to the section's heading and calls onNavigate. On a phone the links are in a sheet that closes itself before the scroll. The mark links to brandHref ("#top" scrolls to the top and drops the hash of the section you were in); a call to action with href="#contact" scrolls like the rest. onNavigate is a function, so use the bar from a Client Component.

entries.name: navbar-transparent
entries.title: Transparent navbar
entries.description: A navbar that sits over the hero with no background and turns solid with a hairline as soon as the page scrolls.

components.name: NavbarTransparent
components.summary: A navbar that sits over the hero with no background of its own, so the hero fills the screen, and turns solid with a hairline as soon as the page has scrolled past a threshold (24px by default). One passive scroll listener sets data-scrolled on the header for your own styling, and the state starts from the real scroll position. Text keeps AA contrast in both states: with tone "light" the bar is light on the photograph and takes the foreground token once solid. The phone menu opens on a solid sheet, so links never sit directly on an image, and under reduced motion the change is instant. Put a dark hero under it, or pass tone="dark" over a light one.

props.name: actions
props.doc: Sign in, a call to action: shown on the right, and at the foot of the phone menu.

props.name: tone
props.doc: What the bar sits on at rest: "light" is light text over a dark hero (the default), "dark" is dark text over a light one.

props.name: threshold
props.doc: How far the page scrolls, in px, before the bar turns solid.

entries.docs: The bar is fixed to the top of the window and see-through at rest, so put it over a hero that is already dark (tone="light", the default) or light (tone="dark"). Once the page has scrolled past threshold (24px) it takes the page colour and a hairline. One passive scroll listener sets data-scrolled on the header for your own styling, and the state starts from the real scroll position. At rest with a light tone the text is white and the bar speaks the dark theme's tokens, so buttons you pass as actions are legible on a photograph; a theme with no dark tokens should give those buttons colours of their own. Once solid the bar hands everything back to the page. The phone menu opens on a solid sheet; navLabel names the navigation landmark, and menuLabel the menu button and the title of the sheet. In a layout that scrolls inside a container, the bar follows that container instead of the window…

components.name: NavbarTwoRow
components.summary: A header in two rows, for shops, marketplaces and publishers with more than six sections: the mark, a search field in the middle and the account links on top, the main categories underneath with the current one underlined and a trailing link to everything. On scroll the first row slips away and only the categories stay pinned, so the bar costs about 48px of height instead of 112px; that is plain CSS (a sticky bar with a negative top, the fixed height of the first row), so it needs no script and no scroll listener and your mark must fit that height. Under md the search field takes a row of its own and the categories become one scrolling line with fade edges and the current category scrolled into view. Keyboard focus on the first row brings it back into view: the whole bar unpins while keyboard focus is inside that row (CSS :has and :focus-visible, still no script), and pins again as soon…
