entries.docs: Put the search field in search (a SearchTrigger, a form), the account, help and bag in utilities and the categories in categories; catalogue is the trailing link to everything. The header is sticky with a negative top, the height of the first row, so on scroll the first row slides away and only the categories stay: plain CSS, no scroll listener. While keyboard focus is inside the first row the whole bar unpins (CSS :has and :focus-visible), so a control you tab to is never out of sight above the window, and it pins again as soon as focus moves on. It counts on the first row's fixed height (56px on a phone, 48px more with the search row, 64px from md), so keep your mark within it, and it works when the header sits in the container that scrolls, the page or a layout of your own. entries.docs: The field is a real button: it calls onSearchOpen, so open your own command palette or search overlay there and the bar keeps no search logic. It shows the shortcut for the platform (the Command symbol on a Mac, Ctrl elsewhere) with the letter from shortcutKey, and the shortcut works anywhere on the page, also below lg where the field gives way to an icon button named by searchLabel. Under md the links move into a sheet with the actions at its foot. onSearchOpen is a function, so use the bar from a Client Component, next to the palette it opens. components.summary: A smart banner for phones that points to your app in a store: its icon, its name and a line about it, a star rating with the count of reviews, one button that reads Get or Open depending on whether the app is installed, and a close. It is for apps that live in a store, with a link to the store page, and not for installing a web app, which is a different prompt. It shows on phones only by default, and it is padded for the notch and the home indicator when the page uses viewport-fit=cover. Closing hands the choice back to you, so you can keep it away for thirty days. The rating is words as well as stars: "Rated 4.8 out of 5 from 12,400 reviews".

entries.docs: Give it the name, a pitch, the icon (or let it draw a monogram of the name), the rating with its count, and storeHref. When you know the app is installed, pass installed and openHref, a deep link such as atlas://home: the button then reads Open. onAction tells you which button was followed, and onDismiss is where you store the choice and keep the banner away for thirty days; the banner hides itself when it is closed. showOn is "phones" by default (below 640px), "tablets" (below 1024px) or "all", and position says which page edge it sits on, "top" or "bottom": it picks the border side and pads the banner for the notch or the home indicator when the page sets viewport-fit=cover, while you place the banner in your layout yourself. The status is text first and a dot second, so it never leans on colour. On a phone only the phone link and the status stay; the rest belong in the main menu, and a bar left with nothing to show on a phone is not drawn at all. The bar stays one row from a tablet up: the email makes way for the links between md and lg. It is deliberately not an announcement: it is calm, not inverted, and holds only what is true every day. No state of its own, so it renders on the server.

entries.docs: Give it phone, email, status and links. The phone and the email are tel: and mailto: links whose text is the number and the address themselves, so they can be read, copied and printed; phoneHref sets another tel: address for a number with an extension. status is the shape OpeningHours takes, { open, text }, worked out on your side from your clock in the business's time zone: the bar shows your words with a filled dot when open and a hollow one when closed, so it never leans on colour. Below sm only the phone and the status show; the email appears from sm and the links, which belong in the main menu on a phone, from md. Between md and lg the email makes way for the links, so the bar stays one row on a tablet, and it returns from lg. entries.name: top-loading-bar
entries.title: Top loading bar
entries.description: A thin bar across the top that races to 80 percent while a page or action is pending, then sweeps to the end and fades. Work shorter than a delay never shows it.

components.name: TopLoadingBar
components.summary: The route-change and async-action indicator: a thin bar that races to about 80 percent while something is pending, keeps creeping so it never looks stuck, then sweeps to the end and fades when the work is done. Pass `active` from a transition or a form action. Work shorter than `delay` never shows the bar at all. It is announced once as a polite status, and under reduced motion it is a still line that appears and disappears.

props.name: active
props.doc: True while a navigation, request or action is pending.

props.name: tone
props.doc: `default` follows the text colour, `muted` is quieter, `destructive` marks a run that is failing.

props.name: height
props.doc: Thickness of the bar in pixels.

props.name: delay
props.doc: Milliseconds of pending work to ignore, so a fast response never flashes the bar.

props.name: label
props.doc: What a screen reader hears while the bar is showing.

entries.docs: Pass active from a router transition, a form action or a pending flag; mount one bar near the top of the layout. It is fixed to the viewport by default: give it className="absolute" inside a relatively positioned panel. The bar waits delay milliseconds (150 by default) before it shows, so fast work never flashes it, and it is announced once as a polite status with the label you give it. Under reduced motion it is a still line that appears and disappears. Switch tone to destructive just before a failing run ends.

entries.name: auto-height
entries.title: Auto height
entries.description: A container that glides to its new height when its content changes, for form steps, inline errors and swapped panels, without ever clipping a focus ring.

components.name: AutoHeight
components.summary: A container that glides to its new height instead of jumping, for form steps, inline errors, swapped panels and anything else that grows or shrinks. It watches its content with a ResizeObserver, so it follows images that load and text that wraps as well as your own state changes. Height is only pinned while it moves: afterwards it is `auto` again and overflow is released, so focus rings and shadows are never clipped. Reduced motion applies the change at once.

props.name: children
props.doc: The content whose height changes.

props.name: duration
props.doc: Milliseconds the height takes to settle.

props.name: as
props.doc: The element to render.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Switch the animation off and let the height change at once.

entries.docs: Wrap the part of a layout whose height changes. A ResizeObserver watches the content, so it follows your own state, images that load and text that wraps. Height is pinned only while it moves; afterwards it is auto again and overflow is released, so focus rings and shadows are never clipped. Give it aria-live="polite" when what appears is a message (an inline error), and keep the element mounted so the region exists before its content does. Reduced motion applies the change at once; pass disabled to turn the glide off.

entries.name: count-up
entries.title: Count up
entries.description: A number that counts up from zero the first time it is mostly on screen, with prefix, suffix, decimals and locale, and the final value in the page from the start.

components.name: CountUp
components.summary: A number that counts up the first time it is mostly on screen: for the figures on a stats band, a pricing claim or a results page. The final value is in the page from the first render, for screen readers, search engines and print, and the visible digits sit in a box as wide as that final value, so nothing shifts while they run. Reduced motion, a browser without IntersectionObserver, or a number that is already on screen when the page hydrates simply show the final value.

props.name: value
props.doc: The number to count to.

props.name: from
props.doc: Where the count starts.

props.name: duration
props.doc: Milliseconds the count takes.

props.name: delay
props.doc: Milliseconds to wait after the number has scrolled into view.

props.name: prefix
props.doc: Text before the number: "$".

props.name: suffix
props.doc: Text after the number: "%", "k", " orders".

props.name: decimals
props.doc: Digits after the decimal point.

props.name: locale
props.doc: BCP 47 locale for digits and separators. Pass your application locale.

props.name: format
props.doc: More number formatting, such as `{ notation: "compact" }`. Set after `decimals`, so it wins.

props.name: once
props.doc: Count once (the default), or count again every time the number comes back into view.

entries.docs: The final value is in the page from the first render, in text for screen readers, search engines and print; the visible digits sit in a box as wide as that value, so nothing shifts while they run. It counts when 40 percent of the number is on screen. A number that is already on screen when the page hydrates keeps its final value, one that mounts in the browser always counts. Reduced motion and browsers without IntersectionObserver show the final value at once. Pass your application locale.

entries.name: crossfade
entries.title: Crossfade
entries.description: Swap content with a soft crossfade and no layout jump: tab panels, loaded states and changing values, with the leaving content made inert.

components.name: Crossfade
components.summary: Swaps content with a soft crossfade and no jump: tab panels, a skeleton becoming its content, a step in a form. Old and new share one grid cell, so while they overlap the container is as tall as the taller of the two; put an AutoHeight around it when the two differ and the rest of the page should glide instead of snapping at the end. The leaving content is made inert and hidden from assistive technology at once, the new content takes focus only when `moveFocus` asks for it, and reduced motion swaps instantly.

props.name: activeKey
props.doc: Identifies what is showing. When it changes, the content fades over to the new children.

props.name: children
props.doc: The content for the current key. Only this is rendered; the previous content stays until it has faded out.

props.name: duration
props.doc: Milliseconds of each fade.

props.name: mode
props.doc: `overlap` fades both at once; `wait` lets the old content leave before the new arrives.

props.name: moveFocus
props.doc: Move focus to the new content after a change, for a step or panel the reader has just asked for.

entries.docs: Render the content for the current key as children and change activeKey when it changes; the previous content stays mounted just long enough to fade out. Old and new share one grid cell, so during the fade the box is as tall as the taller of the two. When the heights differ, wrap Crossfade in AutoHeight so the rest of the page glides to the new height instead of snapping once the fade ends. The leaving content is inert and hidden from assistive technology the moment it starts leaving. Pass moveFocus to move focus to the new content after a change. mode="wait" lets the old content leave before the new arrives. Reduced motion swaps instantly.

entries.name: fade-in
entries.title: Fade in
entries.description: A wrapper that fades and lifts its content in once when it enters view, with direction, delay and duration. Visible without JavaScript and under reduced motion.

components.name: FadeIn
components.summary: A once-only entrance for any block: it fades in and rises a few pixels the first time it is on screen, on its own clock. Reveal follows the scroll; FadeIn plays and is done, which suits cards and copy the reader will not scrub. The server renders it fully visible, so there is no hidden content without JavaScript and none before hydration; a block that is already on screen when the page hydrates simply stays, and one that mounts in the browser (a route change, a conditional) always plays. Only opacity and transform move, so layout never shifts, and reduced motion and print show everything at rest.

props.name: direction
props.doc: The way the block travels as it arrives: `up` rises into place, `left` slides in from the right.

props.name: distance
props.doc: Travel in pixels.

props.name: delay
props.doc: Milliseconds to wait once the block is visible: the way to line a row of them up.

props.name: duration
props.doc: Milliseconds the entrance takes.

props.name: once
props.doc: Play once (the default), or play again every time the block comes back into view.

props.name: amount
props.doc: How much of the block (0 to 1) must be on screen before it plays.

props.name: as
props.doc: The element to render.

entries.docs: Reveal is tied to the scroll position; FadeIn plays on its own clock, which suits cards and copy the reader will not scrub. The server renders the block fully visible, so nothing is hidden without JavaScript or before hydration. A block that is already on screen when the page hydrates stays as it is; one that mounts in the browser, such as a route change or a conditional, always plays. Use delay to line a row of blocks up. Only opacity and transform move, so layout never shifts, and reduced motion and print show everything at rest.

entries.name: fill-bar
entries.title: Fill bar
entries.description: A labelled bar that fills to its value when it scrolls into view, for skills, quotas and survey results, built on Progress so the real value is always in the page.

components.name: FillBar
components.summary: A labelled bar that fills to its value when it scrolls into view, for skills, quotas and survey results. It is the Progress primitive underneath, so the progressbar role and the real value are in the page from the first render and only the drawing animates. Bars in a list stagger through `order`; reduced motion, and a bar that is already on screen when the page hydrates, show the final width at once.

props.name: value
props.doc: How far along it is. A value past `max` draws a full bar, one below zero an empty bar, and the text still shows the real number.

props.name: max
props.doc: The value that means full.

props.name: label
props.doc: What the bar measures: "TypeScript", "API requests".

props.name: showValue
props.doc: Show the value at the right of the label.

props.name: format
props.doc: How the value reads: "percent" (62%), "value" (7,420) or "fraction" (7,420 of 10,000).

props.name: valueText
props.doc: Replaces the value text entirely, for anything the formats do not cover: "7.2 of 10 GB".

props.name: locale
props.doc: BCP 47 locale for the numbers. Pass your application locale.

props.name: duration
props.doc: Milliseconds the fill takes.

props.name: order
props.doc: Position in a list of bars: each step starts the fill a little later, so a group lands in sequence.

props.name: tone
props.doc: `muted` is for the bars that are not the point, `destructive` for a limit that has been hit.

props.name: once
props.doc: Fill once (the default), or fill again every time the bar comes back into view.

entries.usage:
import { IconRefresh } from "@rhs-ui/icons"; import { Button } from "@rhs-ui/primitives/button"; import { FillBar } from "@rhs-ui/motion/fill-bar"; const SURVEY = [ { label: "Very easy", value: 54 }, { label: "Easy", value: 28 }, { label: "Neutral", value: 11 }, { label: "Hard", value: 5 }, { label: "Very hard", value: 2 }, ] as const; export default function Demo(): React.JSX.Element { const [run, setRun] = useState(0); return (

Fill on view

Bars fill once, in turn, when they scroll into view.

Plan usage

Northwind Pro, renews on 1 November.

How was onboarding?

Survey of 1,204 new customers.

{SURVEY.map((row, index) => ( ))}
); }
entries.docs: It renders the Progress primitive, so the progressbar role, its name and the true value are present from the first render and only the drawing animates. Give bars in a group an increasing order to land them in sequence. format is percent, value or fraction; pass valueText for anything else ("7.2 of 10 GB"). Use tone="muted" for the rows that are not the point and tone="destructive" for a limit that has been hit, and say so in the value text too. A value past max draws a full bar and one below zero an empty bar, while the text still shows the real number. Reduced motion, and a bar already on screen when the page hydrates, show the final width at once.

entries.name: stagger-list
entries.title: Stagger list
entries.description: A list whose items enter one after another when it scrolls into view, with a step, a cap on the wait and real list semantics that stay intact.

components.name: StaggerList
components.summary: A list whose items arrive one after another when it scrolls into view. It renders the element you choose and leaves its children alone, so a ul or ol keeps its role and its item count for assistive technology (it carries an explicit role="list", because Safari with VoiceOver drops the semantics of a list that has no bullets). Each child gets an index-based delay that is capped by `maxDelay`. The server renders every item visible, so nothing is hidden before hydration or without JavaScript; a list already on screen when the page hydrates stays as it is, and one that mounts in the browser always plays. Reduced motion and print show every item at once.

props.name: step
props.doc: Milliseconds between one item starting and the next.

props.name: maxDelay
props.doc: The longest any item waits, so a long list never makes anyone wait.

props.name: duration
props.doc: Milliseconds each item takes to arrive.

props.name: direction
props.doc: The way items travel as they arrive: `up` rises into place, `left` slides in from the right.

props.name: distance
props.doc: Travel in pixels.

props.name: once
props.doc: Play once (the default), or play again every time the list comes back into view.

props.name: as
props.doc: The element to render. Use `ul` or `ol` for list semantics and give it `li` children.

entries.docs: Render it as ul or ol and give it li children; it adds no wrapper, and a ul or ol carries an explicit role="list", so assistive technology (Safari with VoiceOver included) still announces the list and its item count. Each child waits index times step milliseconds, never longer than maxDelay. Any element can be an item. The server renders every item visible; a list already on screen when the page hydrates stays as it is, one that mounts in the browser always plays. Reduced motion and print show every item at once.

entries.name: drag-scroll
entries.title: Drag scroll
entries.description: A horizontal strip you can drag with a mouse, with optional snap and edge arrows, and full keyboard support. Touch keeps its native scroll.

components.name: DragScroll
components.summary: A horizontal strip of cards, chips or thumbnails that also scrolls by grabbing it with a mouse or pen, with a short glide when you let go, or by snapping to the next item when `snap` is on. A drag never clicks the item under it. Touch keeps its native scrolling; the strip is a labelled region that scrolls by item with the arrow keys, Home and End; the wheel moves it sideways only while the pointer is over it, no modifier is held and there is room to move, so the page is never trapped.

props.name: children
props.doc: The items in the strip: cards, chips or thumbnails. Give them a width; they never shrink.

props.name: label
props.doc: Names the strip for assistive technology. It is a focusable region you can scroll with the arrow keys.

props.name: snap
props.doc: Settle on the start edge or the centre of an item as you scroll.

props.name: gap
props.doc: Space between items, in pixels.

props.name: arrows
props.doc: Previous and next buttons at the edges. They appear only on devices with a fine pointer, and only where there is more to scroll.

props.name: className
props.doc: Styles the wrapper. Every other prop goes to the scrolling strip.

entries.docs: Mouse and pen drag the strip with a short glide when released; a drag never clicks the item under it. Touch keeps native scrolling. The strip is a focusable region named by label: arrow keys move by an item, Home and End jump to the ends. The wheel moves it sideways only while the pointer is over it, no modifier is held and there is room that way, so the page is never trapped. snap settles on the start or centre of an item. arrows adds previous and next buttons, shown only on devices with a fine pointer and only where there is more to scroll. className styles the wrapper; other props go to the strip.

entries.name: edge-fade-scroller
entries.title: Edge fade scroller
entries.description: A scroll container that fades its edges only where there is more to scroll, for chip rows, menus and long lists, and never covers text.

components.name: EdgeFadeScroller
components.summary: A scroll box that softens its edges only where there is more to see: chip rows, menus, long lists. The fade is a CSS mask whose width follows the scroll position (a pixel of scroll is a pixel of fade, up to `fadeSize`), so it never covers text or catches a click, grows as you move away from an edge, and is gone when nothing overflows. Scrolling itself is native: keyboard, wheel and touch are untouched, and an item focused with the keyboard scrolls to a spot clear of the fade.

props.name: children
props.doc: The content that scrolls.

props.name: orientation
props.doc: The direction it scrolls.

props.name: fadeSize
props.doc: How wide the fade is, in pixels, once you are at least that far from the edge. Closer in, it is proportionally smaller.

props.name: onReachEnd
props.doc: Called when the scroll reaches the end, once per arrival: load the next page here.

props.name: label
props.doc: Makes the box a labelled region you can focus and scroll with the keyboard. Use it when nothing inside is focusable.

props.name: hideScrollbar
props.doc: Hide the browser scrollbar, as for a row of chips. Defaults to true for horizontal, false for vertical.

entries.docs: The fade is a CSS mask, so it works on any background and never covers text or catches a click. Its width follows the scroll position, so it grows as you leave an edge and is gone when nothing overflows. Scrolling stays native: keyboard, wheel and touch are untouched, and an item focused with the keyboard scrolls to a spot clear of the fade. When nothing inside is focusable, pass label to make the box a labelled region you can scroll with the keyboard; its focus ring is drawn outside the fade. onReachEnd fires once each time the end is reached, for loading the next page. Give a horizontal row a flex layout through className.

entries.name: parallax-layer
entries.title: Parallax Layer
entries.description: A layer that travels at its own pace while the page scrolls past, with optional zoom and turn.

components.name: ParallaxLayer
components.summary: A layer that moves at its own pace while the page scrolls past it, for depth in heroes, product shots and collages. Pure CSS on a view timeline; reduced motion and browsers without scroll timelines keep it in place.

props.name: speed
props.doc: How much faster (positive) or slower (negative) than the page the layer travels. 0.2 is subtle, 0.6 is dramatic.

props.name: zoom
props.doc: Extra scale added by the time the layer leaves the screen: 0.15 grows it by 15% on the way through.

props.name: rotate
props.doc: Turn in degrees over the whole passage.

entries.usage:
import { ParallaxLayer } from "@rhs-ui/motion/parallax-layer"; export default function Demo(): React.JSX.Element { return (

Scroll inside this panel

Depth, not decoration

Every layer at its own pace.

); }
entries.docs: Put layers with different speeds in one relatively positioned section. Keep speeds between -0.6 and 0.6 for text, and use the stronger values for shapes and images. Clip a parent with overflow: clip, never overflow: hidden: a hidden overflow makes that parent the scroll container the timeline follows, and the animation stands still.

entries.name: reading-time-left
entries.title: Reading time left
entries.description: A reading-time readout that counts down as you read an article, from its real word count, ending in a quiet Done. Screen readers hear the total once and are never interrupted.

components.name: ReadingTimeLeft
components.summary: How long an article will still take, counted down as you read: "6 min read" at the top, "4 min left" a little later, a quiet "Done" at the end. It counts the real words of the target and follows the reader's position through it, redrawing at most once a second and never announcing the change, so a screen reader hears the total once and is left alone. It pairs with a progress bar rather than replacing one, and it renders no text on the server.

props.name: target
props.doc: The article: a ref to its element, or a CSS selector. Its words and its scroll position drive the readout.

props.name: wpm
props.doc: Words per minute. Adults read prose at about 230.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words, for another language. `{minutes}` stands for the number.

props.name: format
props.doc: Takes over the text completely.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Locale for the number of minutes.

entries.docs: Point target at the article with a ref or a CSS selector: its words are counted and the reader's position through it drives the readout. It shows the total at the top ("3 min read"), counts the minutes left, and ends on Done. It redraws at most once a second and is never announced; a screen reader gets the total once. It renders no text on the server. It pairs with Scroll progress rather than replacing it. Translate it with labels (use {minutes} for the number) or take over completely with format.

entries.name: render-on-view
entries.title: Render on view
entries.description: Mounts heavy content such as a map, a chart or an embed only when it nears the viewport, holding its space so nothing shifts.

components.name: RenderOnView
components.summary: Holds back heavy content (a map, a chart, an embed) until it is about to be seen. The placeholder reserves the final height, so the page never jumps, and the content mounts a screen early, so it is ready when the reader gets there. A browser without IntersectionObserver renders at once. Keep headings and landmarks outside it: only the expensive part waits, and the outline of the page is always complete.

props.name: children
props.doc: The expensive part: a map, a chart, an embed. Nothing of it renders until the placeholder is near the screen.

props.name: fallback
props.doc: What stands in until then. Defaults to a quiet skeleton that fills the reserved space.

props.name: minHeight
props.doc: Height to hold, in pixels or any CSS length. Match what the content will measure and nothing shifts when it arrives.

props.name: ratio
props.doc: Hold the height by proportion instead, as width / height (16 / 9). Wins over `minHeight`.

props.name: rootMargin
props.doc: How early to start, as a CSS `rootMargin`. The default is one screen above and below, so it is ready on arrival.

props.name: once
props.doc: Keep the content once it has rendered. Turn it off to unmount it again when it is far away; the space is kept.

props.name: onVisible
props.doc: Called each time the content mounts, for analytics or to start a clock.

props.name: forceRender
props.doc: Render now, for print, crawlers and tests. Printing renders everything on its own as well.

entries.docs: Give it the height the content will have, as minHeight or ratio, so the page does not jump when it arrives. Keep headings, landmarks and anything a crawler must read outside it, and use forceRender for print, bots and tests. With once off the content unmounts again when it is far away and the space it measured is kept. Inside a scrolling panel the margin cannot reach past the panel's own edge, so content there mounts as it enters the panel.

entries.name: reveal
entries.title: Reveal
entries.description: Brings an element forward as it scrolls into view, tied to the scroll: rise, tilt, scale, blur or slide.

components.name: Reveal
components.summary: Brings an element forward as it scrolls into view, tied to the scroll itself: scroll back and it steps back. Pure CSS (scroll-driven animations), no JavaScript and no layout shift; the server renders the element at rest, so nothing is hidden before hydration or without support.

props.name: effect
props.doc: How the element arrives. `tilt` swings it forward in 3D, like a screen lifting off the page.

props.name: distance
props.doc: Travel in pixels for rise, tilt, blur and the slides.

props.name: order
props.doc: Position in a row of reveals: each step starts a little later, so a grid lands in sequence.

props.name: range
props.doc: The scroll range as CSS `animation-range`. The default finishes when the element is a third of the way up the screen.

entries.docs: Pure CSS scroll-driven animation: nothing is hidden before hydration, and reduced motion or a browser without scroll timelines shows the element at rest. Give a row of reveals an increasing order to land them in sequence. Clip a parent with overflow: clip, never overflow: hidden: a hidden overflow makes that parent the scroll container the timeline follows, and the animation stands still.

entries.name: scroll-aware-header
entries.title: Scroll aware header
entries.description: A sticky header that hides on the way down and returns on the way up, or condenses, or turns solid, without trapping focus or shifting the page.

components.name: ScrollAwareHeader
components.summary: A sticky header that gets out of the way: it hides on the way down and returns on the way up, or condenses, or turns solid, once the page has scrolled. It never hides while anything inside it has focus, while a menu in it is open, or at the top of the page. It moves on transform only and toggles instantly under reduced motion; the scroll listener is passive and coalesced into one frame. Condensing trades padding for margin, so the page below never shifts.

props.name: behavior
props.doc: `hide` slides away while you scroll down and returns when you scroll up. `condense` shrinks its padding and gains a hairline. `solid` turns from transparent to solid.

props.name: threshold
props.doc: Pixels of scroll before the header reacts. Defaults to 80 for `hide` and 12 for the others.

props.name: offset
props.doc: Pixels to stop short of the top of the scroll area, for something fixed above it.

entries.docs: Make it a direct child of the page or scroll area it should stick in. behavior="hide" slides away while scrolling down and returns on scroll up; condense shrinks its padding and gains a hairline; solid turns from transparent to solid. It never hides at the top, while anything inside it has focus, or while a menu in it is open (an element with aria-expanded="true"). Tabbing into a hidden header brings it back. Only transform animates for hide, and condensing trades padding for margin so the page below never moves. Set the padding with --rhs-header-py and --rhs-header-py-condensed. Scroll handling is passive and runs once per frame; reduced motion toggles instantly.

entries.name: scroll-away
entries.title: Scroll away
entries.description: The exit counterpart to Reveal: hero text and headers fade, lift and soften as they scroll off the top, in pure CSS with no scroll handler.

components.name: ScrollAway
components.summary: The exit counterpart to Reveal: content that fades, lifts and softens as it scrolls off the top, so a hero or a page header makes way instead of being cut by the edge of the screen. Pure CSS on a view timeline, no scroll handler and no layout shift; the server renders the element at rest, and reduced motion or a browser without scroll timelines keeps it fully visible.

props.name: effect
props.doc: How it leaves. `fade` only dims, `lift` rises as it dims, `scale` shrinks away.

props.name: distance
props.doc: Travel in pixels for `lift`, a third of it for `scale`.

props.name: blur
props.doc: Blur in pixels reached by the time it is gone: 0 stays sharp, 6 to 10 softens it.

props.name: range
props.doc: When it runs, as CSS `animation-range`. The default starts as the element reaches the top of the screen and ends when 80% of it has gone.

props.name: asChild
props.doc: Put the effect on your own element (a heading, a link) instead of a wrapping div.

entries.docs: Pure CSS on a view timeline: nothing is hidden before hydration, and reduced motion or a browser without scroll timelines leaves the content fully visible. It ends invisible and, once it has, ignores the pointer, so a link you can still see always works and one that has gone cannot be pressed. Pair it with Reveal (Reveal outside, ScrollAway inside) for something that arrives and leaves with the scroll. It owns opacity, transform and filter while it runs; put your own on a child. Clip a parent with overflow: clip, never overflow: hidden: a hidden overflow makes that parent the scroll container the timeline follows, and the animation stands still.

entries.name: scroll-focus-list
entries.title: Scroll focus list
entries.description: A list where the item at the reading line is at full strength and the rest step back, for steps, features and long lists, always at readable contrast.

components.name: ScrollFocusList
components.summary: A list read at a line. As the reader scrolls, the item crossing a reading line near the middle of the screen is at full strength and the others step back, for steps, features and long lists. It watches a thin band with an IntersectionObserver, so there is no scroll listener, and the current item carries `aria-current`. Text only steps back as far as your muted-foreground, so it stays readable, and the description of the current item steps up toward your foreground while the rest stay put; without JavaScript, or under reduced motion, no item is dimmed.

props.name: items
props.doc: The rows, in reading order.

props.name: lineAt
props.doc: Where the reading line sits, from the top (0) to the bottom (1) of the scroll area.

props.name: dim
props.doc: How far the other items step back, 0 to 1. Their text never goes lighter than your muted-foreground, so contrast stays at AA.

props.name: onActiveChange
props.doc: Called when a different item reaches the reading line.

props.name: render
props.doc: Your own content for an item. The list still owns the state: `aria-current` and `data-active` stay on the row.

props.name: as
props.doc: The element to render. Rows are `li`, or `div` when this is `div`.

entries.docs: It watches a thin band at lineAt (0.45 by default) with an IntersectionObserver, in the nearest scrolling box or the page, so there is no scroll listener. The row at the line gets aria-current and data-active; render lets you draw your own rows and read that state. Other rows step back only as far as your muted-foreground, never lighter, so contrast stays at AA, and the description of the current row steps up toward your foreground; dim sets how far. Space the rows with the --rhs-focus-gap variable, and leave room above the first and below the last so each can reach the line. Under reduced motion the other rows are not dimmed, and without JavaScript nothing is.

entries.name: scroll-progress
entries.title: Scroll Progress
entries.description: A thin reading bar that fills as you scroll the page or a scrolling panel.

components.name: ScrollProgress
components.summary: A thin bar that fills as you read. Place it at the top of the page or of a scrolling panel (it is sticky; position it with className). Driven by a CSS scroll timeline where the browser has one, by a passive scroll listener where it does not. Decorative: hidden from assistive technology.

props.name: source
props.doc: `page` follows the whole document; `nearest` follows the closest scrolling box, for a panel or a reader.

entries.docs: Sticky at the top of its container. Uses a CSS scroll timeline where available and a passive scroll listener elsewhere. Decorative, so hidden from assistive technology.

entries.name: smooth-scroll
entries.title: Smooth scroll
entries.description: Optional eased, inertial scrolling for the page or one box, on Lenis, that never fights the browser: scrollbar, Page keys and anchors still work.

components.name: SmoothScroll
components.summary: Eased, inertial wheel scrolling for the page or for one scrolling box, built on Lenis. It only drives the scroll position the browser already has, so content works if the script fails, and it steps aside for everyone who does not want it: touch screens, reduced motion, nested scrollers, open dialogs. The scrollbar, Page Up and Down, Home and End and anchors keep their native feel, and an ease that is running hands over the moment one of them takes the scroll, so the page never snaps back.

props.name: duration
props.doc: Seconds a wheel step takes to settle, on an expo-out ease. The default 1.2 is unhurried; 0.8 is brisk.

props.name: lerp
props.doc: Instead of a duration: the share of the remaining distance covered each frame, from 0 to 1. 0.1 is gentle, 0.2 is snappy.

props.name: wheelMultiplier
props.doc: Scales how far one wheel notch travels.

props.name: root
props.doc: `true` smooths the page. `false` smooths this element's own scrolling: give it a height with `className`.

props.name: anchors
props.doc: Glide to same-page #links with the same ease, update the address and move focus as a normal jump would.

props.name: enabled
props.doc: Turn the smoothing off without removing the provider. `scrollTo` still works, as a plain jump.

entries.docs: Wrap the app once for page scrolling, or wrap one box with root={false} and give it a height. It eases the wheel only, and turns itself off on touch screens, under reduced motion and when enabled is false; scrollTo then falls back to a plain jump, so a button that calls it never goes dead. It lets go when the scrollbar, Page Down or an anchor takes the scroll mid-ease, pauses while a dialog locks the page, and leaves nested scrollers, menus and dialogs alone; mark any other area with data-lenis-prevent. Do not combine it with CSS scroll-behavior: smooth or scroll snap on the same scroller. Use one page-level provider, and read scrollTo and active with useSmoothScroll.

entries.name: snap-pages
entries.title: Snap pages
entries.description: Full-height sections that snap into place as you scroll, with a dot rail and keyboard paging, on native CSS scroll snap.

components.name: SnapPages
components.summary: Full-height pages that settle into place as you scroll, for product stories and walk-throughs. Native CSS scroll snap does the snapping, so it is as smooth as the browser's own scrolling. A dot rail marks the current page and each dot links to its page; Page Up, Page Down, Home and End move between pages. A page taller than the screen scrolls normally before the next page takes over, and reduced motion softens the snap and ends the gliding.

props.name: pages
props.doc: The pages, top to bottom. Each one is as tall as the screen at least and snaps into place as you scroll.

props.name: indicator
props.doc: Show the dot rail on the right.

props.name: snapType
props.doc: `mandatory` always settles on a page. `proximity` only snaps when you stop close to one. Reduced motion always uses proximity.

props.name: onPageChange
props.doc: Called when another page becomes the current one, not on the first render.

props.name: label
props.doc: Accessible name of the set of pages.

props.name: className
props.doc: Sizes the component; it is one screen tall (`h-dvh`) by default, so give it `h-full` to fill a parent instead.

entries.docs: One screen tall by default (h-dvh); give it h-full to fill a parent. Give each page its own className for a background, and flex items-center to centre what it holds. Keep the right edge of a page free for the dot rail, around 4rem on a phone. A page taller than the screen scrolls normally and the keys follow it: Page Down moves on only when its end is in view. Reduced motion softens mandatory snapping to proximity and switches off gliding.

entries.name: stick-to-bottom
entries.title: Stick to bottom
entries.description: A scroll area for chats and logs that follows new content while you are at the end, and offers a Jump to latest button once you scroll up.

components.name: StickToBottom
components.summary: A scroll area for chats, logs and activity feeds that follows new content for as long as the reader is at the end. Scroll up to read and it stops following, and a button offers the way back with a count of what arrived. A bottom sentinel and a ResizeObserver keep it pinned when content grows after the fact (an image loads, a line wraps). New items are announced politely, but only while it follows; while the reader is away, the count of what arrived is announced instead.

props.name: children
props.doc: The items, oldest first: messages, log lines, events.

props.name: label
props.doc: Accessible name of the log, read when it is focused: "Conversation with Mara".

props.name: onAtBottomChange
props.doc: Called with true when the reader reaches the end and the area starts following again, with false when they scroll away.

props.name: newCount
props.doc: Items that arrived while the reader was away, shown on the button. Leave it out and the items added to your list since they left the end are counted.

props.name: behavior
props.doc: How the area follows new content and how the button scrolls. Reduced motion is always instant.

props.name: jumpLabel
props.doc: The button's words. The default reads "3 new messages", or "Jump to latest" when nothing new has arrived.

entries.docs: Give it a height with className (h-80, or h-full inside a flex column). It follows only while the reader is at the end: scroll up and it lets go, and the button counts what arrived (pass newCount to count yourself, for example when you trim old items). Items are announced politely, and only while it follows; while the reader is away, the count of what arrived is announced as a status instead, at most every few seconds. Growth that arrives later, such as an image that loads, is followed too. A stream that updates many times a second reads best with behavior="instant". To pull the reader to the end after they send something, scroll an element at the end of your list into view. Under reduced motion every jump is instant.

entries.name: sticky-section-header
entries.title: Sticky section header
entries.description: Section headings that stick under the page header while their section scrolls, with a hairline and solid background only when stuck.

components.name: StickySectionHeader
components.summary: The heading of a section in a long grouped list: a changelog by month, contacts by letter, a settings page. It sticks to the top of the scroll area while its section is in view and the next heading pushes it away. It is plain `position: sticky`, so Page Down, find in page and screen magnifiers behave, and the heading keeps its level. A sentinel and one IntersectionObserver tell it when it is stuck, so the bottom hairline and the solid background appear only then, with no scroll handler.

props.name: children
props.doc: The heading text: "March 2026", "B", "Notifications".

props.name: aside
props.doc: Something to put at the end of the bar, outside the heading: a count, a link, an action.

props.name: offset
props.doc: Pixels to stop short of the top of the scroll area, for a fixed navbar above.

props.name: level
props.doc: The heading level of the text.

props.name: as
props.doc: The element of the bar itself.

entries.docs: Put one header at the top of each section, as a direct child of the section: it sticks while its section is in view and the next one pushes it away. It is native position: sticky, so Page Down, find in page and screen magnifiers behave. Set offset to the height of a fixed navbar above. Sticking needs no overflow: hidden between the header and its scroll area; use overflow: clip instead. Give the scroll area a scroll-padding-top equal to the header height so focused items are never hidden behind it.

entries.name: text-reveal
entries.title: Text Reveal
entries.description: A statement that lights up word by word as it scrolls through the screen.

components.name: TextReveal
components.summary: A statement that lights up word by word as it scrolls through the screen, for the one sentence a page is built around. Screen readers get the sentence whole; the words are presentation. Pure CSS on a view timeline; reduced motion and browsers without one show every word at full strength.

props.name: text
props.doc: The sentence to reveal. Plain text: it is split into words.

props.name: dim
props.doc: How dim a word is before its turn, 0 to 1.

entries.docs: For the one sentence a page is built around. Screen readers read the sentence whole. Give it room above and below, so the words have scroll to light up in. Clip a parent with overflow: clip, never overflow: hidden: a hidden overflow makes that parent the scroll container the timeline follows, and the animation stands still.

entries.name: view-video
entries.title: View video
entries.description: A muted video that plays while it is mostly in view and rests when it is not, with a pause button that is always there and a poster.

components.name: ViewVideo
components.summary: A muted loop or product demo that only plays while it is in view. It starts when at least half of it is on screen and pauses when it leaves, or when the tab goes to the background, so it costs no battery or data while nobody watches. Only metadata loads until it is a screen away. A pause button is always there (WCAG 2.2.2), pausing it yourself sticks, and under reduced motion it never starts by itself: the poster stays until you press play.

props.name: src
props.doc: The clip. For several formats use `sources` instead. Pass another file and the new clip loads and plays in its place.

props.name: sources
props.doc: The same clip in more formats, best first: WebM, then MP4 as the fallback. Pass another list and the new clip loads and plays in its place.

props.name: poster
props.doc: A still of the clip. It shows until the clip plays and stands in for it under reduced motion.

props.name: label
props.doc: What the clip shows. It names the video and its pause button.

props.name: loop
props.doc: Loop the clip.

props.name: threshold
props.doc: How much of the video must be on screen before it plays, from 0 to 1.

props.name: controls
props.doc: Add the browser's own controls (seek, volume, fullscreen) next to the pause button.

props.name: ratio
props.doc: Width over height of the frame, 16 / 9 by default. It holds the space before the clip loads.

props.name: onPlayingChange
props.doc: Called with true when the clip starts playing and false when it stops (scrolled away, paused, tab hidden), for a status label or analytics.

entries.docs: For loops and product demos with no sound: the video is always muted and inline. Give it a poster that matches the first frame, so playback starts without a jump, and a label that says what the clip shows. Pass sources with WebM first and MP4 as the fallback. It plays at half visible (threshold), rests off screen and in a background tab, and a pause you press sticks until you press play. Under reduced motion it never starts by itself. Only metadata loads until the video is a screen away. onPlayingChange tells you when it starts and stops, for a status label or analytics. The control stays a dark disc with a light glyph in every theme, so it reads over any frame.

entries.name: add-to-calendar-button
entries.title: Add to calendar button
entries.description: Adds an event to the calendar people use, Google, Outlook, Apple or an .ics file, built from one event object with the time zone handled.

components.name: AddToCalendarButton
components.summary: A button with a menu that turns one event into every format people need: Google Calendar and Outlook open a prefilled form in a new tab, Apple and a plain .ics file are built in the browser (RFC 5545: escaped text, folded lines, times converted to UTC, a UID that stays the same) and downloaded, with no server involved. The menu header repeats the event with its time zone, so nobody has to guess, and each choice says in words whether it opens a tab or downloads a file. An event that cannot be read disables the button and says why next to it. The builders are exported from calendar.ts for testing.

props.name: event
props.doc: The event: title, start, end or durationMinutes, timeZone, location, description, url, allDay.

props.name: providers
props.doc: Which calendars to offer, in this order. Default: Google, Outlook, Apple and an .ics file.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Language of the date and time in the menu header. Default "en-US".

props.name: label
props.doc: The button's text. Default "Add to calendar".

props.name: onAdd
props.doc: Called after a provider is chosen, with which one. The web links and the download start on their own.

props.name: variant
props.doc: Any Button variant. Default "outline".

props.name: size
props.doc: Any Button size.

entries.docs: A start without an offset (2026-11-12T19:00) is read in the event's timeZone; a Date or a string ending in Z or +01:00 is an exact moment. Give end or durationMinutes (default 60). All-day events take a date, and end is the last day. buildIcs, buildGoogleUrl and buildOutlookUrl are pure functions in calendar.ts that return null for an event that cannot be read. Pass uid so an edited event updates the first one in the calendar.

entries.name: approval-buttons
entries.title: Approval buttons
entries.description: Approve and Reject as one decision: a reason when rejecting, who decided and when, and a short window to change your mind.

components.name: ApprovalButtons
components.summary: A decision control for approvals: expenses, pull requests, leave requests. Pending shows Approve and Reject at equal weight; Reject opens a small reason field inline and commits only when it is confirmed (the button, or Ctrl or Cmd with Enter). Once decided, the pair is replaced by a status line ("Approved by Dana Whitfield, 14:20") with a Change decision button that stays for a short window you set, with a thin line running down along its edge; in a narrow space the button drops under the sentence instead of squeezing it. Each action has its own busy and error state, the buttons name their subject ("Approve expense"), and the final state is announced politely. It holds no form of its own, so it can sit inside yours.

props.name: status
props.doc: Controlled: the decision so far. Update it in `onApprove`, `onReject` and `onChangeDecision`.

props.name: defaultStatus
props.doc: Where an uncontrolled control starts. Default "pending".

props.name: onApprove
props.doc: Called when Approve is pressed. The button shows its own busy state; if this rejects, a line says so and nothing is decided.

props.name: onReject
props.doc: Called with the reason when a rejection is confirmed. Same rules as `onApprove`.

props.name: onChangeDecision
props.doc: Called when "Change decision" is pressed: take the decision back and ask again. Uncontrolled, the buttons come back by themselves.

props.name: requireReason
props.doc: A rejection needs a reason. Off, the field is optional. Default true.

props.name: decidedBy
props.doc: Who made the decision, as it reads in the status line. Uncontrolled it names the person pressing; default "you".

props.name: decidedAt
props.doc: When it was decided. Uncontrolled, it is the moment of the press. Without it a decision made elsewhere counts from when this control first sees it. A time given here is always printed with its date, so a page rendered on the server reads the same once it has loaded.

props.name: reason
props.doc: The reason given for a rejection, shown in the status line. Uncontrolled, it is the text that was sent.

props.name: subject
props.doc: What is being decided, for the names: "expense" gives "Approve expense". Default "request".

props.name: undoWindow
props.doc: How many seconds "Change decision" stays available after a decision. 0 turns it off. Default 30.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Language of the time. Default "en-US".

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: Time zone of the time, so the server and the browser agree. Default "UTC".

props.name: size
props.doc: 32, 36 or 44px buttons. Default "default".

entries.docs: Uncontrolled it runs by itself: Approve and Reject call onApprove and onReject (each may return a promise and shows its own busy and error state), then the status line takes over with Change decision for undoWindow seconds. Controlled, pass status, decidedBy, decidedAt and reason, and set status back to pending in onChangeDecision. Reject always asks for a reason first (requireReason makes it required). Pass locale and timeZone so the time reads the same on the server and in the browser. A decision made here shows just the time on the day it was made and adds the date on any other day; a time you pass in decidedAt always carries its date, so a page rendered on the server reads the same once it has loaded. In a narrow space Change decision drops under the sentence. The control holds no form of its own, so it can sit inside yours, and Ctrl or Cmd with Enter confirms a rejection.

entries.name: bulk-select-menu
entries.title: Bulk select menu
entries.description: The header checkbox with a menu for choosing what to select: all, none, unread, starred, with the mixed state and the count in words.

components.name: BulkSelectMenu
components.summary: The select-all control of an inbox, a table or a file list: a checkbox that toggles between all and none and shows a dash while only some rows are chosen, joined to a chevron whose menu offers other ways to choose (All, None, Unread, Starred) with the number each would select. A count in words sits beside it ("12 of 248 selected"), and after every choice a polite message says what was selected. The menu is a real menu: arrow keys move, typing jumps to an item and Escape closes it.

props.name: state
props.doc: How much of the list is selected: nothing, some of it, or all of it.

props.name: onSelectAll
props.doc: Select every row. Runs from the checkbox when nothing is selected, and from the "All" item.

props.name: onSelectNone
props.doc: Clear the selection. Runs from the checkbox when some or all rows are selected, and from the "None" item.

props.name: criteria
props.doc: More ways to choose rows, each with the number it would select.

props.name: total
props.doc: How many rows there are. Shown next to "All" and in the count.

props.name: selectedCount
props.doc: How many rows are selected now, for the count beside the checkbox.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Language of the numbers. Default "en-US".

props.name: label
props.doc: The checkbox's accessible name. Default "Select all".

props.name: menuLabel
props.doc: The chevron's accessible name. Default "Choose what to select".

props.name: showCount
props.doc: Show "12 of 248 selected" beside the control. Default true.

props.name: size
props.doc: The height: 32 or 36px.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Turns the checkbox and the menu off, for a list that is loading or has no rows.

entries.docs: Controlled: derive state (none, some or all) from your own selection and keep the selection in your callbacks. The checkbox runs onSelectAll when nothing is selected and onSelectNone otherwise. Each criterion shows the number it would select and is disabled at 0. After every choice a polite message says what was selected.

entries.name: copy-as-menu
entries.title: Copy as menu
entries.description: Copy the same thing in the format the next tool wants: a split button whose menu offers Markdown, JSON, cURL or plain text and remembers the last choice.

components.name: CopyAsMenu
components.summary: A copy button for data that other tools want in other shapes, like an API response, a console log or a table: Markdown for the README, JSON for the script, cURL for the terminal, CSV for the spreadsheet. The main button copies in the current format and confirms with a check and the format's name ("Copied as cURL"); the chevron opens a menu of formats with one line on what each produces, and picking one copies in it and keeps it as the current format. Formats are made only when asked for, so a large table is turned into CSV only when someone picks CSV. ArrowDown opens the menu, Enter copies, and the result is read out in a live region.

props.name: formats
props.doc: The formats on offer, in menu order. The first one is the default.

props.name: format
props.doc: The current format, controlled. Pair it with `onFormatChange`.

props.name: defaultFormat
props.doc: The format an uncontrolled menu starts with. Default: the first.

props.name: onFormatChange
props.doc: Called with the id when someone picks a format, so the parent can keep the last choice.

props.name: onCopy
props.doc: Called with the format and the text once it is on the clipboard.

props.name: onError
props.doc: Called when the text could not be produced or the browser refused to copy it.

props.name: size
props.doc: The height: 32, 36 or 44px.

props.name: variant
props.doc: The look of both buttons. Default "outline".

props.name: menuLabel
props.doc: The chevron's accessible name. Default "Choose a format to copy as".

entries.docs: Each format's serialize() runs only when someone copies in that format, and may return a promise. Pass format and onFormatChange to keep the last choice yourself (in local storage, say), or defaultFormat to leave it to the button. Picking a format in the menu copies in it at once. Set as on a format when it reads badly after Copy as: "plain text" for Plain text. Formats carry functions, so build them in a client component.

entries.name: copy-field
entries.title: Copy Field
entries.description: A selectable code field with clipboard feedback and an error fallback.

components.name: CopyField
components.extends: { value: string; label?: string; className?: string }

entries.usage:
import { CopyField } from "@rhs-ui/application/copy-field"; export default function Demo(): React.JSX.Element { return

Install a little motion.

; }

entries.name: directions-button
entries.title: Directions button
entries.description: Get directions in the maps app people use: Apple Maps on iPhone, Google Maps elsewhere, Waze if they prefer, and the address to copy as a fallback.

components.name: DirectionsButton
components.summary: A button that hands a place to a maps app. The main button is a real link to the app people use: Apple Maps on an iPhone or iPad, Google Maps everywhere else, worked out after the page has loaded so server and browser markup agree. A small chevron opens the other apps and "Copy address". The place's name goes into the query, so the pin is labelled; links are built by exported pure functions with proper encoding. Every external link says it opens a new tab, and a place without an address or coordinates disables the button and says why.

props.name: destination
props.doc: The place to go to: an address (with its name, so the pin is labelled) or latitude and longitude.

props.name: origin
props.doc: Where the route starts. Leave it out to start from the person's own position.

props.name: mode
props.doc: How they travel. Waze only drives, so it is left out for the other modes. Default "driving".

props.name: apps
props.doc: The apps to offer, in order of preference. Without it: Apple Maps first on iPhone and iPad, Google Maps first everywhere else.

props.name: label
props.doc: The button's text. Default "Get directions".

props.name: onOpen
props.doc: Called when a maps link is opened, with the app.

props.name: variant
props.doc: Any Button variant. Default "outline".

props.name: size
props.doc: Any Button size.

entries.docs: Give the destination an address (with its name, so the pin is labelled) or latitude and longitude; a name alone is not enough and disables the button with the reason. Without apps, Apple Maps comes first on iPhone and iPad and Google Maps elsewhere, decided after mount. Waze only drives. The link builders in directions.ts are pure and return null for a place that cannot be used.

entries.name: follow-button
entries.title: Follow button
entries.description: Follow, Following and Requested in one button: optimistic, with a follower count, a clear way to unfollow and a rollback message when the request fails.

components.name: FollowButton
components.summary: A button for following people, topics or projects. It answers at once and settles afterwards: pressing Follow shows Following (and one more follower) right away, and if the request fails it rolls back with a short line saying so. Hovering or focusing Following shows the unfollow action, but the pressed state only ever changes when the button is pressed, and a press is ignored while a request is on its way. A private account shows Requested and asks for one confirmation before unfollowing. The count uses tabular numbers that count up and down, and a polite announcement says the result, "Following Maya Okafor, 1,204 followers".

props.name: status
props.doc: Where things stand: not following, following, or waiting for the person to approve. Controlled: update it, and `count`, in your callbacks before they resolve.

props.name: defaultStatus
props.doc: Where an uncontrolled button starts. Default "none".

props.name: onFollow
props.doc: Called when Follow is pressed. The button changes at once; if this rejects, it rolls back and says so. Resolve with "requested" when the account turned out to need approval.

props.name: onUnfollow
props.doc: Called when Following (or Requested) is pressed again. Same rules: at once, then settle or roll back.

props.name: count
props.doc: How many people follow. It moves with the button, and counts up or down. Leave it out to show no count.

props.name: name
props.doc: Who or what is followed, for the accessible name: "Maya Okafor" gives "Follow Maya Okafor".

props.name: isPrivate
props.doc: A private account: following asks for approval ("Requested"), and unfollowing asks once to confirm.

props.name: noun
props.doc: What the count counts, singular and plural. Default follower and followers.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Language of the numbers. Default "en-US".

props.name: variant
props.doc: The look of the Follow button; once following it turns into an outline. Default "default".

props.name: size
props.doc: Any Button size.

entries.docs: Controlled: keep status and count in state and update both in onFollow and onUnfollow before they resolve. The button answers at once and rolls back with a message if the promise rejects; presses are ignored while a request is pending. Resolve onFollow with "requested" when the account needs approval, or pass isPrivate to ask for it up front; unfollowing a private account asks once. defaultStatus leaves the status to the button, and the count then stays as given for that starting status and moves with the button. The error line is wider than the button and widens the control with it, so where you right-align the button pass className="items-end" (or sm:items-end) and it keeps its right edge when a request fails. The accessible name stays "Follow <name>" and aria-pressed carries the state, while the visible word changes to Following or Requested.

entries.name: keep-awake-toggle
entries.title: Keep awake toggle
entries.description: A switch that keeps the screen on for recipes, scripts and slides with the Wake Lock API, taking it again after a tab switch.

components.name: KeepAwakeToggle
components.summary: A switch that keeps the screen on for recipes, scripts and slides, using the Wake Lock API. It asks for the lock when turned on, asks again when the tab comes back (browsers let go of it while a tab is hidden), lets go when it is turned off or the page goes, and if the browser refuses, such as on a low battery or under a permissions policy, the switch returns to off with one line saying why. Where the API does not exist it renders nothing, so a page never shows a switch that cannot work. The state is `aria-checked` on a real switch, a polite message confirms "Screen will stay on", and nothing is requested on load.

props.name: on
props.doc: Controlled: whether the screen is kept on. Pair it with `onChange`; a refused request calls `onChange(false)`.

props.name: defaultOn
props.doc: Where an uncontrolled switch starts. Default false. Nothing is requested on load: a switch that starts on (here or through `on`) asks for the lock at the first touch or key press, because a wake lock is a promise to a person who is there.

props.name: onChange
props.doc: Called with the new state when the switch is turned, and with false when the browser refuses or drops the request.

props.name: label
props.doc: The switch's label. Default "Keep screen on".

props.name: description
props.doc: A line under the label on why you would: "Stops the screen from dimming while you cook."

props.name: size
props.doc: The size of the row and its switch. Default "default".

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables the switch.

props.name: wakeLock
props.doc: Where wake locks come from. Defaults to `navigator.wakeLock`.

entries.docs: The lock is requested when the switch is turned on, requested again when the tab becomes visible (browsers let go of it while a tab is hidden) and released when it is turned off or the page goes. Nothing is requested on load: a switch that starts on (defaultOn or on) asks for the lock at the first touch or key press. If the browser refuses, the switch returns to off, onChange(false) is called and one line says why. Where the Wake Lock API does not exist the component renders nothing. Pass wakeLock to supply your own source.

entries.name: like-button
entries.title: Like button
entries.description: A like button where the count is the point: it answers at once, rolls the number, plays one quiet ring and tells screen readers the exact count.

components.name: LikeButton
components.summary: A like button where the count is the point. It answers at once and settles afterwards: pressing it fills the icon, plays one quiet ring on the way in (never on unlike, never under reduced motion) and rolls the count to the new number; if the request fails, icon and count roll back and a short line says so beside the button, on the side that has room. The state is `aria-pressed` on a button named with the exact count ("Like this post, 1,204 likes") while the eye reads "1.2K", so it never rests on colour or an abbreviation; a tooltip shows that exact count too. A polite message confirms the result, and `names` turns the tooltip into "Liked by Maya and 41 others".

props.name: liked
props.doc: Whether the signed-in person has liked it. Controlled: update it, and `count`, in `onToggle` before it resolves.

props.name: defaultLiked
props.doc: Where an uncontrolled button starts. Default false.

props.name: count
props.doc: How many likes there are, yours included when `liked`. It moves with the button, one up or down. Leave it out to show no number.

props.name: onToggle
props.doc: Called with the next state when the button is pressed. The button flips at once; if this rejects it rolls back, count and all, and says so. Presses are ignored while a request is on its way.

props.name: label
props.doc: What pressing does, for the accessible name: "Like this post" gives "Like this post, 42 likes". Default "Like".

props.name: icon
props.doc: The glyph, drawn filled once liked. Default a heart. Any `@rhs-ui/icons` glyph works: a thumb, a star.

props.name: compact
props.doc: A smaller button without a border, for rows of comments.

props.name: showCount
props.doc: Show the number. Default true.

props.name: names
props.doc: People who liked it besides you, most relevant first. The tooltip, which otherwise shows the exact count behind an abbreviated one, then reads "Liked by Maya and 41 others".

props.name: noun
props.doc: What the count counts, singular and plural. Default like and likes.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Language of the numbers and of the list of names. Default "en-US".

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables the button.

entries.docs: Controlled: keep liked and count in state and update both in onToggle once the request has succeeded; the button already shows the new state while it waits, and rolls back with a message if onToggle rejects. defaultLiked leaves the state to the button, and count then stays as written for that starting state and moves with the button. Counts above 999 abbreviate by locale (1.2K, 1,2 Mio.) while the accessible name and the tooltip keep the exact number. Pass names to make the tooltip read "Liked by ...", and any @rhs-ui/icons glyph as icon: it is drawn filled once liked.

entries.name: listen-button
entries.title: Listen button
entries.description: Listen to this article with the browser's own speech: play, pause and stop, a choice of speed, and the sentence being read highlighted.

components.name: ListenButton
components.summary: Listen to this article: the browser's own speech, with no file and no server. One press reads the text aloud, sentence by sentence; the same button pauses and resumes, a second one stops, and a small menu picks the speed. When the text is an element on the page, the sentence being read is highlighted so people can follow along. Reading in sentences also sidesteps Chrome stopping long utterances. A page has one voice: pressing a second button stops the first, and if anything else cuts the speech off the button goes back to rest. It stops when the page is hidden or leaves, shows progress as "Sentence 4 of 31" instead of a time (a speech engine cannot know one), announces each change politely and, where the browser cannot speak, renders nothing.

props.name: text
props.doc: What to read. Use this, or `targetRef`.

props.name: targetRef
props.doc: An element whose text is read sentence by sentence, with the sentence being read highlighted. It wins over `text`.

props.name: lang
props.doc: The language of the text, as a BCP 47 tag: "en-GB". It picks the voice and how sentences are cut. Default "en-US".

props.name: rates
props.doc: The speeds in the menu, as multiples of normal: 0.9, 1, 1.25. Default 0.75, 1, 1.25 and 1.5.

props.name: defaultRate
props.doc: The speed it starts at. Default 1, or the first of `rates`.

props.name: onStateChange
props.doc: Called whenever the state changes, and with "unavailable" where the browser cannot speak.

props.name: voice
props.doc: A voice by name or `voiceURI`. Without it the browser picks one for `lang`.

props.name: label
props.doc: What the button says at rest. Default "Listen".

props.name: size
props.doc: 32, 36 or 44px. Default "default".

props.name: variant
props.doc: Any Button variant. Outline by default.

props.name: locale
props.doc: Language of the speed and progress figures. Default "en-US".

props.name: engine
props.doc: Where speech comes from. Defaults to `window.speechSynthesis`.

entries.docs: Pass text, or targetRef for an element whose text is read sentence by sentence (the sentence being read is highlighted with the CSS Custom Highlight API, without touching your markup; mark anything that should not be read with data-listen-skip). lang picks the voice and how sentences are cut. The button reads in sentences, which also avoids Chrome stopping long utterances, and stops when the page is hidden or unmounts. Progress is shown as sentences, not time. A page has one voice: pressing a second button stops the first, and if anything else cuts the speech off the button goes back to rest. Where the browser has no speech synthesis it renders nothing; pass engine to supply your own.

entries.name: pay-button
entries.title: Pay button
entries.description: The checkout button with its whole life: the amount on it, locked until the form is valid, processing, the bank step, paid, and failed with a safe retry.

components.name: PayButton
components.summary: The one button a checkout cannot get wrong. It reads "Pay 49.00" in tabular numbers and stays aria-disabled, with the reason under it, until the form is valid. Once pressed it locks and says "Processing payment, do not close this page"; the bank step has its own wording, paid shows a check and the amount, and a failure names the reason in words and offers "Try again" without resetting the form. A double submit is impossible by construction: the first press locks the button before anything renders, and every press carries its own attempt id so your server can make the charge idempotent.

props.name: amount
props.doc: What is charged, in minor units: 4900 is 49.00.

props.name: currency
props.doc: ISO 4217 code: "EUR", "USD", "GBP".

props.name: locale
props.doc: Always pass your application locale, so the server and the browser print the same amount.

props.name: status
props.doc: Drive the state yourself, from your payment provider. Leave it out and the button runs the whole cycle from the promise `onPay` returns.

props.name: onPay
props.type: (attemptId: string, step: { authenticating: () => void }) => void | Promise<void>
props.doc: Called when the button is pressed while ready (or failed). It gets a fresh attempt id for every press: send it to your server as the idempotency key, so a retried request can never charge twice. Return the promise and the button stays locked until it settles; call `step.authenticating()` when the bank asks for a confirmation.

props.name: disabledReason
props.doc: Why the button cannot be pressed yet: "Enter your card number". It shows under the button, which stays focusable but aria-disabled. Leave it out once the form is valid.

props.name: label
props.doc: The verb before the amount. Put {amount} in it to place the figure elsewhere: "Pay {amount} now".

props.name: error
props.doc: What went wrong, in words, while the status is failed. Without it the thrown Error's message is used, then a general line.

props.name: onRetry
props.doc: Called by "Try again". In a controlled button it replaces `onPay` for the retry; otherwise it is called and the payment runs again.

props.name: note
props.doc: An optional quiet line under the button: "Payments are encrypted".

props.name: size
props.doc: "lg", the default, is the tall checkout button.

props.name: type
props.doc: Use "submit" inside a checkout form: pressing Enter in a field then pays through `onPay`, and the form never submits natively.

props.name: form
props.doc: The id of the form this button belongs to, when it sits outside it.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words, for another language.

props.name: buttonClassName
props.doc: Extra classes for the button itself; `className` styles the wrapper around it.

entries.docs: Send every press's attempt id to your server as the idempotency key. Pass disabledReason while the form is invalid, status from your payment provider (or let the promise from onPay drive it), and call step.authenticating() when the bank asks for a confirmation. Inside a checkout form use type="submit".

entries.name: reaction-bar
entries.title: Reaction bar
entries.description: Emoji reactions under a message or comment: counts, your own pressed, who reacted on hover, and an add button with a palette you walk with arrow keys.

components.name: ReactionBar
components.summary: Emoji reactions under a message or a comment. Each chip is a toggle with the emoji and a count, your own reactions pressed, and a tooltip that says who reacted. The add button opens a compact palette you can walk with the arrow keys. Presses are optimistic: the chip answers at once, and a rejected `onToggle` puts the count back and explains why in words. Read only keeps the counts and the who-reacted tooltip at full strength (the chips stay focusable and say they are disabled) and dims just the add button.

props.name: reactions
props.doc: What is on the message now: one entry per emoji, in the order the chips should appear.

props.name: onToggle
props.doc: You pressed a chip or picked from the palette. `reacted` is the state you asked for. Save it and update `reactions`; if the promise rejects, the bar puts everything back and says so.

props.name: palette
props.doc: The emoji offered by the add button, sixteen by default. Eight per row.

props.name: max
props.doc: The most different reactions one message can carry. At the limit the palette only lets you toggle what is already there. Default 12.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Shows the reactions but lets nobody change them: an archived thread, a read-only role. The chips keep their full contrast, their tooltip and their place in the tab order; only the add button is dimmed.

props.name: locale
props.doc: For the list of names in the tooltip. Default "en-US".

props.name: label
props.doc: The group's name for screen readers. Default "Reactions".

entries.docs: Keep reactions in state and update it in onToggle (applyReaction does the bookkeeping). The bar shows your press at once; if onToggle rejects it puts the count back and says so in words, and a request in flight blocks a second press on the same emoji. users lists the other people who reacted, so the tooltip can read 'You, Ana Reyes and 2 others'; it may hold only the first few names. max is the most different reactions one message can carry. disabled makes the bar read only: the chips keep full contrast, their tooltip and their place in the tab order (they are aria-disabled, not disabled) and only the add button is dimmed.

entries.name: save-contact-button
entries.title: Save contact button
entries.description: Save a person or business to the address book: it builds a vCard in the browser from one contact object and downloads it, with no server involved.

components.name: SaveContactButton
components.summary: A button that saves a person or a business to the address book. It builds a vCard 3.0 file in the browser from one contact object (escaped text, folded lines, labelled phone and email types) and hands it over as a download, with no server involved; on an iPhone the file opens the Add Contact sheet. The label says what happens, the accessible name adds who ("Save to contacts, Maya Okafor"), and a contact with no name disables the button and says why. The pure buildVCard function is exported from vcard.ts, for testing or for turning the same card into a QR code.

props.name: contact
props.doc: The person or business: name, organisation, title, phones, emails, url, address, note, photoUrl.

props.name: fileName
props.doc: The name of the downloaded file. ".vcf" is added when it is missing. Default: the contact's name.

props.name: label
props.doc: The button's text. It says what happens. Default "Save to contacts".

props.name: doneLabel
props.doc: The text for the moment after the file has been handed over. Default "Downloaded".

props.name: onSave
props.doc: Called with the contact and the vCard text once the file has been handed to the browser.

props.name: variant
props.doc: Any Button variant. Default "outline".

props.name: size
props.doc: Any Button size.

entries.docs: The file is a vCard 3.0 with escaped text, lines folded at 75 octets and labelled phone, email and address types. On an iPhone it opens the Add Contact sheet. The accessible name adds who it is for, and a contact without a name disables the button with the reason. buildVCard in vcard.ts is pure and returns null without a name, so the same text can become a QR code.

entries.name: social-sign-in-buttons
entries.title: Social sign-in buttons
