entries.name: batch-progress
entries.title: Batch progress
entries.description: Progress for work on many items at once: one bar, a count of done, failed and waiting, and a Cancel that stops the rest.

components.name: BatchProgress
components.summary: Progress for work on many items at once: an import, a bulk delete, a resize of a whole folder. One bar fills as items finish, and the failed ones take the end of it as a hatch, so a failure differs in pattern and not only in colour. Under the bar a line reads "42 of 120 done, 2 failed, 76 waiting" in tabular numbers, each count with a swatch of its part of the bar. The bar is a real progressbar with its own text ("42 of 120 done, 2 failed, 76 waiting"), and the counts are never a live region: a status line is spoken only at each ten per cent, and when the batch is cancelled or done, so a fast batch cannot flood a screen reader. Cancel stops the rest; on completion it gives way to "Done".

props.name: total
props.doc: How many items the batch holds.

props.name: done
props.doc: How many finished well. Failed items are counted apart, so done plus failed is how far it has got.

props.name: failed
props.doc: How many finished badly. They fill the end of the bar with a hatch, so they differ in pattern and not only in colour. Default 0.

props.name: label
props.doc: What the batch is doing, as a short line above the bar: "Importing contacts". It also names the progress bar.

props.name: status
props.doc: `running` shows Cancel, `cancelling` shows it busy, `complete` shows "Done" and no button. You own it: change it as the work changes. Default `running`.

props.name: onCancel
props.doc: Called when Cancel is pressed. Stop starting new items, then set `status` to `cancelling` and, once the running ones settle, to `complete`. Leave it out and there is no button.

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the numbers. Default "en-US".

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the panel uses, for translation.

entries.docs: total, done and failed are counts of items; done and failed are kept apart, so the bar shows done plus failed and the rest is waiting. label names the progress bar. status is 'running', 'cancelling' or 'complete'; onCancel adds the Cancel button, and on complete it gives way to Done. The failed share is hatched at the end of the bar, never thinner than 6px, so a few failures in a big batch still show. The bar is a real progressbar with aria-valuetext; the counts line is not a live region, and a status is spoken only at each tenth of the way, when cancelling starts and when the batch is done.

entries.name: bulk-result-summary
entries.title: Bulk result summary
entries.description: The outcome of a batch job in numbers: what worked, what was skipped and what failed, with each failure's reason and a retry.

components.name: BulkResultSummary
components.summary: The outcome of a batch job in numbers: what worked, what was left alone and what failed, with the failures listed one by one. A headline ("Imported 118 of 124 contacts"), a bar in three parts told apart by pattern (solid, dots, hatch) with every count written out under it, and the failed items each with its reason ("Row 17: email is not valid"). Beyond five failures the list folds behind "Show all 9". Retry and Download report are the way on, and they show a spinner while your promise runs; the focus, which a disabled button loses, then goes back to Download report, and after a retry to the panel, so a screen reader reads the new result. When nothing failed the whole panel shrinks to one calm line with a check. The panel takes the focus once when it appears, so a screen reader reads the result the person was waiting for; turn that off for a panel that is part of a page.

props.name: total
props.doc: How many items the job was given.

props.name: succeeded
props.doc: How many worked.

props.name: skipped
props.doc: How many were left alone on purpose: duplicates, rows that were empty. Default 0.

props.name: failures
props.doc: The items that failed, each with the reason. The count of failures is the length of this list. With none, the panel shrinks to one calm line.

props.name: onRetryFailed
props.doc: Called when "Retry n failed" is pressed. Return a promise and the button shows a spinner meanwhile. When it settles the panel takes the focus, so a screen reader reads out the new headline and counts: settle it once the new numbers are in. Leave it out and there is no button.

props.name: onDownloadReport
props.doc: Called when "Download report" is pressed. Return a promise and the button shows a spinner meanwhile, and takes the focus back when it settles. Leave it out and there is no button.

props.name: noun
props.doc: What the items are: "contacts", or `{ one: "contact", other: "contacts" }` so that one item is not "1 contacts". Default items.

props.name: verb
props.doc: What the job did, in the past tense with a capital: "Imported", "Deleted", "Archived". Default "Processed".

props.name: foldAfter
props.doc: How many failures show before the rest fold behind "Show all". Default 5.

props.name: autoFocus
props.doc: Take the focus once, when the panel appears, so a screen reader reads the result. Turn it off for a panel that is part of a page, not the answer to something the person just did. Default true.

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the numbers. Default "en-US".

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the panel uses, for translation.

entries.docs: total, succeeded, skipped and failures ({ id, label, reason }[]) give the counts; a fourth, not processed, appears when they do not add up to total. verb ("Imported") and noun ("contacts", or { one, other }) write the headline. With no failures the panel is one calm line. More than foldAfter (5) failures fold behind Show all n. onRetryFailed and onDownloadReport may return promises and show a spinner meanwhile; when Retry settles the panel takes the focus, so a screen reader reads the new counts (settle it once they are in), and Download report takes its own focus back. The bar never relies on colour: each part has a pattern (solid, dots, hatch) and a written count, and a screen reader hears the counts as the panel's description. The panel takes focus once on mount unless autoFocus is false.

entries.name: coming-soon-state
entries.title: Coming soon state
entries.description: A placeholder for a feature that is not ready: what it will do, roughly when, and a button to be told when it launches.

components.name: ComingSoonState
components.summary: A placeholder for a feature that is not ready: a calm panel with the Soon badge, the feature's name, a sentence or two on what it will do, and "Planned for Q1" when you want to say roughly when. Notify me asks your app to save the sign-up and, once that has worked, turns into "We will email you", and the device remembers it so the button does not come back and nobody signs up twice; if saving fails the panel says so in words instead of pretending. The focus, which the button loses while it saves, goes to the confirmation or back to the button. There is no countdown and no urgency, only honest copy. It fits a tab, a settings page or a sidebar slot, and keeps the button out of the first paint until the device has been asked whether it was already pressed, so a returning visitor never sees it flash.

props.name: title
props.doc: The feature's name: "Scheduled reports". It gets the Soon badge.

props.name: description
props.doc: What it will do, in a sentence or two. Say the benefit, not the build.

props.name: expected
props.doc: Roughly when, in a few words: "Q1", "early 2027". The panel says "Planned for Q1". Leave it out and it promises no window.

props.name: onNotify
props.doc: Called when Notify me is pressed. Return the promise of the sign-up: a rejection shows its message and the button comes back, so nobody is told "we will email you" when nothing was saved.

props.name: notified
props.doc: The person is already on your list (you know it from your server): the panel shows "We will email you" and no button.

props.name: storageKey
props.doc: Where this device remembers the sign-up, in localStorage, so the button does not come back on the next visit. Default one per title.

props.name: icon
props.doc: An icon in the tile above the title, as an element: `<IconRocket />`. Default a sparkle.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The level of the title: 3 by default.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the panel uses, for translation.

entries.docs: title gets the Soon badge, description says what the feature will do and expected completes "Planned for …". onNotify returns the promise of the sign-up: a rejection shows its message and the button comes back; success turns the button into "We will email you" (which takes the focus; after a rejection the button gets it back), remembered in localStorage under storageKey (default one per title). notified shows that state at once for people your server already knows. There is no countdown and no urgency. icon replaces the sparkle in the tile.

entries.name: draft-restored-notice
entries.title: Draft restored notice
entries.description: Tells people their unsaved work came back after a crash or a closed tab: when it was saved, Keep or Start over, plus a useLocalDraft hook.

components.name: DraftRestoredNotice
components.summary: Tells people that their unsaved work came back: "We restored your draft from 10:42", how much it holds ("3 fields changed", "412 words") and two ways on. Keep draft simply dismisses the notice. Start over deletes the draft for good, so it asks for a second press before it calls `onDiscard`. The time is a time element in the zone you pass, and it carries the day too when the draft is not from today. The notice is a polite status: it is spoken once and never takes the focus, and it holds no alert role, so a validation error in the form beside it is always the louder voice. Put it above the form, where `useLocalDraft` (exported from here) reports that a draft exists.

props.name: savedAt
props.doc: When the draft was saved: `draft.savedAt` from `useLocalDraft`, or any Date or ISO moment.

props.name: summary
props.doc: How much the draft holds, in a few words: "3 fields changed", "412 words". It is shown under the sentence.

props.name: onKeep
props.doc: Called when "Keep draft" is pressed. The notice folds away; the draft stays in storage until you save.

props.name: onDiscard
props.doc: Called once "Start over" has been confirmed with its second press. Reset your form and call `clear()` here. Return a promise and the notice waits for it before it folds away.

props.name: onClosed
props.doc: Called after the notice has folded away, whichever button closed it. Stop rendering it here, not before, or it vanishes without its fold.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone the time is written in, so the server and the browser agree. Default "UTC".

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the time. Default "en-US".

props.name: now
props.doc: Pins the moment "today" is worked out from, for previews and tests. Leave it out to use the browser's clock, read once the page is live.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the notice uses, for translation.

entries.docs: DraftRestoredNotice takes savedAt, summary ("3 fields changed", "412 words"), timeZone and locale, onKeep, onDiscard (called after a second press of Start over) and onClosed (after it has folded away). It is a polite status, never an alert, and never takes the focus. useLocalDraft(key, value, { delay, enabled }) returns { draft, clear }: it saves value to localStorage a moment after the last change (and when the tab is hidden), reports a draft found on mount in draft (null on the server and on the first paint), never overwrites it before the form has changed, and clear() deletes it: call it after the form was saved for real, and from Start over. value must survive JSON.

entries.name: empty-state
entries.title: Empty State
entries.description: A considered empty state with a heading, explanation, icon and recovery action.

entries.name: first-run-state
entries.title: First run state
entries.description: The empty state for a brand new account: one promise and two to four ways to begin, as cards in one keyboard group, with a Recommended one and a quiet Skip.

components.name: FirstRunState
components.summary: The empty state for a brand new account: one promise as a heading, a line of context, then two to four ways to begin as cards (a template, an import, an invite) and a quiet "Skip for now". It is deliberately not a checklist: pick one and go. The cards are real buttons or links in one group, and the arrow keys, Home and End move between them while Tab still reaches each. The option most people should choose carries the word "Recommended". Use Empty State when there is nothing to choose, and this when there are good ways to start.

props.name: title
props.doc: The one promise, as the heading: "Welcome to Halcyon".

props.name: description
props.doc: A line of context under it: what they get and that nothing is final.

props.name: options
props.doc: Two to four ways to begin. More than four is a menu, and fewer than two is an Empty State with one action.

props.name: recommendedId
props.doc: The `id` of the option most people should pick. It carries the word "Recommended".

props.name: onSkip
props.doc: Shows a quiet "Skip for now" under the cards and calls this when it is pressed. Leave it out when skipping makes no sense.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: Heading level of the title. Default 2.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the state uses, for translation.

entries.docs: title is the one promise and description a line of context. options are two to four ways to begin ({ id, title, description, icon, onSelect or href }): a card with href is a link, any other is a button. recommendedId puts the word Recommended on one card, and onSkip adds a quiet 'Skip for now'. The cards are one labelled group: Tab reaches each card, and the arrow keys, Home and End move between them, up and down to the nearest card in the row above or below. Two and four cards sit in two columns, three in a row once the container is wide enough, and all stack on a phone. It is deliberately not a checklist: nothing is ticked and nothing counts. Use Empty State when there is nothing to choose.

entries.name: mode-bar
entries.title: Mode bar
entries.description: A bar that says you are in a special mode (test data, viewing as someone else, read-only or beta) and gives the one way out. It cannot be dismissed.

components.name: ModeBar
components.summary: A bar that says you are in a special mode (test data, viewing as someone else, read only, beta) and gives the way out. One row: an icon and the mode's name, a plain statement of what is different, and a single Exit button. It cannot be dismissed, only exited, because a hidden mode is how mistakes on real data happen. Every kind has its own icon, word and weight, so the mode reads without colour. It is a labelled region that screen reader users can jump to, and `sticky` keeps it in view while the page scrolls.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Which mode this is. It decides the icon, the word and how loud the bar is.

props.name: title
props.doc: What comes after the mode's name: for "viewing-as", whose account it is ("Mara Jansen").

props.name: description
props.doc: One plain statement of what is different: "No real payments are taken." Say what changes, not what the mode is called.

props.name: onExit
props.doc: Leaves the mode. The bar has no close button on purpose: a mode that can be hidden is how mistakes on real data happen, so it can only be left. Without `onExit` there is no button, for a mode the person cannot leave themselves.

props.name: sticky
props.doc: Pins the bar under the header while the page scrolls. It sticks at the top of its container; pass `className="top-14"` to sit under a 56px header.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the bar uses, for translation.

entries.docs: kind is 'test', 'viewing-as', 'read-only' or 'beta': each has its own icon, its own word in a chip and its own weight (hatched, inverted, plain, a card), so the mode reads without colour. title adds whose account it is for viewing-as, description says what is different in plain words, and onExit adds the single Exit button, named 'Exit: Test mode' for a screen reader. There is no close button on purpose: a mode that can be hidden is how mistakes on real data happen. Without onExit there is no button at all, for a mode the person cannot leave. The bar is a labelled region, so screen reader users can jump to it. sticky pins it under the header; pass className='top-14' to sit under a 56px header. labels carries every word.

entries.name: needs-setup-state
entries.title: Needs setup state
entries.description: Stands in for a feature that needs one step first: what is missing, why, the steps done and left, and the action that fixes it.

components.name: NeedsSetupState
components.summary: The stand-in for a feature that needs one step before it works: a dashed panel in the place of the feature, with what is missing as the title, a line on why, an optional list of what is done and what is left, and the action that fixes it. Done steps show a check and the word "Done", the first open step is marked "Next" and carries `aria-current="step"`, and the rest are read out as not done. The panel keeps the height you give it, so the page does not jump when setup finishes and the feature takes its place. The main button runs `onAction`; if that returns a promise it shows a spinner and ignores presses until it settles, without losing focus. It is not an onboarding checklist: use it only where a missing prerequisite blocks one specific thing.

props.name: title
props.doc: What is needed, as the action it asks for: "Connect a Stripe account to see revenue".

props.name: description
props.doc: Why it is needed, in a sentence.

props.name: steps
props.doc: The parts of the setup, in order. Leave it out when there is one step and the title says it.

props.name: actionLabel
props.doc: The label of the main button: "Connect Stripe". Leave it out for no button.

props.name: onAction
props.doc: Called when the main button is pressed. Return a promise and the button shows a spinner until it settles; a rejection is yours to show.

props.name: secondary
props.doc: Beside the main button: a link or a quieter button, such as "Read the guide".

props.name: icon
props.doc: An icon in the tile above the title, as an element. Default is a plug.

props.name: minHeight
props.doc: The height of the feature this stands in for: a number of pixels or any CSS length. The panel never gets shorter, so the page does not jump when setup finishes.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the panel uses, for translation.

entries.docs: title says what is needed, as the action it asks for, and description says why. steps is a list of { label, done }: a finished step shows a check and the word Done, the first open step is marked Next and carries aria-current="step", the rest are read out as not done, and a polite status says how many are finished. actionLabel and onAction make the main button; if onAction returns a promise the button shows a spinner and ignores presses until it settles, without losing focus. secondary is a node beside it, such as a link. minHeight is the height of the feature the panel stands in for, in pixels or any CSS length, so the page does not jump when setup finishes. icon replaces the plug. Use it for one missing prerequisite that blocks one specific thing, not for onboarding. labels carries every word.

entries.name: notice-stack
entries.title: Notice stack
entries.description: Several notices in one place: the most urgent on top, the rest folded under '+2 more', each closable on its own.

components.name: NoticeStack
components.summary: Several notices in one place, so a page does not grow a tower of banners when a billing warning, a maintenance note and a trial notice all apply at once. The stack sorts them by urgency (errors, then warnings, then information), shows the first `max` in full and folds the rest under a "+2 more" button, with a hint of the folded cards peeking out beneath. The button unfolds the list in place, and its name carries the count ("Show 2 more notices"). Each notice keeps its own action, and `dismissible` ones have a close button: dismissing one calls `onDismiss`, and when you remove it from `notices` the next one comes forward and focus moves to it instead of dropping to the top of the page. A notice that arrives after the first paint is announced politely; an error is announced once, as an alert. The whole stack is one labelled region.

props.name: notices
props.doc: Everything that applies right now, in any order. The stack sorts it by urgency, and keeps your order within a level.

props.name: onDismiss
props.doc: Called with the id when a notice's close button is pressed. Remove it from `notices` and the next one comes forward.

props.name: max
props.doc: How many notices are shown in full; the rest fold under a button. Default 1.

props.name: label
props.doc: The name of the region for a screen reader. Default "Notices".

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the stack uses, for translation.

entries.docs: notices is a list of { id, tone, title, body, action, dismissible } in any order: the stack sorts it by tone (error, warning, info) and keeps your order within a level. max (default 1) is how many show in full; the rest fold under a +N more button, whose name carries the count and which unfolds them in place. A dismissible notice has a close button that calls onDismiss(id); remove it from notices and the next one comes forward and takes focus. A notice that arrives after the first paint is announced politely, and an error is announced once, as an alert; what is there on load is not announced. Only errors use colour: a warning and information differ by icon, weight and the word read before the title. label names the region. labels carries every word.

entries.name: offline-state
entries.title: Offline state
entries.description: The page-sized 'you are offline' state: what still works on the device, a Try again button, and a Back online moment with an automatic retry.

components.name: OfflineState
components.summary: The page-sized "you are offline" state. While the connection is down it replaces the page with a wifi-off icon, "You are offline", a line on what is safe on the device, what still works (your children) and a Try again button. It follows the browser's online and offline events, or your own `online`. When the connection returns it says "Back online" for a moment, calls `onRetry` once so the page can refetch, and steps aside. It stays out of the way while the browser already knows it is online, including the first paint, and the change is announced politely instead of stealing focus. The title is a heading of the level you choose (2 unless you set `headingLevel`), and the "Still offline" line under the button has its room from the start, so pressing Try again never moves the button.

props.name: online
props.doc: Overrides what the browser says: `false` shows the state, `true` hides it. Leave it out to follow the browser's own online and offline events, for a page that has no better test of the connection.

props.name: onRetry
props.doc: Called once when the connection returns, and each time Try again is pressed. It may return a promise: the button shows a spinner until it settles. Refetch what the page needs here.

props.name: cachedAt
props.doc: When the copy kept on the device was last updated. Written in the locale and the zone, with the zone's name.

props.name: children
props.doc: What still works offline, as a list: "Read your saved projects", "Edit notes (they sync later)". A plain `<ul>` with `<li>` items is spaced for you.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: Heading level of the title. Default 2; use 1 when the state is the whole page.

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the date. Default "en-US".

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone the date is written in, so the server and the browser agree. Default "UTC".

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the state uses, for translation.

entries.docs: It follows the browser's online and offline events, or your own online prop, and it is hidden whenever the browser knows it is online, including the first paint. Offline it shows a wifi-off icon, 'You are offline', what is safe on the device, an optional last-saved line from cachedAt (written in locale and timeZone), your children under 'Still works offline', and a Try again button that calls onRetry, shows a spinner and says 'Still offline' if it did not help, on a line that has its room from the start so the button never moves. When the connection returns it says 'Back online' for a moment, calls onRetry once and steps aside. The change is announced through a polite status region and focus never moves. It is page-sized: cover your page with className='fixed inset-0 z-50 bg-background' or place it in the content area. The title is a heading at headingLevel (2 by default, 1 when the sta…

entries.name: payment-failed-banner
entries.title: Payment failed banner
entries.description: A banner for a failed subscription payment: which card, the date it becomes a problem, and one button to fix it. Turns destructive once access is paused.

components.name: PaymentFailedBanner
components.summary: The banner for a subscription payment that failed: what happened, the date it becomes a problem and one button to fix it. While the plan still works it reads "We could not charge your card ending 4242. Update it by 14 November to keep your plan." in a calm bordered card; once the grace period is over it turns destructive and says that access is paused. The date sits in a time element, written in the time zone you pass, with the full day, time and zone in its title. "Update payment method" runs `onUpdate`, and if that returns a promise (a request for a billing portal link) the button shows a spinner meanwhile and gets the focus back after it, which a disabled button loses. There is no close button on purpose: the problem is real until your app says the payment went through, and then you stop rendering the banner. It is a labelled region, not a live one, so it does not interrupt a screen …

props.name: cardLabel
props.doc: What was charged, as it reads after "your": "card ending 4242", "Visa ending 4242". Leave it out and the banner says "your card".

props.name: graceEndsAt
props.doc: When the plan stops working if nothing changes: the end of the grace period, as a Date or an ISO moment. After it, access is paused.

props.name: status
props.doc: `grace` while the plan still works, `overdue` once access is paused. Overdue turns the banner destructive. Default `grace`.

props.name: onUpdate
props.doc: Called when "Update payment method" is pressed: open your billing portal or the card form here. Return a promise (a request for a portal link, say) and the button shows a spinner until it settles, and then takes the focus back.

props.name: invoiceHref
props.doc: Where the failed invoice is. Adds a quiet "View invoice" link; leave it out for none.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone the date is written in, so the server and the browser agree. Pass the zone the account's billing runs in. Default "UTC".

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the date. Default "en-US".

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the banner uses, for translation.

entries.docs: cardLabel is what follows "your" ("card ending 4242"), graceEndsAt is the end of the grace period and status is 'grace' (the default) or 'overdue', which turns the banner destructive and says that access is paused. onUpdate runs when Update payment method is pressed and may return a promise: the button shows a spinner until it settles and then takes the focus back, which a disabled button loses. invoiceHref adds a quiet View invoice link. The date is a time element written in timeZone and locale, with the full day, time and zone in its title. There is no close button on purpose: render the banner only while the payment is unresolved. The banner is a labelled region, not a live one. labels carries every word.

entries.name: permission-primer
entries.title: Permission primer
entries.description: The soft ask before the browser's permission prompt: why you need notifications, camera, microphone or location, and what to do if blocked.

components.name: PermissionPrimer
components.summary: The soft ask before the browser's own permission prompt. The browser asks once, in words the page does not control, and a "Block" is forever, so the page asks first, in its own words: what you get, with Allow and Not now. The browser's question opens only from the Allow button, never on load, and the card says that it is coming. It reads the permission: not asked yet shows the ask; allowed shows a quiet "Notifications are on"; blocked switches to short steps for turning it back on in the browser's settings, because the prompt cannot be shown again. Not now is remembered on the device for a number of days, so it does not nag, and the card follows a change made in the browser's settings while the page is open. If the browser closes its question without an answer, or cannot ask at all, the card says so, out loud as well, and puts the focus back on Allow so that it can be pressed again. It …

props.name: kind
props.doc: Which permission this asks for.

props.name: benefit
props.doc: Why it is worth saying yes, in one line and in terms of what the person gets: "Hear about replies and mentions when you are in another tab."

props.name: onRequest
props.doc: Asks the browser, and returns its answer. It runs only when Allow is pressed, never on load. For notifications: `() => Notification.requestPermission()`. Leave it out and the card asks the browser itself for the four kinds it knows (the camera and microphone are opened for a moment and let go at once).

props.name: state
props.doc: The permission as you know it, when you track it yourself or want a fixed preview. Leave it out and the card reads the browser (the Permissions API, or `Notification.permission`) and follows changes made in its settings.

props.name: onStateChange
props.doc: Called with the answer after Allow, and when the browser's own settings change the state.

props.name: onDismiss
props.doc: Called when Not now was pressed, after the choice is remembered.

props.name: snoozeDays
props.doc: How many days Not now is remembered. Default 14.

props.name: storageKey
props.doc: Where this device remembers Not now, in localStorage. Default one per kind.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The level of the card's heading: 3 by default.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the card uses, for translation.

entries.docs: kind picks the permission (notifications, camera, microphone or location), with its icon and words; benefit is one line on what the person gets. onRequest asks the browser and returns its answer; leave it out and the card asks the browser itself. state fixes the permission for a preview, or when you track it yourself; otherwise the card reads the browser (the Permissions API, or Notification.permission) and follows changes made in its settings. Not now is remembered in localStorage for snoozeDays (14) under storageKey. The browser's own prompt opens only from the Allow button, never on load, and the card is drawn after the page is live. If the browser closes its prompt without an answer, or cannot ask, the card says so (spoken too) and Allow takes the focus back. labels carries every word, including the steps shown when it is blocked.

entries.name: pwa-install-prompt
entries.title: PWA install prompt
entries.description: A prompt to install your web app: a real Install button where the browser supports it, and share-sheet steps on iPhone.

components.name: PwaInstallPrompt
components.summary: A prompt to install your web app, for the browsers that let a page do it. Where the browser fires `beforeinstallprompt` it shows "Install Acme" with a real Install button, which opens the browser's own dialog; on iPhone and iPad, whose Safari has no such event, it shows the two steps instead (Share, then Add to Home Screen) with the glyphs printed on the Safari button. It is for installable web apps, not for sending people to an app store. It stays hidden when the app already runs standalone, remembers a dismissal for a number of days, and never appears on first paint: it waits for the browser's event, or a beat on iOS. It is a bottom sheet on phones and a card in the corner on wide screens, wherever it is placed, with room for the home indicator. Mount it once, high in the app, so it is listening before the browser fires its event.

props.name: appName
props.doc: The name people know the app by: "Acme".

props.name: icon
props.doc: The app's icon, as an element sized by its box: an `` of your launcher icon. It is drawn in a rounded tile. Default a phone glyph.

props.name: onInstalled
props.doc: Called once the app was installed, whether from this prompt or from the browser's own menu.

props.name: onDismiss
props.doc: Called when Not now was pressed, or the browser's own dialog was dismissed, after the choice is remembered.

props.name: dismissDays
props.doc: How many days a dismissal is remembered, on this device, before the prompt may come back. Default 14.

props.name: platform
props.doc: `auto` (the default) reads the browser: the Install button once it fires `beforeinstallprompt`, share-sheet steps on iOS Safari, nothing anywhere else. `ios` always shows the steps, for a preview or a test.

props.name: delay
props.doc: How long, in ms, the iOS steps wait after the page is live before they appear, since iOS has no event to wait for. Default 2500.

props.name: storageKey
props.doc: Where this device remembers a dismissal, in localStorage. Default one for the site.

props.name: titleAs
props.doc: The level of the heading: 2 by default.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the prompt uses, for translation.

entries.docs: It listens for beforeinstallprompt and shows Install with Not now; on iOS Safari, which has no such event, it shows the Share, then Add to Home Screen steps after delay ms. It is hidden when the app already runs standalone, a dismissal is remembered in localStorage for dismissDays (14), and it never appears on first paint. platform="ios" forces the steps for a preview. The root is a window-sized, click-through box that the card measures itself against: a bottom sheet below 36rem and a corner card above, with safe-area padding; pass className="absolute" to place it inside a box of your own. Mount it once, high in the app, so it is listening before the browser fires its event. icon is an element for the app tile; onInstalled and onDismiss are callbacks.

entries.name: queue-position
entries.title: Queue position
entries.description: A waiting-room panel for being in line: your place, an honest wait range, and a Leave button that asks before it lets go of the spot.

components.name: QueuePosition
components.summary: A waiting-room panel for being in line: ticket drops, exports, rate-limited jobs. It says "You are 14th in line" in large tabular figures that count through whole places to the new place when it changes (the suffix steps aside while it counts, when a place on the way would need another one: "3nd" on the way from 5th to 2nd), a bar of how far you have moved since you joined, and the wait as a range ("About 3 to 5 min"), never a promise. Leave asks for a second press, because it gives up the place. When it is your turn the panel changes to "It is your turn" with the action and the time your spot is held, counting down, and says so if the time runs out. A screen reader is told your place only at friendly steps (every fifth place, then each of the last three) and the hold only when it starts, at thirty seconds and at its end, so a line that moves fast does not flood it.

props.name: position
props.doc: Your place in the line: 1 is next.

props.name: total
props.doc: How many people are in the line, you included. Shown beside the bar.

props.name: joinedAt
props.doc: When you joined, as a Date or an ISO moment. Written as a time, in `timeZone`.

props.name: startPosition
props.doc: Your place when you joined: the bar fills from there to the front. Leave it out and the first place the panel sees is taken as the start; pass it when the page can reload mid-line.

props.name: estimateSeconds
props.doc: How long the wait is likely to be, in seconds, as your server estimates it. It is written as a range ("About 3 to 5 min"), never as a promise.

props.name: status
props.doc: `waiting` shows the place and the wait; `ready` shows that it is your turn, with the action and the time the spot is held. Default `waiting`.

props.name: onLeave
props.doc: Called when "Leave the line" is confirmed: the second press. Return a promise and the button waits for it. Leave it out and there is no Leave button.

props.name: onEnter
props.doc: Called when "Enter now" is pressed. Return a promise and the button shows a spinner meanwhile, and takes the focus back when it settles.

props.name: holdSeconds
props.doc: How long the spot is held once it is your turn, in seconds, counted from when the panel turns `ready`. Default 120.

props.name: holdEndsAt
props.doc: When the held spot is released, as a moment from your server. Use it instead of `holdSeconds` when the page can reload while it is your turn.

props.name: onExpire
props.doc: Called once when the hold runs out. Take the spot away and set `status` back, or show your own message.

props.name: ordinalSuffixes
props.doc: The suffixes for places, by the language's ordinal category: "14th". Default English: st, nd, rd, th.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone the joining time is written in. Default "UTC".

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the numbers and the time. Default "en-US".

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the panel uses, for translation.

entries.docs: position is the place (1 is next); total, joinedAt (written in timeZone), startPosition (the bar fills from there; default the farthest back the panel has seen) and estimateSeconds (written as a range, never a promise) fill in the rest. status 'ready' shows It is your turn with the action (onEnter) and the hold counting down (holdSeconds, or holdEndsAt from your server), then calls onExpire when it runs out. onLeave runs on the second press of Leave the line. The number counts through whole places to each new place, and its suffix steps aside while it counts when a place on the way would need another one (5th to 2nd); Enter now takes the focus back once its promise settles. A screen reader is told the place only every fifth place and for each of the last three, and the hold only at its start, at thirty seconds and at its end.

entries.name: streak-tracker
entries.title: Streak tracker
entries.description: A week of days with the streak count: filled for days done, ringed for today, hollow for what was missed.

components.name: StreakTracker
components.summary: Seven days with the streak count beside them. A circle is filled with a check for a day done, ringed for today and hollow for a day that was missed; days still to come are dashed. Missed days are neutral on purpose: a streak is something to keep going, not a record of failure, so nothing turns red and the line under the count only says what to do next. The week starts on the locale's first weekday. Every day has a name that says its state in words ("Tuesday, done"), so nothing depends on colour, and the count is a status: it is read out when it changes and swells quietly when today is completed, or not at all under reduced motion. With `onDayClick` the days that have come are buttons. The week and the count are worked out from `days` and today, and today comes from the browser's clock in your time zone unless you pin it; a page left open past midnight moves on to the new day by itself.

props.name: days
props.doc: The days that were completed, as "2026-11-05". Pass every one you have, or at least the last run: the count is the run of days in a row that ends today, or yesterday while today is still open.

props.name: today
props.doc: Today as "2026-11-05". Leave it out to read the browser's clock in `timeZone`, once the page is live; until then the card holds its place with empty circles. Pass it when you render on the server, so the first paint is already right.

props.name: weekStartsOn
props.doc: The first day of the week: 0 for Sunday, 1 for Monday up to 6 for Saturday. Default is the locale's own.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone that decides what today is. Default "UTC".

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the weekday letters and names. Default "en-US".

props.name: onDayClick
props.doc: Called when a day that has come is pressed. Without it the days are not buttons.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the tracker uses, for translation.

entries.docs: days lists the completed days as YYYY-MM-DD, and today is the day it is now: leave it out to read the browser's clock in timeZone once the page is live (until then the card holds its place with empty circles, so pass today when you render on the server). The count is the run of days in a row that ends today, or yesterday while today is still open, so it only falls to nothing after a whole day was missed. entries.name: suspicious-activity-alert
entries.title: Suspicious activity alert
entries.description: A 'was this you?' alert for an unfamiliar sign-in, with device and place, and two clear answers: yes, or secure my account.

components.name: SuspiciousActivityAlert
components.summary: The "was this you?" alert for a sign-in from a device nobody has seen before. It shows what is needed to judge it, as a description list: the device, the approximate place (called approximate, because it is guessed from the IP address), the time, and the IP address with its last part hidden, since an address is personal data. Two clear answers follow: "Yes, it was me" folds the alert away, and "No, secure my account" runs your `onSecure` and then shows the next steps (change the password, sign out other sessions), which become buttons when you give them somewhere to go. The destructive answer is never the one that has the focus: nothing is focused when the alert appears, it is announced once as an alert, and focus moves only when the next steps take the place of the answers, or back to the button that was pressed when its answer failed.

props.name: event
props.doc: The sign-in: device, approximate place, time and IP address.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone the time is written in, so the server and the browser agree. Pass the zone the person lives in. Default "UTC".

props.name: onConfirm
props.doc: Called when "Yes, it was me" is pressed. Return a promise and the button waits; once it settles the alert folds away. A rejection keeps the alert and says so.

props.name: onSecure
props.doc: Called when "No, secure my account" is pressed. Do the urgent part here (flag the session, lock it); once it settles the alert shows the next steps. A rejection keeps the alert and says so.

props.name: steps
props.doc: The next steps, in order. Default two instructions, to change the password and to sign out other sessions; give them an `href` or an `onSelect` and they become buttons.

props.name: defaultStep
props.doc: Start on the next steps, for a page that reopens after "No" or a preview. Default "ask".

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the time. Default "en-US".

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the alert uses, for translation.

entries.docs: event is { device, place, at, ip }: the IP address is hidden in part whatever you pass (203.0.x.x), and the place is called approximate. onConfirm (Yes, it was me) folds the alert away; onSecure (No, secure my account) runs and then shows the next steps, by default change your password and sign out other sessions. Pass steps with an href or an onSelect to make them buttons. Both callbacks may return promises and show a spinner, and a rejection is said in words. The alert is announced once as role="alert"; nothing takes the focus when it appears, the heading of the steps takes it after No, and a failed answer or step gives it back to the button that was pressed. defaultStep="secured" opens on the steps.

entries.name: trial-status-bar
entries.title: Trial status bar
entries.description: A header strip counting the days left in a trial, with a thin progress line and an Upgrade button that gets firmer in the last days and after the end.

components.name: TrialStatusBar
components.summary: A header strip that counts the days left in a trial: "Trial: 12 days left", the date it ends, a thin track of how much of the trial has gone, and an Upgrade button. It gets firmer as the end comes: from three days on the sentence changes ("Trial ends in 3 days", "Trial ends tomorrow", "Trial ends today"), the bar turns solid and Upgrade stands out, and after the end it reads "Your trial has ended" with the same action. Days are counted as calendar days in the time zone you give, so the number never flickers around midnight. The strip keeps its height until the browser's clock is read, so the page does not jump, and the track is hidden from assistive technology because the sentence already says the same.

props.name: startedAt
props.doc: When the trial started, as an ISO moment: "2026-10-31T09:00:00Z". It sets how much of the trial has gone.

props.name: endsAt
props.doc: When the trial ends, as an ISO moment. The days left are counted from it in calendar days.

props.name: onUpgrade
props.doc: Called when Upgrade is pressed.

props.name: upgradeHref
props.doc: Makes Upgrade a link to your pricing or checkout instead of a button. `onUpgrade` still runs first.

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone the days are counted in, so the number does not flicker around midnight and the server and the browser agree. Default "UTC". Pass the zone the account lives in.

props.name: now
props.doc: Pins the moment the days are counted from, for previews and tests. Leave it out to use the browser's clock, read once the page is live and then every minute.

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the numbers and of the date. Default "en-US".

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the bar uses, for translation.

entries.docs: startedAt and endsAt are ISO moments, timeZone is the zone days are counted in, and now pins the clock for tests. With four days or more left it reads 'Trial: 12 days left' with the date it ends and an outline Upgrade; from three days on the sentence changes ('Trial ends in 3 days', 'Trial ends tomorrow', 'Trial ends today'), the bar turns solid and Upgrade stands out; after the end it reads 'Your trial has ended' with the same action. Days are calendar days in timeZone, so the number only changes at midnight there. The thin track shows how much of the trial has passed and is hidden from assistive technology. The strip keeps its height until the browser's clock is read, so the page does not jump. onUpgrade is called on press, or give upgradeHref for a link.

entries.name: unavailable-state
entries.title: Unavailable state
entries.description: For a link that no longer works (expired, used, revoked or removed): the reason in words, the date it happened and the next step, with a resend cooldown.

components.name: UnavailableState
components.summary: For a link that no longer works: an invite that expired, a reset link that was already used, a share that was withdrawn, a page that was removed. The icon and the words differ per reason, so people know whether to wait, ask or give up, and the date it happened is written when you pass one. The action fits the reason: ask for a new link (then a cooldown with the seconds left, so it cannot be pressed in a row), sign in, or go home. It never shows a technical code, and the result of asking is said politely, on a line that has its room from the start so the card does not grow when it is said. The title is a heading of the level you choose (2 unless you set `headingLevel`).

props.name: reason
props.doc: What happened to the link: it decides the icon, the words and which action fits.

props.name: subject
props.doc: What the link was, in one or two words: "invite", "reset link", "download link". Default "link".

props.name: occurredAt
props.doc: When it happened. Written in the locale and the zone, with the zone's name. A date-only string such as "2026-10-14" is a day on the calendar and is written without a time.

props.name: onRequestNew
props.doc: Asks for a new link: shown as the main action for an expired link, and for a used one when there is no `signInHref`. It may return a promise: the button shows a spinner until it settles, then waits out the cooldown before it can be pressed again.

props.name: signInHref
props.doc: Where signing in happens: the main action for a link that was already used.

props.name: homeHref
props.doc: Where "Go to the homepage" leads. It is the way out when asking again makes no sense.

props.name: cooldownSeconds
props.doc: How many seconds before a new link can be requested again. Default 30.

props.name: children
props.doc: Anything more under the actions: a line on who to write to, a link to help.

props.name: headingLevel
props.doc: Heading level of the title. Default 2; use 1 when the state is the whole page.

props.name: locale
props.doc: The language of the date. Default "en-US".

props.name: timeZone
props.doc: The time zone the date is written in, so the server and the browser agree. Default "UTC".

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the state uses, for translation.

entries.docs: reason is 'expired', 'used', 'revoked' or 'removed': each has its own icon, title and explanation, and subject names what the link was ('invite', 'reset link'). occurredAt is written as a date in locale and timeZone (a date-only string as a day). The action fits the reason: expired offers onRequestNew, used offers signInHref first, revoked and removed offer homeHref. Asking for a new link shows a spinner while onRequestNew runs, then a cooldown (cooldownSeconds, default 30) with the seconds left, and says politely when the request went through, when it failed and when asking is possible again, on a line that has its room from the start so the card does not grow. It never shows a technical code. children add a line under the actions. The title is a heading at headingLevel (2 by default, 1 when the state is the whole page). labels carries every word.

entries.name: unsupported-browser-notice
entries.title: Unsupported browser notice
entries.description: A calm notice for a browser that cannot run your app: what is missing in plain words, which browsers work, and Continue anyway.

components.name: UnsupportedBrowserNotice
components.summary: The notice for a browser that cannot run your app: what is missing in plain words, the browsers that work with the oldest version of each and a link to the official page, and a way to continue anyway. It checks what you list in `requires` (a function, or `{ css }` and `{ api }` data) and, when it can read the visitor's browser and it is on your list and older, the version too. Feature detection can be wrong, so Continue anyway is always there, and the choice is remembered for the session. The checks run once the page is live: the server renders nothing, and so does a browser that passes every check, so a working browser pays no layout shift. It is a labelled region in the calm info style, with no browser logos; a close button hides it for this page view only. When it goes, focus moves to a quiet message in its place instead of dropping to the top of the page, and the message is spoken.

props.name: requires
props.doc: What the app needs, one entry each. A `test` is a function that returns `false` when the browser lacks it, or data: `{ css: "container-type: inline-size" }`, `{ api: "IntersectionObserver" }`. Data works from a Server Component.

props.name: browsers
props.doc: The browsers that work, with the oldest version of each and the official page to get it. The visitor's browser is compared with this list when it can be read.

props.name: onContinue
props.doc: Called once when the visitor chooses Continue anyway, for a fallback mode or for analytics.

props.name: onDismiss
props.doc: Called once when the visitor closes the notice with its close button (see `dismissible`).

props.name: dismissible
props.doc: Adds a close button that hides the notice for this page view only. Continue anyway is the choice that is remembered. Default `false`.

props.name: storageKey
props.doc: Where Continue anyway is remembered for the session. Give each notice on a site its own. Default "rhs-ui:unsupported-browser-notice".

props.name: userAgent
props.doc: The user agent to read the browser from. Leave it out to use the visitor's own; it is for previews and tests.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the notice uses, for translation.

entries.docs: requires lists what the app needs: each entry has a label, shown when it is missing, and a test, either a function that returns false when the browser lacks it or data such as { css: "container-type: inline-size" } or { api: "IntersectionObserver" }, which also works from a Server Component. browsers lists the browsers that work, each with its name, minVersion and the official href. When the visitor's browser can be read from its user agent, is on the list and is older, the notice says so and its card shows the version it has. The checks run once the page is live, so the server renders nothing, and a browser that passes every check gets no notice and no gap. Continue anyway is always offered, is remembered for the session under storageKey and calls onContinue; dismissible adds a close button that hides it for this page view only and calls onDismiss. Above your content it pushes the page…

entries.name: update-available-bar
entries.title: Update available bar
entries.description: A slim bar saying a new version is ready, with Reload now, Later (remembered for the session) and a link to what changed. Announced once, never steals focus.

components.name: UpdateAvailableBar
components.summary: A slim bar that says a new version is ready: a refresh icon, one sentence ("A new version of Acme is ready"), the version, an optional link to what changed, a quiet Later and a Reload now. Later hides it and remembers the snooze in sessionStorage, so it returns after the interval and not on every navigation; Reload shows a busy state while the page restarts. It is announced once through a status region and never takes focus. At the top it sits in the flow of the page and grows in, so it pushes the page down instead of covering the header, and it scrolls away with the page unless you pass `sticky`, which also hands its height to a sticky header through `--update-bar-height`; at the bottom it is fixed to the viewport, slides in and clears the home indicator on a phone through the safe-area inset. Under reduced motion it simply appears.

props.name: onReload
props.doc: Reloads into the new version. Wire it to your service worker's skipWaiting message and let the page reload when the new worker takes over, or to a plain `location.reload()`. Leave it out and Reload now calls `location.reload()`. It may return a promise; the button shows a spinner while the page restarts, and returns if it settles without one.

props.name: onLater
props.doc: Called when Later was pressed, after the bar has been hidden and the snooze remembered.

props.name: version
props.doc: The version that is ready: "2.4.0". It is written after the sentence, and a snooze is remembered per version, so a newer one asks again at once.

props.name: changesHref
props.doc: Where the release notes are. Adds a quiet "What changed" link after the sentence.

props.name: appName
props.doc: The product's name for the sentence: "A new version of Acme is ready".

props.name: snoozeMinutes
props.doc: How long Later hides the bar, in minutes. Default 60. It is kept in sessionStorage, so it survives navigations and reloads of the tab, and the bar comes back when the time is up.

props.name: position
props.doc: "top" puts the bar in the flow of the page, above everything, where it pushes the page down instead of covering the header and scrolls away with the page (add `sticky` to keep it in view). "bottom" fixes it to the bottom edge of the viewport, over the page, with room for the home indicator (pass `className="absolute"` to place it inside a box of your own). Default "top".

props.name: sticky
props.doc: Keeps a top bar in view while the page scrolls. It then writes its height, as it grows in and out, to `--update-bar-height` on the element it sits in, so a sticky header can hang under it with `className="sticky top-[var(--update-bar-height,0px)]"` instead of being covered. The bar sticks inside its parent: put it in the element that holds the page. The bottom bar is fixed already and ignores this. Default false.

props.name: storageKey
props.doc: The sessionStorage key for the snooze. Default one per version.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the bar uses, for translation.

entries.docs: onReload reloads into the new version: wire it to your service worker's skipWaiting message and reload on controllerchange, or to location.reload(), which is also what the button does without it. Reload shows a busy state while the page restarts. onLater is called after the bar was hidden; Later also remembers the snooze for snoozeMinutes (60 by default) in sessionStorage, per version, so the bar comes back after the interval and not on every navigation. version, appName and changesHref add the version, the product's name and a 'What changed' link. position is 'top' (the default: in the flow of the page, above everything, so it pushes the page down instead of covering the header, and scrolls away with the page) or 'bottom' (fixed over the bottom edge of the viewport, clearing the safe-area inset; className='absolute' places it inside a box of your own). sticky keeps a top bar in view wh…

entries.name: verify-email-banner
entries.title: Verify email banner
entries.description: A banner for unverified accounts that names the address, resends the email with a cooldown that survives a reload, and lets people fix a typo.

components.name: VerifyEmailBanner
components.summary: A banner for an account whose email address is not verified yet. It says what to do and why ("Verify jane@acme.com to start sending invites"), resends the email, and lets people fix a typo in the address without leaving the page. After a send the button counts down ("Resend in 42s") in tabular figures, and the end of that wait is kept in sessionStorage, so refreshing the page does not hand out a fresh minute. A send is confirmed by a polite status ("Email sent") and a failure is written under the buttons in words, without starting the wait. Change address turns the sentence into a field; the new address gets its own email and its own wait. When `verified` turns true the banner swaps to a short "Email verified" and folds away by itself. The countdown is worked out from timestamps and is spoken only when it starts and ends, so a screen reader is not told the time every second.

props.name: email
props.doc: The address that needs verifying. It is shown in bold, and "Change address" turns it into a field.

props.name: reason
props.doc: What verifying unlocks, as the end of the sentence: "to start sending invites". It follows the address. Leave it out for the bare "Verify jane@acme.com".

props.name: verified
props.doc: Set it to true when your app knows the address is confirmed (it polls, or the link was opened in another tab). The banner swaps to a short "Email verified" confirmation and then folds away. If it is true on first render, nothing is drawn.

props.name: onResend
props.doc: Sends the verification email again. Return the promise: the button waits for it, a rejection shows its message in words and does not start the wait.

props.name: onChangeEmail
props.doc: Turns the address into a field and, on submit, sends the verification email to the new address. Return an error message ("That address already has an account.") or nothing: once it resolves the banner shows the new address and the wait starts again. Leave it out and there is no Change address button.

props.name: cooldownSeconds
props.doc: Seconds before another email can be asked for, counted from a send. It is kept in sessionStorage, so a reload does not reset it. Default 60; 0 means no wait.

props.name: storageKey
props.doc: Where the end of the wait is kept in sessionStorage. Default one key for the page; give each banner its own if there are several.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the banner uses, for translation.

entries.docs: email is the address to verify and reason finishes the sentence ("to start sending invites"). onResend returns a promise: a rejection shows its message under the buttons and does not start the wait. After a send the button counts down for cooldownSeconds (60), worked out from timestamps and kept in sessionStorage under storageKey, so a reload does not reset it; the countdown is spoken at its start and its end only, while the button's own name is what it shows ("Resend in 28s"), so voice control can reach it. onChangeEmail(address) turns the address into a field: return an error message to show under it, or nothing, and the new address gets its own email and its own wait. When verified turns true the banner swaps to a short Email verified and folds away; if it is true on first render nothing is drawn. labels carries every word.

entries.name: agreement-scroll
entries.title: Agreement scroll
entries.description: Terms in a scrolling box with a read-progress line; the accept checkbox unlocks at the end, and keyboard users and short texts still work.

components.name: AgreementScroll
components.summary: A contract, licence or consent text in a bordered scrolling region, with a thin line along its top edge that fills as it is read (and keeps the furthest point reached, so scrolling back up never un-reads it) and the acceptance below it. The checkbox stays disabled until the reader reaches the end, with "Scroll to the end to accept" tied to it and replaced by "You can now accept" when it unlocks, announced politely. The region is focusable and named, so the arrow keys, Page Up and Down and End scroll it, and a "Jump to the end" button covers anyone who cannot scroll comfortably. A text that fits unlocks at once, and a ResizeObserver checks again when the width changes, so a rotated phone never strands the reader.

props.name: title
props.doc: The name of the document: "Terms of service". It names the scrolling region for a screen reader.

props.name: version
props.doc: The version of the text, shown beside the title: "3.2".

props.name: children
props.doc: The text to read. `h4`, `p`, `ol` and `ul` are styled for you.

props.name: requireScroll
props.doc: The reader must reach the end before the checkbox unlocks. A text that fits without scrolling unlocks at once. Default true.

props.name: accepted
props.doc: Whether the text is accepted, when you control the checkbox.

props.name: defaultAccepted
props.doc: Whether it is accepted to begin with, when the component keeps that itself.

props.name: onAcceptedChange
props.doc: Called when the checkbox is ticked or cleared.

props.name: acceptLabel
props.doc: The words next to the checkbox. Default "I have read and accept the {title}".

props.name: height
props.doc: The height of the scrolling region: a number of px or any CSS length. Default "16rem".

props.name: name
props.doc: The checkbox's name, for a plain form submit.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Turn the whole thing off.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the component says, for translation.

The checkbox stays disabled until the reader reaches the end of the scrolling region, or at once when the text fits; once reached it stays unlocked, and a text that is already accepted can always be un-accepted. Control it with accepted and onAcceptedChange, or defaultAccepted. requireScroll={false} offers the text without the lock and hides the hint, the percentage and the jump button. A ResizeObserver checks again when the width changes. height sets the region's height (default 16rem), acceptLabel the words by the checkbox, name submits it with a form, and labels translates the fixed words.

entries.name: answer-checklist
entries.title: Answer checklist
entries.description: A checklist where each item gets an answer, Pass, Fail or N/A, or Yes and No, with a note that opens on the answers that need explaining.

components.name: AnswerChecklist
components.summary: A list of statements that each get an answer, for inspections, audits, intake questionnaires and quality checks: Pass, Fail or Not applicable (or Yes and No, or any set you give) on the house segmented control. Every row is a radio group named by its statement, and shows where it stands in words as well as a mark: not answered, the answer, or the answer with a note still to write. Answers listed in `noteOn` open a note field under the row that is required until it has text. A header counts what is left ("7 of 12 answered, 1 note missing") in a polite live region, and a button moves focus to the first row that is still open, to its answer or to its empty note. On a phone the control wraps under the statement at full width.

props.name: items
props.doc: The statements to answer, in order.

props.name: options
props.doc: The answers a statement can get. Default Pass, Fail and Not applicable.

props.name: value
props.doc: The answers and notes so far, by statement id, when you control the checklist.

props.name: defaultValue
props.doc: The answers to begin with, when the checklist keeps them itself.

props.name: onValueChange
props.doc: Called with every answer and note whenever one changes.

props.name: noteOn
props.doc: The `value`s of the options that need a note. Choosing one opens a note field under the row, and the row stays open until it is filled. Default none.

props.name: labels
props.doc: The words the checklist says, for translation.

entries.docs: items are the statements (id, label, hint, notePlaceholder) and options the answers: value, label and an optional tone (pass, fail or skip) that sets the shape of the mark; the default is Pass, Fail and Not applicable. value maps a statement id to { answer, note }, and onValueChange receives the whole map. noteOn lists the answers that need a note: choosing one opens a required textarea under the row, and the row stays open, marked "Note required", until it has text; the note is kept if the answer changes.
